During GRPO generation, each newly decoded token sequence is projected into this spectral space. The policy network's output logits are then subjected to a 'Manifold Repulsion Gate'—a dynamic regularization term applied directly in the attention head that penalizes token generation if the intermediate spectral signature aligns too closely with the current anchor. This creates a continuous anti-correlation pressure that breaks zero-variance states in real-time without storing or re-evaluating full reference trajectories.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1. ZVF behavioral collapse is fundamentally observable in the high-frequency variance of intermediate layer activations (which the spectral projection captures), rather than just the final output tokens. 2. The sequential alignment between the streaming hash space and the policy's latent manifold is sufficiently linear to allow an efficient dot-product repulsion gate. 3. The additional floating-point operations required for the spectral projection impose a negligible latency overhead compared to standard transformer auto-regressive decoding.
ideas.expected_impact: This mechanism will entirely eliminate Zero-Variance Starvation in GRPO without the memory and compute overhead of loading a reference policy or retaining large trajectory batches. By maintaining a steady non-zero advantage variance during deep reinforcement fine-tuning, it will prevent mode collapse, accelerate convergence on reasoning tasks, and enable stable GRPO training on edge hardware with highly constrained VRAM.

ideas.topic: Adaptive Reward-Trajectory Entropy Regularization in Policy Gradient Methods
ideas.title: Cauchy-Schwarz Trajectory Entropy Bound for Mode-Collapse Prevention in On-Policy RL
ideas.problem_statement: Standard policy gradient methods employ maximum entropy regularization to encourage exploration. When the environment contains large, reward-neutral regions (e.g., wide corridors), maximizing marginal entropy leads to policy bifurcation and mode-collapse, where the agent randomly oscillates between disconnected high-return trajectories, destroying the continuity of the policy manifold and destabilizing value estimation.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose replacing the standard marginal Shannon entropy with a trajectory-level Cauchy-Schwarz (CS) entropy bound. The CS divergence naturally penalizes overlaps between distinct sampled trajectories. By maximizing the CS trajectory entropy bound, we formulate an objective that explicitly maximizes the pairwise 'distance' between entire state-action sequences in the trajectory space (pushing the policy to discover diverse high-return paths) while inherently minimizing intra-trajectory variance (ensuring each individual path is smooth, continuous, and deterministic). We implement this via a dual-critic architecture where an auxiliary network approximates the kernel distance between current batch trajectories and a replay bank of previous diverse modes.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1. Bifurcation and mode-collapse in wide state-spaces are primarily driven by the uniform-distribution bias of marginal Shannon entropy. 2. The trajectory-level kernel distance can be accurately approximated using a bounded context window (e.g., the last $K$ states) without suffering from the curse of dimensionality. 3. The computational overhead of the pairwise kernel matrix calculation during the update phase is negligible compared to the cost of environment interaction.
ideas.expected_impact: This regularization will yield highly cohesive multi-modal policies capable of smoothly navigating vast, reward-sparse environments without the 'flickering' behavior characteristic of traditional maximum-entropy methods. It will fundamentally shift policy gradient exploration from state-marginal uniformity to trajectory-level distinctness, resulting in improved sample efficiency and stable convergence in complex continuous control tasks with multiple viable solutions.

ideas.title: Recurrent Sturm-Liouville Eigenfunctions for Continuous Spectral State Routing in Legendre Attention
ideas.problem_statement: Current spectral attention mechanisms rely on static, segment-wise orthogonal polynomial projections (like Legendre polynomials applied to fixed chunk sizes). When computing attention via spectral multiplication, the context window is strictly bounded by the dimensionality of the chosen polynomial basis $N$. Scaling to extremely long contexts (e.g., 100k+ tokens) requires an exponentially larger basis degree, severely degrading the $O(N^2)$ spectral routing complexity and resulting in a rigid, non-adaptive token-to-spectrum assignment that ignores the continuous nature of long-range semantic dependencies.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose formulating the routing mechanism as a time-varying Sturm-Liouville (S-L) eigenvalue problem directly within the attention recurrent state. Instead of projecting fixed token chunks onto a static Legendre basis, we treat the token stream as a continuous signal governed by an S-L differential operator. The network learns the spatially-varying 'weight' and 'diffusion' functions of this operator per attention head. As new tokens arrive, they update the continuous eigenfunctions via a recurrent Legendre-Galerkin step. Attention is then computed by routing queries through the instantaneous S-L eigenvalues (which act as a continuous, topologically-aware frequency bottleneck), dynamically scaling the context retrieval without discrete window truncation.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1) Long-range semantic dependencies in transformer representations can be accurately approximated by the smooth eigenfunctions of a learned differential operator. 2) The continuous S-L eigenstates can be discretized and updated recurrently in linear time $O(N)$ relative to the sequence length via an efficient Legendre-Galerkin approximation. 3) The gradient of the eigenvalues of the S-L operator with respect to the network weights can be effectively optimized via implicit differentiation without causing training instability.
ideas.expected_impact: This mechanism will enable theoretically infinite, dynamically bounded context windows for Transformer architectures. By replacing discrete, chunk-based spectral attention with a continuous eigenstate evolution, we achieve true sub-linear time complexity for attention retrieval during generation, entirely eliminating the need for context window segmentation while establishing a rigorous mathematical bridge between differential equation solvers and large language model architectures.

ideas.topic: Quantum-Inspired Givens Entropic Attention for Sparse KV Noise Elimination
ideas.title: Non-Commutative Itô Calculus for KV-Cache Noise Filtration via Quantum Givens Stochastic Flow
ideas.problem_statement: In autoregressive Large Language Models, the Key-Value (KV) cache suffers from extreme activation noise sparsity—often amplified in long contexts. While quantum-inspired Givens rotations can theoretically compress and filter attention matrices, they currently operate deterministically and fail to model the stochastic, non-commutative nature of attention noise propagation. The problem is that without a mathematical framework to model the cumulative, noisy perturbation of keys and values over time, deterministic Givens entropic attention either over-compresses vital context or fails to eliminate dynamic noise, leading to degraded long-context reasoning.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose modeling the sequential application of Givens rotation matrices ($G_i$) over the KV cache as a Non-Commutative Quantum Itô Stochastic Differential Equation (SDE). By treating the KV cache as a quantum state vector subject to entropic drift and stochastic noise diffusion, the Givens rotations are optimized not just as static orthogonal projectors, but as continuous-time unitary operators. The model derives a modified Itô isometry for the attention head, where the entropic noise elimination boundary is mathematically defined by the commutator $[G_t, dW_t]$, allowing the network to dynamically filter sparse KV noise via the predictable quadratic variation of the attention trajectory.
key_assumptions: The sparse noise present in the KV cache is accurately modeled as a Brownian motion (Wiener process) operating within a complex Hilbert space.
The deterministic baseline of the attention mechanism can be abstracted as the drift component of a quantum SDE.
The baseline Givens rotation matrices can be successfully parameterized as time-ordered unitary operators (analogous to a product formula in stochastic quantum mechanics).
The attention head can be efficiently trained to approximate the predictable quadratic variation of this stochastic process using standard backpropagation through a stochastic computational graph.
ideas.expected_impact: This research will establish a rigorous stochastic-geometric foundation for quantum-inspired attention mechanisms. By allowing the Givens entropic attention to adapt to the statistical variance of KV noise dynamically, it is expected to significantly improve perplexity and retrieval accuracy in infinite-context or heavily quantized settings. Furthermore, defining the noise elimination boundary via Itô calculus will provide a mathematically guaranteed mechanism for preventing the 'over-pruning' of critical context tokens, effectively solving the fidelity-loss bottleneck in extreme KV cache compression.

ideas.topic: Differentiable Memory Manifolds for Dynamic Phase-Space KV-Cache Compression
ideas.title: Symplectic Hamiltonian KV-Cache Compression via Action-Angle Coordinate Transformations
ideas.problem_statement: Standard KV-cache compression methods typically rely on Euclidean norms or static importance scoring (e.g., attention weight magnitude), which fail to dynamically track the evolving energy distribution of long-range token dependencies. In autoregressive generation, these dependencies follow complex, oscillatory trajectories in phase-space. Current compression techniques perturb these trajectories, resulting in non-recoverable catastrophic forgetting of long-term context and structural instabilities in the attention distribution over long generation horizons.
ideas.core_mechanism: We formulate the KV-cache as a classical Hamiltonian dynamical system living on a symplectic manifold. Token representations are mapped into canonical coordinates: 'position' (semantic key states) and 'momentum' (temporal value derivatives). By performing an action-angle coordinate transformation, the oscillatory dynamics of highly attended token pairs are converted into invariant 'action' variables (representing conserved global context energy) and cyclic 'angle' variables. KV-cache compression is then executed as a canonical transformation (specifically, a controlled energy truncation) that selectively discards tokens with negligible action magnitudes. Because symplectic integration exactly preserves the geometric phase-space volume and the system's Hamiltonian invariants, the compression is structurally reversible and non-destructive to the long-term global context topology.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1. The evolution of hidden states in deep autoregressive Transformers can be accurately approximated by Hamiltonian dynamics under residual connections. 2. The global context distribution (the Hamiltonian) evolves continuously across generation steps without severe, abrupt discontinuities, allowing for continuous action-angle transformations. 3. The computational overhead of implicit symplectic integration is mitigated by the drastic reduction in sequence length during subsequent attention operations.
ideas.expected_impact: This approach will establish a novel physics-informed paradigm for memory compression that theoretically guarantees the preservation of global contextual energy. Empirically, it is expected to extend the effective generation length of LLMs by up to 4x at an equivalent KV-cache budget, while significantly reducing the hallucination rate typically caused by conventional destructive cache pruning methods.

ideas.topic: Sub-Linear Randomized SVD State-Space Routing in Transformer Decoding
ideas.title: Sketched Frobenius-Norm Error Bounds for Stochastic Sub-Linear SVD Transformer Routing
ideas.problem_statement: Sub-linear randomized SVD state-space routing requires dynamic low-rank approximation of attention matrices for efficient token routing. However, standard random projections fail to provide rigorous, real-time error bounds on the routing decision matrix, leading to sub-optimal or highly volatile state transitions during generation.
ideas.core_mechanism: We introduce a stochastic error-bound oracle that maps the residual of the randomized sketch (difference between sketched and true attention matrices) to a tight probabilistic Frobenius-norm bound using a Johnson-Lindenstrauss (JL) projection. This bound is evaluated using a finite-sample concentration inequality to provide a confidence interval on the current sub-linear routing decision, allowing the system to dynamically adjust the sketch size or fall back to deterministic attention if the error bound exceeds a theoretical threshold.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1) The attention matrix rows exhibit a sufficiently rapid spectral decay such that a low-rank random projection captures a significant portion of the variance. 2) The JL-transform can be applied to attention residuals during the decoding phase with negligible latency overhead compared to the full attention mechanism.
ideas.expected_impact: This framework will yield the first rigorous, real-time statistical guarantees for sub-linear SVD transformer routing, eliminating routing volatility and providing a mathematically grounded mechanism for adaptively trading off computational efficiency (sketch size) with generation fidelity in large language models.

ideas.topic: Curvature-Aware Gradient Routing for Ill-Conditioned LLM Fine-Tuning
ideas.title: Riemannian Leapfrog Hessian-Vector Products for Curvature-Aligned Momentum in LLM Fine-Tuning
ideas.problem_statement: Standard optimizers like AdamW approximate curvature using diagonal second-moment estimates, completely ignoring the off-diagonal Hessian structure. This forces the optimizer to rely on heavy-tuned learning rates and momentum coefficients to navigate ill-conditioned loss landscapes, often resulting in catastrophic forgetting or training instability during LLM fine-tuning. Capturing exact curvature requires O(N^3) matrix inversions, which is computationally intractable for multi-billion parameter models. The problem is to dynamically guide gradient updates using local curvature *without* explicit Hessian inversion, enabling stable traversal of narrow, steep ravines in the loss landscape.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose Curvature-Aligned Momentum (CAM), an optimizer that leverages implicit Hessian-Vector Products (HVPs) via the Pearlmutter trick to route standard gradients along a Riemannian manifold defined by the local loss geometry. Rather than computing the Hessian inverse, CAM runs a fixed, low-cost number of Lanczos iterations ($k \approx 5$) on the HVP operator to approximate the top-$k$ eigenvectors of the Hessian. The first-moment gradient is then orthogonally projected onto the span of these top-$k$ eigenvectors. To specifically escape sharp local minima and navigate ill-conditioned ravines, the momentum vector is dynamically routed through a Riemannian Leapfrog integrator, adjusting the parameter trajectory step size proportionally to the local principal curvatures (the eigenvalues). This effectively 'warps' the optimization path, elongating steps in directions of low curvature and shortening them in directions of high curvature.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1. The local loss geometry of LLMs during fine-tuning is sufficiently smooth such that the top-$k$ Hessian eigenvectors accurately capture the principal directions of curvature for a given mini-batch. 2. The Pearlmutter HVP can be computed in $O(N)$ time with a minor constant overhead relative to the standard backpropagation pass. 3. The cost of running $k$ Lanczos iterations per step is vastly outweighed by the forward/backward pass of a multi-billion parameter LLM. 4. The top-$k$ principal curvature directions change slowly enough (continuous batch-to-batch geometry) that routing gradients along them does not introduce high-frequency trajectory oscillations.

ideas.topic: Content-Addressed Cryptographic Provenance Verification in Multi-Agent Pipelines
ideas.title: Cayley-Menger Determinantal Codification for Incidence-Algebraic Provenance in Multi-Agent Directed Acyclic Graphs
ideas.problem_statement: In complex multi-agent LLM pipelines, verifying content-addressed provenance requires cryptographic attestation of how discrete token manifolds mutate from one agent to the next. Current approaches either rely on localized, vulnerable cryptographic hashes of local KV-caches—which fail to capture the combinatorial geometry of token-level transformations across agent boundaries—or require expensive zero-knowledge proofs of the entire inference execution. ideas.core_mechanism: We propose embedding the input and output token manifolds of each agent into a high-dimensional metric space. We compute the Cayley-Menger determinant of these $n$-point configurations to generate a volume-based topological invariant (the hypervolume of the token simplicial complex). This geometric invariant is then algebraically hashed using the incidence algebra of the pipeline's Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). The Möbius function of the DAG acts as an invertible operator over the sequence of Cayley-Menger invariants. By taking the inverse zeta transform of the operator, we derive an exact, content-addressed cryptographic fingerprint of the structural transformations. If an intermediate agent in the pipeline alters the semantic core of the text while syntactically masquerading as the original, the discrete hypervolume shifts, irrevocably breaking the Möbius inversion constraint.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1) The latent representations of semantically distinct texts form measurably different volumetric simplicial complexes in high-dimensional embedding space. 2) The Cayley-Menger determinant can be adapted to efficiently scale with the context window size ($N$ tokens) via localized sliding-window volumetric hashing. 3) The topological constraints imposed by the DAG's incidence algebra are sufficiently rigid to prevent second-preimage attacks on the generated invariant.
ideas.expected_impact: This framework introduces an entirely new paradigm for LLM provenance: 'Geometric Cryptography'. It will enable multi-agent pipelines to execute sub-linear time provenance checks without relying on trusted execution environments or full-model zero-knowledge proofs. By proving the exact lineage of semantic transformations via algebraic topology, it resolves the multi-agent 'black-box' attribution problem, paving the way for fully decentralized, trustless autonomous agent networks.

ideas.topic: Consensus-Driven Adversarial Feedback Loops for Automated Code Synthesis
ideas.title: Chevalley-Eilenberg Coboundary Operators for Detecting Non-Transitive Code Execution Consensus
ideas.problem_statement: Consensus-driven adversarial feedback loops in multi-agent code synthesis generally evaluate local, pairwise state transitions using Markovian metrics (e.g., exact match or embedding cosine similarity). This fails to capture non-transitive, cyclical execution contradictions, such as Agent A's code beating Agent B on edge cases, B beating C, but C breaking A due to deep semantic logical loops. Current consensus mechanisms lack the topological resolution to detect these global, multi-agent execution paradoxes, leading to degenerate equilibria in the adversarial training loop.
ideas.core_mechanism: We model the multi-agent code synthesis state space as a Lie algebra, representing adversarial mutations as continuous vector fields over this manifold. We construct a Chevalley-Eilenberg (CE) cochain complex where code states are 0-cochains and pairwise adversarial execution transitions are 1-cochains. The CE coboundary operator ($d^1: C^1 \to C^2$) maps pairwise transitions into 2-cochains on the triangular simplex formed by any three agents. If $d^1$ applied to the pairwise reward differentials yields a non-zero evaluation (a non-trivial 2-cocycle), it algebraically proves a topological obstruction—a non-transitive execution loop. This acts as a structural regularizer: the adversarial feedback loop penalizes policies that generate non-zero $d^1$ evaluations, mathematically forcing the code synthesis consensus toward a homologically trivial, globally stable state.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1) The execution state space of generated code can be smoothly approximated as a differentiable manifold where adversarial gradients act as tangent vector fields forming a Lie algebra. 2) The Chevalley-Eilenberg coboundary operator can be discretely approximated over the simplicial complex formed by the interactions of $N$ code-generating agents. 3) The penalty signal derived from the non-zero 2-cocycles effectively translates into a usable gradient for policy optimization in the underlying RLHF/GRPO framework.

ideas.topic: Dynamic Role Delegation and Tool-Locking Invariants in Multi-Agent Systems

ideas.problem_statement: In multi-agent LLM systems, dynamic role delegation causes non-linear state transitions that frequently violate mutual exclusion properties over external tools (e.g., concurrent database write access), leading to silent data corruption. ideas.core_mechanism: We model the multi-agent system state as a dynamically evolving simplicial complex where $0$-simplexes are agents, $1$-simplexes are delegation boundaries, and $2$-simplexes represent concurrent tool-access requests. We propose the Right-Derived Functor Toolkit ($RT^i$) to systematically discover tool-locking invariants. The mechanism computes the homology groups $H_1(C_ ullet)$ of this contention complex. Any non-trivial generator in the nullspace of $H_1$ (an undetected circular wait-state or 'hole' in the delegation topology) mathematically represents an invariant violation (e.g., a deadlocked or racing tool state). When an agent delegates a role requiring a tool lock, the system dynamically checks if the chain map induced by the delegation results in a non-zero right-derived functor $R^1F$ acting on the tool-access subcomplex. If detected, the lock request is structurally denied, enforcing algebraic mutual exclusion over fluid roles.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1. Agent interactions, tool requests, and role delegations can be strictly discretized and embedded into an abstract simplicial complex ($C_ ullet$) within the execution latency budget. 2. The combinatorial blow-up of computing persistent homology $H_1$ over the dynamic contention complex can be mitigated using sparse boundary matrix reduction algorithms in polynomial time. 3. Concurrency violations (such as circular waits or race conditions) manifest identically as topological cycles that are bound by the nullspace of the boundary operator $\partial_1$.

ideas.topic: Asynchronous Task DAG Orchestration with Fail-Closed Failover Guarantees
ideas.title: Itô Drift-Diffusion Lineage Semilattices for Topology-Aware Fail-Closed DAG Orchestration
ideas.problem_statement: Asynchronous DAG orchestrators currently rely on discrete, topological cycle detection (e.g., dependency graphs) to enforce fail-closed semantics. However, these methods react only after topological violations occur and struggle to predict cascading, non-linear propagation of silent execution failures or timeouts across highly concurrent, heterogeneous execution environments. There is no robust mechanism to model the continuous spatio-temporal drift of failure probabilities across task boundaries to proactively isolate fault domains before systemic contamination occurs.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose modeling the asynchronous DAG execution space as a continuous semilattice manifold subjected to an Itô drift-diffusion process. Each node's state is mapped to coordinates on this manifold, where a theoretically derived drift vector encodes topological dependency gravity (pulling the state toward a fail-closed subspace) and a stochastic diffusion tensor encodes asynchronous execution variance. By calculating the stochastic integral of a task's execution path over the semilattice boundaries, we derive an analytical exit-time probability. If the expected exit-time from the fail-closed safe boundary falls below a dynamically calculated Itô isometry bound, the orchestrator deterministically snaps the entire dependent subgraph into a halted, fail-closed state, pre-empting cascading contamination.
ideas.key_assumptions: The statistical variance of asynchronous task execution times and silent failure rates can be continuously approximated by Brownian motion-derived diffusion tensors. Furthermore, we assume that topological dependencies in the DAG can be strictly ordered and embedded into a meet-semilattice coordinate space without losing the causal integrity of concurrent forks. Finally, we assume the computational cost of evaluating the stochastic exit-time integral is sufficiently low to be performed as a synchronous micro-checkpoint between node executions.
ideas.expected_impact: This framework transforms fail-closed guarantees from a reactive graph-traversal problem into a predictive, continuous stochastic-control problem. It will enable orchestrators to mathematically guarantee isolation under highly chaotic, heterogeneous execution loads, entirely eliminating cascading partial failures and 'zombie' task states in distributed systems. This provides a rigorous mathematical bedrock for safety-critical asynchronous workflows, such as automated financial trading pipelines and distributed ML hyperparameter search.

ideas.topic: Multi-Agent Quality-Diversity Archive Search for Automated Scientific Discovery
ideas.title: Persistent Čech Coboundary Gradients for Topological Conflict Resolution in Multi-Agent Quality-Diversity Archives
ideas.problem_statement: In Multi-Agent Quality-Diversity Archive (MA-QDA) search, autonomous agents explore high-dimensional scientific hypothesis spaces. Because the archives rely on behavioral descriptors (e.g., structural or mechanistic traits of hypotheses), multiple agents frequently converge on adjacent cells, forming dense, overlapping clusters in the descriptor space. ideas.core_mechanism: We introduce a mechanism that mathematically formalizes archive conflicts using Čech cohomology. We model the explored scientific hypotheses of each agent as a topological space (a point cloud) which dynamically forms a Čech complex as the archive expands. When the topological supports of two or more agents overlap, they generate a non-trivial 1-cocycle. We compute the topological gradient of this cocycle using a discrete coboundary operator ($\delta$). By applying a custom backpropagation rule through the simplicial complex, we inject this topological gradient as a repulsive force into the agents' local policy gradients. This forces the interacting agents' search trajectories orthogonally away from the shared boundary (i.e., across the $H_1$ homology class), actively driving them into topologically distinct voids (holes) in the archive to discover maximally distinct scientific paradigms.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1) The behavioral descriptor space of scientific hypotheses can be effectively mapped into a metric space where a nerve theorem accurately captures intersection topology. 2) The discrete coboundary operator yields a gradient signal with sufficient directional information to reliably guide continuous policy optimization without causing catastrophic divergence. 3) The computational overhead of dynamically calculating persistent Čech complexes is tractable for the relatively sparse, high-dimensional descriptor spaces typical in automated scientific discovery.
ideas.expected_impact: This framework will fundamentally transform MA-QDA from a parallel random search into a geometrically coordinated topological exploration. By providing a mathematically rigorous penalty for overlapping scientific hypothesis spaces, it eliminates redundant exploration and actively steers agents toward unexplored mechanistic paradigms. We expect a significant increase in the global entropy of the final archive and a marked reduction in the time required to synthesize highly diverse, novel scientific theories, pushing the boundaries of automated scientific discovery.

ideas.topic: Causal Sub-space Disentanglement via Orthogonal Polynomial Projections
ideas.title: Jacobi-Theta Spectral Sieving: Orthogonal Polynomial Projections for Causal-Invariant Subspace Disentanglement under Non-Stationary Interventions
ideas.problem_statement: Standard causal disentanglement methods assume that the generative factors and their causal graph are stationary, and they typically rely on point-estimate encoders that cannot separate spurious correlations from genuine causal mechanisms when observational data is generated under non-stationary intervention distributions. When multiple interventional environments induce smoothly varying spectral densities over the latent space (e.g., gradual domain shift or soft-policy interventions), existing variational or contrastive objectives entangle the causal content with the environment-specific spectral signatures, leading to representations that fail under compositionally novel interventions.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose decomposing the latent representation space into orthogonal causal subspaces via a continuous family of Jacobi orthogonal polynomial projections. Specifically, given an encoder $\phi$ producing latents $z \in \mathbb{R}^d$, we define a spectral integral operator $\mathcal{K}$ whose kernel is constructed from the weight function $w(x) = (1-x)^{\alpha}(1+x)^{\beta}$ of the Jacobi polynomials $P_n^{(\alpha,\beta)}(x)$. The latent $z$ is projected onto the function space $L^2_w([-1,1])$ via the expansion $\hat{z}(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{N} c_n[z] \cdot P_n^{(\alpha,\beta)}(x)$, where the coefficients $c_n[z]$ are learned projection functionals. We then impose a Jacobi-Theta regularizer $\Theta_{\alpha,\beta} = \sum_{n \neq m} \langle c_n, c_m \rangle^2 / (|n - m|^s)$, which penalizes cross-spectral coupling between polynomial modes. We prove that if the interventional distributions induce shifts that are smooth with respect to the Jacobi weight parameters $(\alpha, \beta)$, then the subspace spanned by the first $k$ polynomial projections $\text{span}\{c_0, \ldots, c_{k-1}\}$ is causally invariant—i.e., the interventional conditional $P(Y | \text{do}(X=x))$ depends only on the projection of $\phi(x)$ onto this low-degree polynomial subspace, while environment-specific confounders are absorbed into higher-degree modes. We enforce this separation through a Sobolev-type adversarial loss that trains a discriminator to predict the intervention environment from high-degree coefficients $\{c_k, \ldots, c_N\}$ while being adversarially fooled on the low-degree causal subspace.
key_assumptions: The true causal generative factors induce spectral representations whose power spectral density is concentrated in low-degree orthogonal polynomial modes, while spurious confounders contribute to higher-degree modes.

Interventional shifts across environments correspond to smooth perturbations in the Jacobi weight parameters $(\alpha, \beta)$, which is valid when the interventions modify conditional distributions via temperature-like or concentration-like reweighting rather than hard structural breaks.
The dimensionality $N$ of the polynomial expansion is sufficient to capture the spectral support of both causal and confounding factors without catastrophic truncation.
The adversarial Sobolev discriminator can reliably identify and isolate environment-specific spectral signatures from the high-degree polynomial coefficients.

ideas.problem_statement: Standard Group Relative Advantage Estimation (GRAE) treats all sample trajectories as residing in a flat Euclidean space, computing pairwise advantages without acknowledging latent hierarchical or taxonomic relationships between behaviors. This forces the optimizer to penalize semantically similar but syntactically distinct successful trajectories as high-variance outliers. By modeling policy behaviors as a continuously expanding tree, the variational baseline is computed as the weighted Fréchet mean of the group in hyperbolic space, rather than the arithmetic mean in parameter/action space. Relative advantages are then computed using the hyperbolic distance metric (which naturally discounts the distance between points near the root and exponentially penalizes divergence near the boundary). This curvature dynamically expands the optimization gradient to explicitly preserve hierarchical taxonomic diversity, structurally anchoring the variational baseline to the semantic behavior tree.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1) The underlying optimal policy structure for complex tasks exhibits a learnable, tree-like hierarchical topology; 2) Standard policy networks can be successfully projected into and optimized over a Riemannian manifold (specifically, a hyperbolic space with constant negative curvature) without severe vanishing gradients; 3) The computational overhead of calculating Fréchet means and hyperbolic distances during the GRPO update is tractable and offset by a significant reduction in required overall sample complexity.
ideas.expected_impact: This framework will transform GRPO from a purely statistical variance-reduction technique into a topologically aware optimizer. It will entirely prevent mode collapse in environments with deep behavioral hierarchies (e.g., robotic tool-use, multi-step logical reasoning), discover naturally branching sub-policies without requiring hard-coded hierarchical reinforcement learning architectures, and establish the first mathematical bridge between Riemannian geometry and group-relative advantage estimation.

Rather than computing the Hessian inverse, CAM runs a fixed, low-cost number of Lanczos iterations ($k \approx 5$) on the HVP operator to approximate the top-$k$ eigenvectors of the Hessian. The first-moment gradient is then orthogonally projected onto the span of these top-$k$ eigenvectors. To specifically escape sharp local minima and navigate ill-conditioned ravines, the momentum vector is dynamically routed through a Riemannian Leapfrog integrator, adjusting the parameter trajectory step size proportionally to the local principal curvatures (the eigenvalues). This effectively 'warps' the optimization path, elongating steps in directions of low curvature and shortening them in directions of high curvature.

By treating the KV cache as a quantum state vector subject to entropic drift and stochastic noise diffusion, the Givens rotations are optimized not just as static orthogonal projectors, but as continuous-time unitary operators. The model derives a modified Itô isometry for the attention head, where the entropic noise elimination boundary is mathematically defined by the commutator $[G_t, dW_t]$, allowing the network to dynamically filter sparse KV noise via the predictable quadratic variation of the attention trajectory.

The baseline Givens rotation matrices can be successfully parameterized as time-ordered unitary operators (analogous to a product formula in stochastic quantum mechanics).
The attention head can be efficiently trained to approximate the predictable quadratic variation of this stochastic process using standard backpropagation through a stochastic computational graph.

ideas.topic: Curvature-Aware Gradient Routing for Ill-Conditioned LLM Fine-Tuning

ideas.problem_statement: Standard optimizers like AdamW approximate curvature using diagonal second-moment estimates, completely ignoring the off-diagonal Hessian structure. This forces the optimizer to rely on heavy-tuned learning rates and momentum coefficients to navigate ill-conditioned loss landscapes, often resulting in catastrophic forgetting or training instability during LLM fine-tuning. Capturing exact curvature requires O(N^3) matrix inversions, which is computationally intractable for multi-billion parameter models. The problem is to dynamically guide gradient updates using local curvature *without* explicit Hessian inversion, enabling stable traversal of narrow, steep ravines in the loss landscape.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose Curvature-Aligned Momentum (CAM), an optimizer that leverages implicit Hessian-Vector Products (HVPs) via the Pearlmutter trick to route standard gradients along a Riemannian manifold defined by the local loss geometry. Rather than computing the Hessian inverse, CAM runs a fixed, low-cost number of Lanczos iterations ($k \approx 5$) on the HVP operator to approximate the top-$k$ eigenvectors of the Hessian. The first-moment gradient is then orthogonally projected onto the span of these top-$k$ eigenvectors. To specifically escape sharp local minima and navigate ill-conditioned ravines, the momentum vector is dynamically routed through a Riemannian Leapfrog integrator, adjusting the parameter trajectory step size proportionally to the local principal curvatures (the eigenvalues). This effectively 'warps' the optimization path, elongating steps in directions of low curvature and shortening them in directions of high curvature.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1. The local loss geometry of LLMs during fine-tuning is sufficiently smooth such that the top-$k$ Hessian eigenvectors accurately capture the principal directions of curvature for a given mini-batch. 2. The Pearlmutter HVP can be computed in $O(N)$ time with a minor constant overhead relative to the standard backpropagation pass. 3. The cost of running $k$ Lanczos iterations per step is vastly outweighed by the forward/backward pass of a multi-billion parameter LLM. 4. The top-$k$ principal curvature directions change slowly enough (continuous batch-to-batch geometry) that routing gradients along them does not introduce high-frequency trajectory oscillations.

ideas.topic: Kullback-Leibler Divergence Constrained Policy Search in Non-Stationary Environments
ideas.title: Bregman-Duality Symplectic Integration of Information-Geometric Drift for KL-Constrained Policy Tracking under Hölder Transition Shifts
ideas.problem_statement: Existing KL-constrained policy search methods (e.g., TRPO, its variants) fail catastrophically in non-stationary environments. They implicitly assume a static environmental MDP, causing the learned policy to collapse into local optima when the transition dynamics drift. The core issue is that standard Trust Region Policy Optimization evaluates the KL divergence between the current and old policies using a static Euclidean geometry, treating the policy distribution as a fixed point in state-space rather than a dynamically evolving entity coupled to environmental shifts. There is no mechanism to organically align the policy's KL-constrained update step with the underlying Hölder-continuous drift of the environment's transition kernel.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose modeling the policy search trajectory not as discrete gradient steps, but as a continuous symplectic Hamiltonian flow over the Fisher-Rao Information Metric manifold. The algorithm, Hölder-Aware Symplectic Policy Flow (HASPF), reparameterizes the standard KL constraint as a Hamiltonian energy function. To handle non-stationarity, we introduce a Bregman divergence-based dual estimator that dynamically estimates the Hölder continuity exponent ($\alpha \in (0,1)$) of the transition kernel's shift between timesteps. This estimated $\alpha$ acts as a symplectic integrator time-scaling factor $h \propto \alpha^{-1}$, which continuously warps the local Fisher metric. When the environment shifts abruptly ($\alpha \to 0$), the symplectic integration step expands the Riemannian volume element, explicitly enlarging the KL trust region to allow rapid policy adaptation. Conversely, during stable periods ($\alpha \to 1$), the integration step contracts, mathematically enforcing tighter KL constraints to guarantee stable monotonic improvement.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1. The non-stationary shifts in the environment's transition kernel $P(s'|s,a)$ are locally Hölder continuous in time, meaning the degree of environmental drift exhibits measurable, estimable bounds over finite horizons. 2. The underlying dynamics of the policy network parameters can be continuously approximated by a symplectic manifold, allowing reversible leapfrog integration without structural dissipation of the information geometry. 3. A reliable auxiliary estimator network can implicitly infer the instantaneous Hölder exponent $\alpha$ from high-dimensional state representations without requiring explicit environmental reward signals.
ideas.expected_impact: HASPF will theoretically guarantee bounded regret even under adversarial non-stationary shifts by mathematically tying the adaptive KL trust region bound to the true intrinsic drift of the environment. Empirically, it is expected to eliminate the catastrophic forgetting and brittle collapse currently observed in TRPO-based algorithms operating in non-stationary MDPs, yielding significant sample efficiency improvements and yielding a robust, dynamically scaling policy search paradigm for real-world, drifting environments.

ideas.topic: Self-Refining Multi-Objective Evaluation for Complex Reasoning Tasks
ideas.title: Riesz s-Energy Equilibrium on Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces for Pareto-Optimal Self-Refinement of Reasoning Chains
ideas.problem_statement: Existing self-refining multi-objective evaluation methods treat objectives (e.g., factual accuracy, logical coherence, fluency) as independently weighted scalar rewards. This additive aggregation fails to capture non-linear objective trade-offs, leading to self-refinement trajectories that over-optimize easily distinguishable surrogate metrics while fundamentally degrading the complex structural reasoning capabilities. There is no mathematical guarantee that the self-refinement process converges to a Pareto-optimal frontier that properly balances multi-objective trade-offs without catastrophic forgetting of specific reasoning skills.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose mapping the LLM's reasoning state (represented by its Chain-of-Thought hidden representations) into a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS) structured as a Riesz s-energy equilibrium. Each active evaluation objective $i$ exerts a virtual repulsive force field defined by a kernel-induced potential $V_i(x) = \sum_{j \neq i} \frac{w_j}{d_\mathcal{H}(x_i, x_j)^s}$, where $s$ is an adaptively tuned repulsion exponent based on the current reward gradient entropy. The self-refinement generation step is formulated as seeking the variational minimizer of the total energy $E(x) = \sum_{i \neq j} \frac{1}{d_\mathcal{H}(x_i, x_j)^s}$. Instead of applying a linearized update to maximize scalar reward, the model samples the next reasoning token by projecting the locally estimated Pareto gradient onto the tangent space of this Riesz energy manifold. This forces the reasoning chain to dynamically distribute its semantic mass across the objective axes, mathematically guaranteeing a well-spaced exploration of the Pareto frontier via the equilibrium properties of the s-energy potential.

ideas.expected_impact: This framework will fundamentally shift multi-objective LLM evaluation from static scalar weighting to dynamic, geometry-aware equilibrium seeking. It is expected to eliminate the 'reward hacking' phenomenon where one metric dominates self-refinement, ensuring that generated reasoning chains strictly reside on the true Pareto frontier. This will result in significantly higher data efficiency for self-refining loops and improved structural integrity in complex reasoning tasks (e.g., mathematical or logical deduction) where objective trade-offs are highly non-linear.

ideas.problem_statement: Reward models (RMs) in RLHF are notoriously overconfident on out-of-distribution (OOD) prompts, leading to reward hacking. Existing uncertainty-weighted ensembles rely on scalar variance or heuristic disagreement metrics, which fail to distinguish epistemic uncertainty (lack of knowledge) from aleatoric ambiguity (inherent prompt subjectivity). We evaluate these trajectories using a statistical Mahalanobis-Wasserstein Depth (MWD) metric. The MWD continuously tracks the geometric trajectory of the ensemble's output distribution across decoder layers, quantifying the shape and divergence of the reward manifold. Deep MWD trajectories indicate concentrated, high-confidence agreement (aleatoric), while shallow trajectories indicate dispersed, OOD disagreement (epistemic). We then use a conformal prediction wrapper dynamically calibrated by the MWD volume to output a bounded credal set (a set of plausible reward intervals) rather than a point estimate. The RLHF policy gradient is constrained to strictly operate within the intersection of these conformal bounds, causing gradient masking to automatically zero out updates that violate the conformal guarantee.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1. The continuous reward signals provided by the ensemble members can be meaningfully L1-normalized and projected into a Dirichlet distribution over the probability simplex without breaking temporal coherence across transformer layers. 2. The Mahalanobis-Wasserstein depth of the ensemble's hidden-state trajectory provides a strictly more informative geometric signal for differentiating aleatoric vs. epistemic uncertainty than unidirectional output scalar variance. 3. The computational overhead of computing MWD and conformal bounds online is amortizable through asynchronous ensemble forward-passes and does not introduce training instabilities during PPO.
ideas.expected_impact: This research will fundamentally shift RM calibration from point-estimate variance minimization to geometric trajectory depth analysis. By guaranteeing distribution-free conformal coverage adapted to the ensemble's Wasserstein geometry, the policy will demonstrably eliminate catastrophic reward hacking on OOD prompts while maintaining fast convergence on well-defined alignment tasks, bridging the gap between statistical conformal prediction and practical LLM alignment.

ideas.problem_statement: In complex multi-agent LLM pipelines, verifying content-addressed provenance requires cryptographic attestation of how discrete token manifolds mutate from one agent to the next. Current approaches either rely on localized, vulnerable cryptographic hashes of local KV-caches—which fail to capture the combinatorial geometry of token-level transformations across agent boundaries—or require expensive zero-knowledge proofs of the entire inference execution. There is currently no mathematically rigorous mechanism to cryptographically bind the structural mutation of a text sequence to its exact lineage using the manifold geometry of the latent token space.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose embedding the input and output token manifolds of each agent into a high-dimensional metric space. We compute the Cayley-Menger determinant of these $n$-point configurations to generate a volume-based topological invariant (the hypervolume of the token simplicial complex). This geometric invariant is then algebraically hashed using the incidence algebra of the pipeline's Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). The Möbius function of the DAG acts as an invertible operator over the sequence of Cayley-Menger invariants. By taking the inverse zeta transform of the operator, we derive an exact, content-addressed cryptographic fingerprint of the structural transformations. If an intermediate agent in the pipeline alters the semantic core of the text while syntactically masquerading as the original, the discrete hypervolume shifts, irrevocably breaking the Möbius inversion constraint.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1) The latent representations of semantically distinct texts form measurably different volumetric simplicial complexes in high-dimensional embedding space. 2) The Cayley-Menger determinant can be adapted to efficiently scale with the context window size ($N$ tokens) via localized sliding-window volumetric hashing. 3) The topological constraints imposed by the DAG's incidence algebra are sufficiently rigid to prevent second-preimage attacks on the generated invariant.
ideas.expected_impact: This framework introduces an entirely new paradigm for LLM provenance: 'Geometric Cryptography'. It will enable multi-agent pipelines to execute sub-linear time provenance checks without relying on trusted execution environments or full-model zero-knowledge proofs. By proving the exact lineage of semantic transformations via algebraic topology, it resolves the multi-agent 'black-box' attribution problem, paving the way for fully decentralized, trustless autonomous agent networks.

ideas.topic: Consensus-Driven Adversarial Feedback Loops for Automated Code Synthesis
ideas.title: Chevalley-Eilenberg Coboundary Operators for Detecting Non-Transitive Code Execution Consensus
ideas.problem_statement: Consensus-driven adversarial feedback loops in multi-agent code synthesis generally evaluate local, pairwise state transitions using Markovian metrics (e.g., exact match or embedding cosine similarity). This fails to capture non-transitive, cyclical execution contradictions, such as Agent A's code beating Agent B on edge cases, B beating C, but C breaking A due to deep semantic logical loops. Current consensus mechanisms lack the topological resolution to detect these global, multi-agent execution paradoxes, leading to degenerate equilibria in the adversarial training loop.
ideas.core_mechanism: We model the multi-agent code synthesis state space as a Lie algebra, representing adversarial mutations as continuous vector fields over this manifold. We construct a Chevalley-Eilenberg (CE) cochain complex where code states are 0-cochains and pairwise adversarial execution transitions are 1-cochains. The CE coboundary operator ($d^1: C^1 \to C^2$) maps pairwise transitions into 2-cochains on the triangular simplex formed by any three agents. If $d^1$ applied to the pairwise reward differentials yields a non-zero evaluation (a non-trivial 2-cocycle), it algebraically proves a topological obstruction—a non-transitive execution loop. This acts as a structural regularizer: the adversarial feedback loop penalizes policies that generate non-zero $d^1$ evaluations, mathematically forcing the code synthesis consensus toward a homologically trivial, globally stable state.

ideas.problem_statement: Asynchronous DAG orchestrators currently rely on discrete, topological cycle detection (e.g., dependency graphs) to enforce fail-closed semantics. Each node's state is mapped to coordinates on this manifold, where a theoretically derived drift vector encodes topological dependency gravity (pulling the state toward a fail-closed subspace) and a stochastic diffusion tensor encodes asynchronous execution variance. By calculating the stochastic integral of a task's execution path over the semilattice boundaries, we derive an analytical exit-time probability. If the expected exit-time from the fail-closed safe boundary falls below a dynamically calculated Itô isometry bound, the orchestrator deterministically snaps the entire dependent subgraph into a halted, fail-closed state, pre-empting cascading contamination.

Furthermore, we assume that topological dependencies in the DAG can be strictly ordered and embedded into a meet-semilattice coordinate space without losing the causal integrity of concurrent forks. Finally, we assume the computational cost of evaluating the stochastic exit-time integral is sufficiently low to be performed as a synchronous micro-checkpoint between node executions.

ideas.problem_statement: In Multi-Agent Quality-Diversity Archive (MA-QDA) search, autonomous agents explore high-dimensional scientific hypothesis spaces. We model the explored scientific hypotheses of each agent as a topological space (a point cloud) which dynamically forms a Čech complex as the archive expands. When the topological supports of two or more agents overlap, they generate a non-trivial 1-cocycle. We compute the topological gradient of this cocycle using a discrete coboundary operator ($\delta$). By applying a custom backpropagation rule through the simplicial complex, we inject this topological gradient as a repulsive force into the agents' local policy gradients. This forces the interacting agents' search trajectories orthogonally away from the shared boundary (i.e., across the $H_1$ homology class), actively driving them into topologically distinct voids (holes) in the archive to discover maximally distinct scientific paradigms.

ideas.expected_impact: This framework will fundamentally transform MA-QDA from a parallel random search into a geometrically coordinated topological exploration. By providing a mathematically rigorous penalty for overlapping scientific hypothesis spaces, it eliminates redundant exploration and actively steers agents toward unexplored mechanistic paradigms. The steering intervention is formulated as the exponential map $\exp_p(v)$ of a computed bracket-corrected control vector $v$ at the activation point $p$. This non-linear, curvature-aware steering vector is injected into the residual stream, dynamically forcing the trajectory to follow the intrinsic geodesics of the non-collapsed reasoning space rather than an arbitrary linear interpolation that intersects degenerate policy regions.

ideas.topic: Causal Sub-space Disentanglement via Orthogonal Polynomial Projections
ideas.title: Jacobi-Theta Spectral Sieving: Orthogonal Polynomial Projections for Causal-Invariant Subspace Disentanglement under Non-Stationary Interventions
ideas.problem_statement: Standard causal disentanglement methods assume that the generative factors and their causal graph are stationary, and they typically rely on point-estimate encoders that cannot separate spurious correlations from genuine causal mechanisms when observational data is generated under non-stationary intervention distributions. When multiple interventional environments induce smoothly varying spectral densities over the latent space (e.g., gradual domain shift or soft-policy interventions), existing variational or contrastive objectives entangle the causal content with the environment-specific spectral signatures, leading to representations that fail under compositionally novel interventions.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose decomposing the latent representation space into orthogonal causal subspaces via a continuous family of Jacobi orthogonal polynomial projections. Specifically, given an encoder $\phi$ producing latents $z \in \mathbb{R}^d$, we define a spectral integral operator $\mathcal{K}$ whose kernel is constructed from the weight function $w(x) = (1-x)^{\alpha}(1+x)^{\beta}$ of the Jacobi polynomials $P_n^{(\alpha,\beta)}(x)$. The latent $z$ is projected onto the function space $L^2_w([-1,1])$ via the expansion $\hat{z}(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{N} c_n[z] \cdot P_n^{(\alpha,\beta)}(x)$, where the coefficients $c_n[z]$ are learned projection functionals. We then impose a Jacobi-Theta regularizer $\Theta_{\alpha,\beta} = \sum_{n \neq m} \langle c_n, c_m \rangle^2 / (|n - m|^s)$, which penalizes cross-spectral coupling between polynomial modes. We prove that if the interventional distributions induce shifts that are smooth with respect to the Jacobi weight parameters $(\alpha, \beta)$, then the subspace spanned by the first $k$ polynomial projections $\text{span}\{c_0, \ldots, c_{k-1}\}$ is causally invariant—i.e., the interventional conditional $P(Y | \text{do}(X=x))$ depends only on the projection of $\phi(x)$ onto this low-degree polynomial subspace, while environment-specific confounders are absorbed into higher-degree modes. We enforce this separation through a Sobolev-type adversarial loss that trains a discriminator to predict the intervention environment from high-degree coefficients $\{c_k, \ldots, c_N\}$ while being adversarially fooled on the low-degree causal subspace.
key_assumptions: The true causal generative factors induce spectral representations whose power spectral density is concentrated in low-degree orthogonal polynomial modes, while spurious confounders contribute to higher-degree modes.

Interventional shifts across environments correspond to smooth perturbations in the Jacobi weight parameters $(\alpha, \beta)$, which is valid when the interventions modify conditional distributions via temperature-like or concentration-like reweighting rather than hard structural breaks.
The dimensionality $N$ of the polynomial expansion is sufficient to capture the spectral support of both causal and confounding factors without catastrophic truncation.
The adversarial Sobolev discriminator can reliably identify and isolate environment-specific spectral signatures from the high-degree polynomial coefficients.
ideas.expected_impact: This approach provides the first rigorous connection between orthogonal polynomial spectral theory and causal invariance, offering a constructive (rather than purely constraint-based) method for identifying causally sufficient subspaces. By leveraging the three-parameter tunability $(\alpha, \beta, N)$ of Jacobi polynomials, practitioners can adaptively control the causal-confounding spectral boundary without retraining the encoder. We expect measurable improvements in out-of-distribution generalization on benchmarks with smooth intervention families (e.g., procedural environment generation), and we anticipate the Jacobi-Theta regularizer will yield interpretable spectral fingerprints of confounding, enabling post-hoc diagnostics of which latent modes are causally relevant versus environment-specific artifacts.

ideas.topic: Von Neumann Entropy Density Heatmaps for Sparse Attention Pruning

ideas.problem_statement: Existing attention head pruning methods rely on scalar saliency proxies (e.g., L1 norms, gradient magnitude, or marginal attention weight entropy) that fail to capture the structural interaction between a head's query-key correlation geometry and its information bottleneck capacity. Rather than computing von Neumann entropy S(ρ_i) = -Tr(ρ_i log ρ_i) in isolation, we embed all heads into the Bures-Wasserstein manifold of density operators and compute the geodesic distance D_BW(ρ_i, ρ_j) between every pair. This yields a Riemannian metric tensor field over the attention head population. The pruning objective then selects a maximal diversity subset of heads by solving a facility-location problem on this manifold: minimize total Bures-Wasserstein distance from pruned heads to their nearest surviving representative, subject to a constraint that the sum of surviving heads' von Neumann entropies exceeds a Chebyshev bound on the approximation error of the full attention output. Crucially, the Bures metric D_BW²(ρ_i, ρ_j) = Tr(ρ_i) + Tr(ρ_j) - 2·Tr((√ρ_i ρ_j √ρ_i)^{1/2}) preserves the positive-semidefinite structure of density operators that Euclidean or KL-based distances violate, enabling principled interpolation along the geodesic to reconstruct pruned heads' contributions as weighted Fréchet means of surviving heads.

ideas.expected_impact: This approach transforms attention pruning from a per-head scalar selection problem into a Riemannian submodular optimization on the quantum state manifold, yielding pruning sets that are maximally diverse in correlation geometry while provably preserving information capacity. We expect 15-25% greater FLOP reduction at iso-perplexity compared to entropy-thresholding baselines, plus a theoretical guarantee that the reconstructed attention output's total variation distance from the dense model is bounded by the Bures-Wasserstein covering radius of the surviving head subset.

The contrastive loss is formulated as the Frechet distance between the eigenvalue distributions of these Hankel matrices, allowing step alignment in $O(N \log N)$ time via Fast Fourier Transform convolutions, while remaining invariant to step permutations within logical sub-spaces.

When the environment shifts abruptly ($\alpha \to 0$), the symplectic integration step expands the Riemannian volume element, explicitly enlarging the KL trust region to allow rapid policy adaptation. Conversely, during stable periods ($\alpha \to 1$), the integration step contracts, mathematically enforcing tighter KL constraints to guarantee stable monotonic improvement.

Empirically, it is expected to eliminate the catastrophic forgetting and brittle collapse currently observed in TRPO-based algorithms operating in non-stationary MDPs, yielding significant sample efficiency improvements and yielding a robust, dynamically scaling policy search paradigm for real-world, drifting environments.

There is no mathematical guarantee that the self-refinement process converges to a Pareto-optimal frontier that properly balances multi-objective trade-offs without catastrophic forgetting of specific reasoning skills.

Each active evaluation objective $i$ exerts a virtual repulsive force field defined by a kernel-induced potential $V_i(x) = \sum_{j \neq i} \frac{w_j}{d_\mathcal{H}(x_i, x_j)^s}$, where $s$ is an adaptively tuned repulsion exponent based on the current reward gradient entropy. The self-refinement generation step is formulated as seeking the variational minimizer of the total energy $E(x) = \sum_{i \neq j} \frac{1}{d_\mathcal{H}(x_i, x_j)^s}$. Instead of applying a linearized update to maximize scalar reward, the model samples the next reasoning token by projecting the locally estimated Pareto gradient onto the tangent space of this Riesz energy manifold. This forces the reasoning chain to dynamically distribute its semantic mass across the objective axes, mathematically guaranteeing a well-spaced exploration of the Pareto frontier via the equilibrium properties of the s-energy potential.

ideas.expected_impact: This framework will fundamentally shift multi-objective LLM evaluation from static scalar weighting to dynamic, geometry-aware equilibrium seeking. It is expected to eliminate the 'reward hacking' phenomenon where one metric dominates self-refinement, ensuring that generated reasoning chains strictly reside on the true Pareto frontier. This will result in significantly higher data efficiency for self-refining loops and improved structural integrity in complex reasoning tasks (e.g., mathematical or logical deduction) where objective trade-offs are highly non-linear.

ideas.topic: Reward Model Calibration via Uncertainty-Weighted Ensemble Variance

Existing uncertainty-weighted ensembles rely on scalar variance or heuristic disagreement metrics, which fail to distinguish epistemic uncertainty (lack of knowledge) from aleatoric ambiguity (inherent prompt subjectivity). We evaluate these trajectories using a statistical Mahalanobis-Wasserstein Depth (MWD) metric. The MWD continuously tracks the geometric trajectory of the ensemble's output distribution across decoder layers, quantifying the shape and divergence of the reward manifold. Deep MWD trajectories indicate concentrated, high-confidence agreement (aleatoric), while shallow trajectories indicate dispersed, OOD disagreement (epistemic). We then use a conformal prediction wrapper dynamically calibrated by the MWD volume to output a bounded credal set (a set of plausible reward intervals) rather than a point estimate. The RLHF policy gradient is constrained to strictly operate within the intersection of these conformal bounds, causing gradient masking to automatically zero out updates that violate the conformal guarantee.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1. The continuous reward signals provided by the ensemble members can be meaningfully L1-normalized and projected into a Dirichlet distribution over the probability simplex without breaking temporal coherence across transformer layers. 2. The Mahalanobis-Wasserstein depth of the ensemble's hidden-state trajectory provides a strictly more informative geometric signal for differentiating aleatoric vs. epistemic uncertainty than unidirectional output scalar variance. 3. The computational overhead of computing MWD and conformal bounds online is amortizable through asynchronous ensemble forward-passes and does not introduce training instabilities during PPO.
ideas.expected_impact: This research will fundamentally shift RM calibration from point-estimate variance minimization to geometric trajectory depth analysis. ideas.problem_statement: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures suffer from representation collapse, where the router consistently over-utilizes a small fraction of experts for semantically similar inputs, causing capacity bottlenecks and leaving other experts under-trained. This network dynamically parameterizes the OT dual potentials $f(x)$ and $g(y)$ for tokens and experts respectively. The routing mechanism is computed as the exact c-transform of these dual potentials, yielding a transport plan that inherently satisfies marginal capacity constraints. We optimize the potentials by minimizing the $L^2$-norm of the marginal violation (the equilibrium gap), replacing standard auxiliary load-balancing losses entirely.

Constraining the gradient updates to minimize the equilibrium gap of the marginal constraints is strictly more efficient for load balancing than penalizing variance across expert dispatch frequencies.

We then use a conformal prediction wrapper dynamically calibrated by the MWD volume to output a bounded credal set (a set of plausible reward intervals) rather than a point estimate. This geometric invariant is then algebraically hashed using the incidence algebra of the pipeline's Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). The Möbius function of the DAG acts as an invertible operator over the sequence of Cayley-Menger invariants. By taking the inverse zeta transform of the operator, we derive an exact, content-addressed cryptographic fingerprint of the structural transformations. If an intermediate agent in the pipeline alters the semantic core of the text while syntactically masquerading as the original, the discrete hypervolume shifts, irrevocably breaking the Möbius inversion constraint.

ideas.problem_statement: Existing self-refining multi-objective evaluation methods treat objectives (e.g., factual accuracy, logical coherence, fluency) as independently weighted scalar rewards. This additive aggregation fails to capture non-linear objective trade-offs, leading to self-refinement trajectories that over-optimize easily distinguishable surrogate metrics while fundamentally degrading the complex structural reasoning capabilities. There is no mathematical guarantee that the self-refinement process converges to a Pareto-optimal frontier that properly balances multi-objective trade-offs without catastrophic forgetting of specific reasoning skills.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose mapping the LLM's reasoning state (represented by its Chain-of-Thought hidden representations) into a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS) structured as a Riesz s-energy equilibrium. Each active evaluation objective $i$ exerts a virtual repulsive force field defined by a kernel-induced potential $V_i(x) = \sum_{j \neq i} \frac{w_j}{d_\mathcal{H}(x_i, x_j)^s}$, where $s$ is an adaptively tuned repulsion exponent based on the current reward gradient entropy. The self-refinement generation step is formulated as seeking the variational minimizer of the total energy $E(x) = \sum_{i \neq j} \frac{1}{d_\mathcal{H}(x_i, x_j)^s}$. Instead of applying a linearized update to maximize scalar reward, the model samples the next reasoning token by projecting the locally estimated Pareto gradient onto the tangent space of this Riesz energy manifold. This forces the reasoning chain to dynamically distribute its semantic mass across the objective axes, mathematically guaranteeing a well-spaced exploration of the Pareto frontier via the equilibrium properties of the s-energy potential.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1) The complex reasoning capabilities of the model can be effectively embedded into an RKHS where semantic distances $d_\mathcal{H}$ accurately reflect functional differences in multi-objective outputs. 2) The gradient signals from independent evaluation models (or reward heads) can be locally approximated as conservative vector fields equivalent to virtual repulsive forces. 3) The computational overhead of approximating the pairwise Riesz potential online during decoding is tractable via random Fourier feature approximations of the RKHS kernel.
ideas.expected_impact: This framework will fundamentally shift multi-objective LLM evaluation from static scalar weighting to dynamic, geometry-aware equilibrium seeking. It is expected to eliminate the 'reward hacking' phenomenon where one metric dominates self-refinement, ensuring that generated reasoning chains strictly reside on the true Pareto frontier. This will result in significantly higher data efficiency for self-refining loops and improved structural integrity in complex reasoning tasks (e.g., mathematical or logical deduction) where objective trade-offs are highly non-linear.

ideas.topic: Reward Model Calibration via Uncertainty-Weighted Ensemble Variance
ideas.title: Conformal Dirichlet-Calibrated Credal Reward Ensembles via Mahalanobis-Wasserstein Depth Trajectories
ideas.problem_statement: Reward models (RMs) in RLHF are notoriously overconfident on out-of-distribution (OOD) prompts, leading to reward hacking. Existing uncertainty-weighted ensembles rely on scalar variance or heuristic disagreement metrics, which fail to distinguish epistemic uncertainty (lack of knowledge) from aleatoric ambiguity (inherent prompt subjectivity). Scalar variance collapses the multi-dimensional disagreement trajectory of the ensemble into a single noisy scalar, providing no geometric guarantees on coverage or calibration, ultimately resulting in the policy exploiting transient, spurious reward peaks.
ideas.core_mechanism: We introduce Conformal Dirichlet Calibration (CDC), which models the ensemble's continuous reward output trajectories not as independent scalars, but as a multivariate Dirichlet distribution mapped onto a probability simplex. We evaluate these trajectories using a statistical Mahalanobis-Wasserstein Depth (MWD) metric. The MWD continuously tracks the geometric trajectory of the ensemble's output distribution across decoder layers, quantifying the shape and divergence of the reward manifold. Deep MWD trajectories indicate concentrated, high-confidence agreement (aleatoric), while shallow trajectories indicate dispersed, OOD disagreement (epistemic). We then use a conformal prediction wrapper dynamically calibrated by the MWD volume to output a bounded credal set (a set of plausible reward intervals) rather than a point estimate. The RLHF policy gradient is constrained to strictly operate within the intersection of these conformal bounds, causing gradient masking to automatically zero out updates that violate the conformal guarantee.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1. The continuous reward signals provided by the ensemble members can be meaningfully L1-normalized and projected into a Dirichlet distribution over the probability simplex without breaking temporal coherence across transformer layers. 2. The Mahalanobis-Wasserstein depth of the ensemble's hidden-state trajectory provides a strictly more informative geometric signal for differentiating aleatoric vs. epistemic uncertainty than unidirectional output scalar variance. 3. The computational overhead of computing MWD and conformal bounds online is amortizable through asynchronous ensemble forward-passes and does not introduce training instabilities during PPO.
ideas.expected_impact: This research will fundamentally shift RM calibration from point-estimate variance minimization to geometric trajectory depth analysis. By guaranteeing distribution-free conformal coverage adapted to the ensemble's Wasserstein geometry, the policy will demonstrably eliminate catastrophic reward hacking on OOD prompts while maintaining fast convergence on well-defined alignment tasks, bridging the gap between statistical conformal prediction and practical LLM alignment.

ideas.topic: Entropy-Regularized Optimal Transport Routing in Sparse Mixture-of-Experts
ideas.title: Kantorovich Dual Network Pruning via Optimal Transport Discrepancy Equilibrium in Sparse MoE Gating
ideas.problem_statement: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures suffer from representation collapse, where the router consistently over-utilizes a small fraction of experts for semantically similar inputs, causing capacity bottlenecks and leaving other experts under-trained. Current routing solutions rely on auxiliary load-balancing losses or greedy top-$k$ token assignment, which fail to capture global distributional discrepancies between the token demand and the actual expert capacity supply.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose modeling the MoE routing objective as a regularized Optimal Transport (OT) problem between a continuous measure of token representations (demand) and a discrete measure of expert capacities (supply). Instead of standard entropy-regularized OT (e.g., Sinkhorn iterations) which adds a static temperature constant, we introduce a learnable, attention-driven Kantorovich Dual Network. This network dynamically parameterizes the OT dual potentials $f(x)$ and $g(y)$ for tokens and experts respectively. The routing mechanism is computed as the exact c-transform of these dual potentials, yielding a transport plan that inherently satisfies marginal capacity constraints. We optimize the potentials by minimizing the $L^2$-norm of the marginal violation (the equilibrium gap), replacing standard auxiliary load-balancing losses entirely.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1. The representations of input tokens in a sequence form a continuous probability measure that can be optimally transported to the discrete expert capacity manifold. 2. The dual potentials of the Kantorovich OT problem can be accurately parameterized by a lightweight, shared multi-layer perceptron rather than requiring iterative fixed-point algorithms like Sinkhorn. 3. Constraining the gradient updates to minimize the equilibrium gap of the marginal constraints is strictly more efficient for load balancing than penalizing variance across expert dispatch frequencies.
ideas.expected_impact: This mechanism will mathematically eliminate routing collapse and eliminate the need to tune load-balancing penalty hyperparameters, leading to strictly enforced expert capacity utilization. By leveraging dynamic dual potentials rather than static entropic regularization, the model will achieve lower transport cost (higher specialization efficiency), yielding lower perplexity and more robust generalization on downstream tasks without increasing inference latency.

Using a lightweight online controller, the system continuously interpolates the moduli set based on the real-time estimated information curvature of the incoming token. This dynamically scales the effective bit-width to a continuous floating value (e.g., exactly 3.7 bits for a specific token), effectively folding the token's state into an optimal continuous-integer hypersphere.

ideas.problem_statement: Zero-Variance Failure (ZVF) in GRPO occurs when an exploration policy collapses onto a single trajectory, causing the group advantage variance to drop to zero and ceasing gradient flow. During GRPO generation, each newly decoded token sequence is projected into this spectral space. The policy network's output logits are then subjected to a 'Manifold Repulsion Gate'—a dynamic regularization term applied directly in the attention head that penalizes token generation if the intermediate spectral signature aligns too closely with the current anchor. This creates a continuous anti-correlation pressure that breaks zero-variance states in real-time without storing or re-evaluating full reference trajectories.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1. ZVF behavioral collapse is fundamentally observable in the high-frequency variance of intermediate layer activations (which the spectral projection captures), rather than just the final output tokens. 2. The sequential alignment between the streaming hash space and the policy's latent manifold is sufficiently linear to allow an efficient dot-product repulsion gate. 3. The additional floating-point operations required for the spectral projection impose a negligible latency overhead compared to standard transformer auto-regressive decoding.
ideas.expected_impact: This mechanism will entirely eliminate Zero-Variance Starvation in GRPO without the memory and compute overhead of loading a reference policy or retaining large trajectory batches. ideas.topic: Adaptive Reward-Trajectory Entropy Regularization in Policy Gradient Methods
ideas.title: Cauchy-Schwarz Trajectory Entropy Bound for Mode-Collapse Prevention in On-Policy RL
ideas.problem_statement: Standard policy gradient methods employ maximum entropy regularization to encourage exploration. However, this objective optimizes the marginal state entropy, creating an 'exploration distribution' that is uniform across the state space. When the environment contains large, reward-neutral regions (e.g., wide corridors), maximizing marginal entropy leads to policy bifurcation and mode-collapse, where the agent randomly oscillates between disconnected high-return trajectories, destroying the continuity of the policy manifold and destabilizing value estimation.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose replacing the standard marginal Shannon entropy with a trajectory-level Cauchy-Schwarz (CS) entropy bound. The CS divergence naturally penalizes overlaps between distinct sampled trajectories. By maximizing the CS trajectory entropy bound, we formulate an objective that explicitly maximizes the pairwise 'distance' between entire state-action sequences in the trajectory space (pushing the policy to discover diverse high-return paths) while inherently minimizing intra-trajectory variance (ensuring each individual path is smooth, continuous, and deterministic). We implement this via a dual-critic architecture where an auxiliary network approximates the kernel distance between current batch trajectories and a replay bank of previous diverse modes.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1. Bifurcation and mode-collapse in wide state-spaces are primarily driven by the uniform-distribution bias of marginal Shannon entropy. 2. The trajectory-level kernel distance can be accurately approximated using a bounded context window (e.g., the last $K$ states) without suffering from the curse of dimensionality. 3. The computational overhead of the pairwise kernel matrix calculation during the update phase is negligible compared to the cost of environment interaction.
ideas.expected_impact: This regularization will yield highly cohesive multi-modal policies capable of smoothly navigating vast, reward-sparse environments without the 'flickering' behavior characteristic of traditional maximum-entropy methods. It will fundamentally shift policy gradient exploration from state-marginal uniformity to trajectory-level distinctness, resulting in improved sample efficiency and stable convergence in complex continuous control tasks with multiple viable solutions.
