ideas.problem_statement: Standard Group Relative Advantage Estimation (GRAE) treats all sample trajectories as residing in a flat Euclidean space, computing pairwise advantages without acknowledging latent hierarchical or taxonomic relationships between behaviors. By modeling policy behaviors as a continuously expanding tree, the variational baseline is computed as the weighted Fréchet mean of the group in hyperbolic space, rather than the arithmetic mean in parameter/action space. Relative advantages are then computed using the hyperbolic distance metric (which naturally discounts the distance between points near the root and exponentially penalizes divergence near the boundary). This curvature dynamically expands the optimization gradient to explicitly preserve hierarchical taxonomic diversity, structurally anchoring the variational baseline to the semantic behavior tree.

ideas.topic: Dynamic Token Pruning via Layer-Wise Information Density Truncation

ideas.problem_statement: Current spectral attention mechanisms rely on static, segment-wise orthogonal polynomial projections (like Legendre polynomials applied to fixed chunk sizes). When computing attention via spectral multiplication, the context window is strictly bounded by the dimensionality of the chosen polynomial basis $N$. Scaling to extremely long contexts (e.g., 100k+ tokens) requires an exponentially larger basis degree, severely degrading the $O(N^2)$ spectral routing complexity and resulting in a rigid, non-adaptive token-to-spectrum assignment that ignores the continuous nature of long-range semantic dependencies.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose formulating the routing mechanism as a time-varying Sturm-Liouville (S-L) eigenvalue problem directly within the attention recurrent state. Instead of projecting fixed token chunks onto a static Legendre basis, we treat the token stream as a continuous signal governed by an S-L differential operator. The network learns the spatially-varying 'weight' and 'diffusion' functions of this operator per attention head. As new tokens arrive, they update the continuous eigenfunctions via a recurrent Legendre-Galerkin step. Attention is then computed by routing queries through the instantaneous S-L eigenvalues (which act as a continuous, topologically-aware frequency bottleneck), dynamically scaling the context retrieval without discrete window truncation.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1) Long-range semantic dependencies in transformer representations can be accurately approximated by the smooth eigenfunctions of a learned differential operator. 2) The continuous S-L eigenstates can be discretized and updated recurrently in linear time $O(N)$ relative to the sequence length via an efficient Legendre-Galerkin approximation. 3) The gradient of the eigenvalues of the S-L operator with respect to the network weights can be effectively optimized via implicit differentiation without causing training instability.
ideas.expected_impact: This mechanism will enable theoretically infinite, dynamically bounded context windows for Transformer architectures. By replacing discrete, chunk-based spectral attention with a continuous eigenstate evolution, we achieve true sub-linear time complexity for attention retrieval during generation, entirely eliminating the need for context window segmentation while establishing a rigorous mathematical bridge between differential equation solvers and large language model architectures.

ideas.topic: Quantum-Inspired Givens Entropic Attention for Sparse KV Noise Elimination
ideas.title: Non-Commutative Itô Calculus for KV-Cache Noise Filtration via Quantum Givens Stochastic Flow
ideas.problem_statement: In autoregressive Large Language Models, the Key-Value (KV) cache suffers from extreme activation noise sparsity—often amplified in long contexts. While quantum-inspired Givens rotations can theoretically compress and filter attention matrices, they currently operate deterministically and fail to model the stochastic, non-commutative nature of attention noise propagation. The problem is that without a mathematical framework to model the cumulative, noisy perturbation of keys and values over time, deterministic Givens entropic attention either over-compresses vital context or fails to eliminate dynamic noise, leading to degraded long-context reasoning.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose modeling the sequential application of Givens rotation matrices ($G_i$) over the KV cache as a Non-Commutative Quantum Itô Stochastic Differential Equation (SDE). By treating the KV cache as a quantum state vector subject to entropic drift and stochastic noise diffusion, the Givens rotations are optimized not just as static orthogonal projectors, but as continuous-time unitary operators. The model derives a modified Itô isometry for the attention head, where the entropic noise elimination boundary is mathematically defined by the commutator $[G_t, dW_t]$, allowing the network to dynamically filter sparse KV noise via the predictable quadratic variation of the attention trajectory.
key_assumptions: The sparse noise present in the KV cache is accurately modeled as a Brownian motion (Wiener process) operating within a complex Hilbert space.
The deterministic baseline of the attention mechanism can be abstracted as the drift component of a quantum SDE.
The baseline Givens rotation matrices can be successfully parameterized as time-ordered unitary operators (analogous to a product formula in stochastic quantum mechanics).
The attention head can be efficiently trained to approximate the predictable quadratic variation of this stochastic process using standard backpropagation through a stochastic computational graph.
ideas.expected_impact: This research will establish a rigorous stochastic-geometric foundation for quantum-inspired attention mechanisms. By allowing the Givens entropic attention to adapt to the statistical variance of KV noise dynamically, it is expected to significantly improve perplexity and retrieval accuracy in infinite-context or heavily quantized settings. Furthermore, defining the noise elimination boundary via Itô calculus will provide a mathematically guaranteed mechanism for preventing the 'over-pruning' of critical context tokens, effectively solving the fidelity-loss bottleneck in extreme KV cache compression.

ideas.topic: Differentiable Memory Manifolds for Dynamic Phase-Space KV-Cache Compression
ideas.title: Symplectic Hamiltonian KV-Cache Compression via Action-Angle Coordinate Transformations
ideas.problem_statement: Standard KV-cache compression methods typically rely on Euclidean norms or static importance scoring (e.g., attention weight magnitude), which fail to dynamically track the evolving energy distribution of long-range token dependencies. In autoregressive generation, these dependencies follow complex, oscillatory trajectories in phase-space. Current compression techniques perturb these trajectories, resulting in non-recoverable catastrophic forgetting of long-term context and structural instabilities in the attention distribution over long generation horizons.
ideas.core_mechanism: We formulate the KV-cache as a classical Hamiltonian dynamical system living on a symplectic manifold. Token representations are mapped into canonical coordinates: 'position' (semantic key states) and 'momentum' (temporal value derivatives). By performing an action-angle coordinate transformation, the oscillatory dynamics of highly attended token pairs are converted into invariant 'action' variables (representing conserved global context energy) and cyclic 'angle' variables. KV-cache compression is then executed as a canonical transformation (specifically, a controlled energy truncation) that selectively discards tokens with negligible action magnitudes. Because symplectic integration exactly preserves the geometric phase-space volume and the system's Hamiltonian invariants, the compression is structurally reversible and non-destructive to the long-term global context topology.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1. The evolution of hidden states in deep autoregressive Transformers can be accurately approximated by Hamiltonian dynamics under residual connections. 2. The global context distribution (the Hamiltonian) evolves continuously across generation steps without severe, abrupt discontinuities, allowing for continuous action-angle transformations. 3. The computational overhead of implicit symplectic integration is mitigated by the drastic reduction in sequence length during subsequent attention operations.
ideas.expected_impact: This approach will establish a novel physics-informed paradigm for memory compression that theoretically guarantees the preservation of global contextual energy. Empirically, it is expected to extend the effective generation length of LLMs by up to 4x at an equivalent KV-cache budget, while significantly reducing the hallucination rate typically caused by conventional destructive cache pruning methods.

ideas.topic: Curvature-Aware Gradient Routing for Ill-Conditioned LLM Fine-Tuning
ideas.title: Riemannian Leapfrog Hessian-Vector Products for Curvature-Aligned Momentum in LLM Fine-Tuning
ideas.problem_statement: Standard optimizers like AdamW approximate curvature using diagonal second-moment estimates, completely ignoring the off-diagonal Hessian structure. This forces the optimizer to rely on heavy-tuned learning rates and momentum coefficients to navigate ill-conditioned loss landscapes, often resulting in catastrophic forgetting or training instability during LLM fine-tuning. Capturing exact curvature requires O(N^3) matrix inversions, which is computationally intractable for multi-billion parameter models. The problem is to dynamically guide gradient updates using local curvature *without* explicit Hessian inversion, enabling stable traversal of narrow, steep ravines in the loss landscape.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose Curvature-Aligned Momentum (CAM), an optimizer that leverages implicit Hessian-Vector Products (HVPs) via the Pearlmutter trick to route standard gradients along a Riemannian manifold defined by the local loss geometry. Rather than computing the Hessian inverse, CAM runs a fixed, low-cost number of Lanczos iterations ($k \approx 5$) on the HVP operator to approximate the top-$k$ eigenvectors of the Hessian. The first-moment gradient is then orthogonally projected onto the span of these top-$k$ eigenvectors. To specifically escape sharp local minima and navigate ill-conditioned ravines, the momentum vector is dynamically routed through a Riemannian Leapfrog integrator, adjusting the parameter trajectory step size proportionally to the local principal curvatures (the eigenvalues). This effectively 'warps' the optimization path, elongating steps in directions of low curvature and shortening them in directions of high curvature.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1. The local loss geometry of LLMs during fine-tuning is sufficiently smooth such that the top-$k$ Hessian eigenvectors accurately capture the principal directions of curvature for a given mini-batch. 2. The Pearlmutter HVP can be computed in $O(N)$ time with a minor constant overhead relative to the standard backpropagation pass. 3. The cost of running $k$ Lanczos iterations per step is vastly outweighed by the forward/backward pass of a multi-billion parameter LLM. 4. The top-$k$ principal curvature directions change slowly enough (continuous batch-to-batch geometry) that routing gradients along them does not introduce high-frequency trajectory oscillations.

ideas.topic: Content-Addressed Cryptographic Provenance Verification in Multi-Agent Pipelines
ideas.title: Cayley-Menger Determinantal Codification for Incidence-Algebraic Provenance in Multi-Agent Directed Acyclic Graphs
ideas.problem_statement: In complex multi-agent LLM pipelines, verifying content-addressed provenance requires cryptographic attestation of how discrete token manifolds mutate from one agent to the next. Current approaches either rely on localized, vulnerable cryptographic hashes of local KV-caches—which fail to capture the combinatorial geometry of token-level transformations across agent boundaries—or require expensive zero-knowledge proofs of the entire inference execution. We compute the Cayley-Menger determinant of these $n$-point configurations to generate a volume-based topological invariant (the hypervolume of the token simplicial complex). This geometric invariant is then algebraically hashed using the incidence algebra of the pipeline's Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). The Möbius function of the DAG acts as an invertible operator over the sequence of Cayley-Menger invariants. By taking the inverse zeta transform of the operator, we derive an exact, content-addressed cryptographic fingerprint of the structural transformations. If an intermediate agent in the pipeline alters the semantic core of the text while syntactically masquerading as the original, the discrete hypervolume shifts, irrevocably breaking the Möbius inversion constraint.

It will enable multi-agent pipelines to execute sub-linear time provenance checks without relying on trusted execution environments or full-model zero-knowledge proofs. By proving the exact lineage of semantic transformations via algebraic topology, it resolves the multi-agent 'black-box' attribution problem, paving the way for fully decentralized, trustless autonomous agent networks.

ideas.topic: Consensus-Driven Adversarial Feedback Loops for Automated Code Synthesis
ideas.title: Chevalley-Eilenberg Coboundary Operators for Detecting Non-Transitive Code Execution Consensus
ideas.problem_statement: Consensus-driven adversarial feedback loops in multi-agent code synthesis generally evaluate local, pairwise state transitions using Markovian metrics (e.g., exact match or embedding cosine similarity). This fails to capture non-transitive, cyclical execution contradictions, such as Agent A's code beating Agent B on edge cases, B beating C, but C breaking A due to deep semantic logical loops. Current consensus mechanisms lack the topological resolution to detect these global, multi-agent execution paradoxes, leading to degenerate equilibria in the adversarial training loop.
ideas.core_mechanism: We model the multi-agent code synthesis state space as a Lie algebra, representing adversarial mutations as continuous vector fields over this manifold. We construct a Chevalley-Eilenberg (CE) cochain complex where code states are 0-cochains and pairwise adversarial execution transitions are 1-cochains. The CE coboundary operator ($d^1: C^1 \to C^2$) maps pairwise transitions into 2-cochains on the triangular simplex formed by any three agents. If $d^1$ applied to the pairwise reward differentials yields a non-zero evaluation (a non-trivial 2-cocycle), it algebraically proves a topological obstruction—a non-transitive execution loop. This acts as a structural regularizer: the adversarial feedback loop penalizes policies that generate non-zero $d^1$ evaluations, mathematically forcing the code synthesis consensus toward a homologically trivial, globally stable state.

If detected, the lock request is structurally denied, enforcing algebraic mutual exclusion over fluid roles.

By calculating the stochastic integral of a task's execution path over the semilattice boundaries, we derive an analytical exit-time probability. If the expected exit-time from the fail-closed safe boundary falls below a dynamically calculated Itô isometry bound, the orchestrator deterministically snaps the entire dependent subgraph into a halted, fail-closed state, pre-empting cascading contamination.

Finally, we assume the computational cost of evaluating the stochastic exit-time integral is sufficiently low to be performed as a synchronous micro-checkpoint between node executions.

We compute the topological gradient of this cocycle using a discrete coboundary operator ($\delta$). By applying a custom backpropagation rule through the simplicial complex, we inject this topological gradient as a repulsive force into the agents' local policy gradients. This forces the interacting agents' search trajectories orthogonally away from the shared boundary (i.e., across the $H_1$ homology class), actively driving them into topologically distinct voids (holes) in the archive to discover maximally distinct scientific paradigms.

ideas.topic: Causal Sub-space Disentanglement via Orthogonal Polynomial Projections
ideas.title: Jacobi-Theta Spectral Sieving: Orthogonal Polynomial Projections for Causal-Invariant Subspace Disentanglement under Non-Stationary Interventions
ideas.problem_statement: Standard causal disentanglement methods assume that the generative factors and their causal graph are stationary, and they typically rely on point-estimate encoders that cannot separate spurious correlations from genuine causal mechanisms when observational data is generated under non-stationary intervention distributions. When multiple interventional environments induce smoothly varying spectral densities over the latent space (e.g., gradual domain shift or soft-policy interventions), existing variational or contrastive objectives entangle the causal content with the environment-specific spectral signatures, leading to representations that fail under compositionally novel interventions.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose decomposing the latent representation space into orthogonal causal subspaces via a continuous family of Jacobi orthogonal polynomial projections. Specifically, given an encoder $\phi$ producing latents $z \in \mathbb{R}^d$, we define a spectral integral operator $\mathcal{K}$ whose kernel is constructed from the weight function $w(x) = (1-x)^{\alpha}(1+x)^{\beta}$ of the Jacobi polynomials $P_n^{(\alpha,\beta)}(x)$. The latent $z$ is projected onto the function space $L^2_w([-1,1])$ via the expansion $\hat{z}(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{N} c_n[z] \cdot P_n^{(\alpha,\beta)}(x)$, where the coefficients $c_n[z]$ are learned projection functionals. We then impose a Jacobi-Theta regularizer $\Theta_{\alpha,\beta} = \sum_{n \neq m} \langle c_n, c_m \rangle^2 / (|n - m|^s)$, which penalizes cross-spectral coupling between polynomial modes. We prove that if the interventional distributions induce shifts that are smooth with respect to the Jacobi weight parameters $(\alpha, \beta)$, then the subspace spanned by the first $k$ polynomial projections $\text{span}\{c_0, \ldots, c_{k-1}\}$ is causally invariant—i.e., the interventional conditional $P(Y | \text{do}(X=x))$ depends only on the projection of $\phi(x)$ onto this low-degree polynomial subspace, while environment-specific confounders are absorbed into higher-degree modes. We enforce this separation through a Sobolev-type adversarial loss that trains a discriminator to predict the intervention environment from high-degree coefficients $\{c_k, \ldots, c_N\}$ while being adversarially fooled on the low-degree causal subspace.
key_assumptions: The true causal generative factors induce spectral representations whose power spectral density is concentrated in low-degree orthogonal polynomial modes, while spurious confounders contribute to higher-degree modes.

Interventional shifts across environments correspond to smooth perturbations in the Jacobi weight parameters $(\alpha, \beta)$, which is valid when the interventions modify conditional distributions via temperature-like or concentration-like reweighting rather than hard structural breaks.
The dimensionality $N$ of the polynomial expansion is sufficient to capture the spectral support of both causal and confounding factors without catastrophic truncation.
The adversarial Sobolev discriminator can reliably identify and isolate environment-specific spectral signatures from the high-degree polynomial coefficients.

This estimated $\alpha$ acts as a symplectic integrator time-scaling factor $h \propto \alpha^{-1}$, which continuously warps the local Fisher metric. When the environment shifts abruptly ($\alpha \to 0$), the symplectic integration step expands the Riemannian volume element, explicitly enlarging the KL trust region to allow rapid policy adaptation. Conversely, during stable periods ($\alpha \to 1$), the integration step contracts, mathematically enforcing tighter KL constraints to guarantee stable monotonic improvement.

We then use a conformal prediction wrapper dynamically calibrated by the MWD volume to output a bounded credal set (a set of plausible reward intervals) rather than a point estimate. ideas.problem_statement: Standard Group Relative Advantage Estimation (GRAE) treats all sample trajectories as residing in a flat Euclidean space, computing pairwise advantages without acknowledging latent hierarchical or taxonomic relationships between behaviors. This forces the optimizer to penalize semantically similar but syntactically distinct successful trajectories as high-variance outliers. In environments with multi-modal hierarchical solution spaces, this Euclidean assumption leads to the catastrophic collapse of intermediate structural behaviors, destroying the learned policy's behavioral tree in favor of a single, locally optimal flat trajectory.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose embedding the group's sampled trajectories into the Poincaré disk model of hyperbolic space prior to advantage calculation. By modeling policy behaviors as a continuously expanding tree, the variational baseline is computed as the weighted Fréchet mean of the group in hyperbolic space, rather than the arithmetic mean in parameter/action space. Relative advantages are then computed using the hyperbolic distance metric (which naturally discounts the distance between points near the root and exponentially penalizes divergence near the boundary). This curvature dynamically expands the optimization gradient to explicitly preserve hierarchical taxonomic diversity, structurally anchoring the variational baseline to the semantic behavior tree.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1) The underlying optimal policy structure for complex tasks exhibits a learnable, tree-like hierarchical topology; 2) Standard policy networks can be successfully projected into and optimized over a Riemannian manifold (specifically, a hyperbolic space with constant negative curvature) without severe vanishing gradients; 3) The computational overhead of calculating Fréchet means and hyperbolic distances during the GRPO update is tractable and offset by a significant reduction in required overall sample complexity.
ideas.expected_impact: This framework will transform GRPO from a purely statistical variance-reduction technique into a topologically aware optimizer. It will entirely prevent mode collapse in environments with deep behavioral hierarchies (e.g., robotic tool-use, multi-step logical reasoning), discover naturally branching sub-policies without requiring hard-coded hierarchical reinforcement learning architectures, and establish the first mathematical bridge between Riemannian geometry and group-relative advantage estimation.

ideas.topic: Deterministic Multi-Agent Replay and Gradient Receipt Auditing for Fail-Closed RL
ideas.title: Topological Consensus Z-Vector Detection via Cech Complex Filtration in Multi-Agent Replay
ideas.problem_statement: In multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) distributed training, a single agent's hardware fault (e.g., a drifting weight or silent NaN gradient) generates localized Zero-Vector Force (ZVF) artifacts that poison the shared global trajectory replay buffer. Existing gradient clipping or norm-based anomaly detection fails to isolate these faults because the poisoned transitions often exhibit perfectly normal gradient magnitudes, making fail-closed enforcement impossible without discarding massive amounts of legitimate exploration data.
ideas.core_mechanism: We introduce Topological Replay Auditing (TRA), a mechanism that constructs a dynamic Čech complex filtration from the point-cloud of per-agent gradient update vectors at each training epoch. By tracking the birth and death of topological holes (1-dimensional homology classes) in this gradient complex, TRA identifies 'topological consensus'. A localized ZVF artifact caused by a deterministic replay fault alters the local geometry of the policy update, creating an anomalous topological void that breaks the expected Betti numbers for consensus. When TRA detects an unexpected homology class, it deterministically traces the bounding simplices back to their exact agent and replay timestep, triggering a fail-closed rollback specifically for the compromised agent.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1) In a healthy, highly-coupled MARL environment, the local policy update gradients of agents form a topological manifold (specifically, a connected 1-cycle) that remains structurally consistent across epochs. 2) Silent localized faults and ZVF injections alter the angular trajectory of specific agent gradients sufficiently to tear this manifold, creating detectable 1-dimensional homology classes. 3) The computational overhead of tracking 1-dimensional Čech complex persistence across periodic replay updates is mitigated by the fail-closed guarantee, as topological auditing is only executed on asynchronous gradient sync intervals.
ideas.expected_impact: This research will enable mathematical fail-closed isolation of single-agent faults in decentralized MARL without requiring a global training halt or rolling back the entire multi-agent replay buffer. By shifting anomaly detection from magnitude-based heuristics to topological invariants, distributed RL systems can achieve provable integrity against silent data corruption, significantly increasing the reliability of large-scale policy training.

ideas.topic: Absorbing State Identification in Reward-Trajectory Quotient Spaces
ideas.title: Persistent Homology-based Quasi-Cycle Detection in Persistent Entropy Quotient Spaces
ideas.problem_statement: When analyzing complex RL trajectories, traditional absorbing state identification methods rely on discrete, exact state-matching techniques. This fails to recognize 'practically absorbing' sets—regions where the agent exhibits perpetual cyclic behavior (e.g., pacing in a corner) without technically triggering a terminal state. Furthermore, mapping trajectories with vastly different syntactic structures but similar underlying intents into a single quotient space often obscures these behavioral sinks due to high-frequency syntactic noise, making them indistinguishable from purposeful exploratory trajectories.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose modeling the reward-trajectory quotient space as a time-varying simplicial complex derived from k-nearest-neighbor graphs of quotient-embedded trajectory segments. We apply persistent homology to compute the 1-dimensional Betti numbers ($\beta_1$) to identify topological loops. Instead of looking for strict terminal states, we define an 'Absorbing Quasi-Cycle' as a topological feature whose persistence interval (lifetime) exceeds a dynamically scaled threshold based on the system's persistent entropy. When a trajectory enters a region of the quotient space that generates a high-persistence 1-dimensional hole, we mathematically identify this as a functional absorbing state, despite the lack of an explicit terminal signal.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1) Meaningless cyclic behaviors (behavioral sinks) manifest as closed loops in the chosen reward-trajectory quotient embedding, whereas purposeful exploration forms contractible paths. 2) The topological noise of syntactic variations can be filtered out using persistence diagrams without erasing the signal of true behavioral loops. 3) The computational overhead of computing Betti numbers on sliding windows of trajectory embeddings is tractable when accelerated via sparse Ricci flow graph pre-processing.
ideas.expected_impact: This research will fundamentally shift absorbing state detection from a discrete, syntactic-level event to a robust, topological-level phenomenon. It will allow RL practitioners to automatically detect and prevent agent oscillation, pacing, and infinite loops in sparse-reward or glitched environments. Furthermore, it provides a mathematically rigorous method for equivalence-class partitioning in trajectory quotient spaces, ensuring that functional failure modes are identified even when disguised by stochastic environmental noise.

ideas.topic: Hierarchical Spectral Legendre Routing for Sub-Linear Long-Context Attention

ideas.problem_statement: Current spectral attention mechanisms rely on static, segment-wise orthogonal polynomial projections (like Legendre polynomials applied to fixed chunk sizes). When computing attention via spectral multiplication, the context window is strictly bounded by the dimensionality of the chosen polynomial basis $N$. Scaling to extremely long contexts (e.g., 100k+ tokens) requires an exponentially larger basis degree, severely degrading the $O(N^2)$ spectral routing complexity and resulting in a rigid, non-adaptive token-to-spectrum assignment that ignores the continuous nature of long-range semantic dependencies.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose formulating the routing mechanism as a time-varying Sturm-Liouville (S-L) eigenvalue problem directly within the attention recurrent state. Instead of projecting fixed token chunks onto a static Legendre basis, we treat the token stream as a continuous signal governed by an S-L differential operator. The network learns the spatially-varying 'weight' and 'diffusion' functions of this operator per attention head. As new tokens arrive, they update the continuous eigenfunctions via a recurrent Legendre-Galerkin step. Attention is then computed by routing queries through the instantaneous S-L eigenvalues (which act as a continuous, topologically-aware frequency bottleneck), dynamically scaling the context retrieval without discrete window truncation.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1) Long-range semantic dependencies in transformer representations can be accurately approximated by the smooth eigenfunctions of a learned differential operator. 2) The continuous S-L eigenstates can be discretized and updated recurrently in linear time $O(N)$ relative to the sequence length via an efficient Legendre-Galerkin approximation. 3) The gradient of the eigenvalues of the S-L operator with respect to the network weights can be effectively optimized via implicit differentiation without causing training instability.
ideas.expected_impact: This mechanism will enable theoretically infinite, dynamically bounded context windows for Transformer architectures. By replacing discrete, chunk-based spectral attention with a continuous eigenstate evolution, we achieve true sub-linear time complexity for attention retrieval during generation, entirely eliminating the need for context window segmentation while establishing a rigorous mathematical bridge between differential equation solvers and large language model architectures.

ideas.topic: Quantum-Inspired Givens Entropic Attention for Sparse KV Noise Elimination
ideas.title: Non-Commutative Itô Calculus for KV-Cache Noise Filtration via Quantum Givens Stochastic Flow
ideas.problem_statement: In autoregressive Large Language Models, the Key-Value (KV) cache suffers from extreme activation noise sparsity—often amplified in long contexts. While quantum-inspired Givens rotations can theoretically compress and filter attention matrices, they currently operate deterministically and fail to model the stochastic, non-commutative nature of attention noise propagation. The problem is that without a mathematical framework to model the cumulative, noisy perturbation of keys and values over time, deterministic Givens entropic attention either over-compresses vital context or fails to eliminate dynamic noise, leading to degraded long-context reasoning.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose modeling the sequential application of Givens rotation matrices ($G_i$) over the KV cache as a Non-Commutative Quantum Itô Stochastic Differential Equation (SDE). By treating the KV cache as a quantum state vector subject to entropic drift and stochastic noise diffusion, the Givens rotations are optimized not just as static orthogonal projectors, but as continuous-time unitary operators. The model derives a modified Itô isometry for the attention head, where the entropic noise elimination boundary is mathematically defined by the commutator $[G_t, dW_t]$, allowing the network to dynamically filter sparse KV noise via the predictable quadratic variation of the attention trajectory.
key_assumptions: The sparse noise present in the KV cache is accurately modeled as a Brownian motion (Wiener process) operating within a complex Hilbert space.
The deterministic baseline of the attention mechanism can be abstracted as the drift component of a quantum SDE.
The baseline Givens rotation matrices can be successfully parameterized as time-ordered unitary operators (analogous to a product formula in stochastic quantum mechanics).
The attention head can be efficiently trained to approximate the predictable quadratic variation of this stochastic process using standard backpropagation through a stochastic computational graph.
ideas.expected_impact: This research will establish a rigorous stochastic-geometric foundation for quantum-inspired attention mechanisms. By allowing the Givens entropic attention to adapt to the statistical variance of KV noise dynamically, it is expected to significantly improve perplexity and retrieval accuracy in infinite-context or heavily quantized settings. Furthermore, defining the noise elimination boundary via Itô calculus will provide a mathematically guaranteed mechanism for preventing the 'over-pruning' of critical context tokens, effectively solving the fidelity-loss bottleneck in extreme KV cache compression.

Token representations are mapped into canonical coordinates: 'position' (semantic key states) and 'momentum' (temporal value derivatives). By performing an action-angle coordinate transformation, the oscillatory dynamics of highly attended token pairs are converted into invariant 'action' variables (representing conserved global context energy) and cyclic 'angle' variables. KV-cache compression is then executed as a canonical transformation (specifically, a controlled energy truncation) that selectively discards tokens with negligible action magnitudes. Because symplectic integration exactly preserves the geometric phase-space volume and the system's Hamiltonian invariants, the compression is structurally reversible and non-destructive to the long-term global context topology.

The global context distribution (the Hamiltonian) evolves continuously across generation steps without severe, abrupt discontinuities, allowing for continuous action-angle transformations. 3. The computational overhead of implicit symplectic integration is mitigated by the drastic reduction in sequence length during subsequent attention operations.

ideas.topic: Curvature-Aware Gradient Routing for Ill-Conditioned LLM Fine-Tuning
ideas.title: Riemannian Leapfrog Hessian-Vector Products for Curvature-Aligned Momentum in LLM Fine-Tuning
ideas.problem_statement: Standard optimizers like AdamW approximate curvature using diagonal second-moment estimates, completely ignoring the off-diagonal Hessian structure. This forces the optimizer to rely on heavy-tuned learning rates and momentum coefficients to navigate ill-conditioned loss landscapes, often resulting in catastrophic forgetting or training instability during LLM fine-tuning. Capturing exact curvature requires O(N^3) matrix inversions, which is computationally intractable for multi-billion parameter models. The problem is to dynamically guide gradient updates using local curvature *without* explicit Hessian inversion, enabling stable traversal of narrow, steep ravines in the loss landscape.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose Curvature-Aligned Momentum (CAM), an optimizer that leverages implicit Hessian-Vector Products (HVPs) via the Pearlmutter trick to route standard gradients along a Riemannian manifold defined by the local loss geometry. Rather than computing the Hessian inverse, CAM runs a fixed, low-cost number of Lanczos iterations ($k \approx 5$) on the HVP operator to approximate the top-$k$ eigenvectors of the Hessian. The first-moment gradient is then orthogonally projected onto the span of these top-$k$ eigenvectors. To specifically escape sharp local minima and navigate ill-conditioned ravines, the momentum vector is dynamically routed through a Riemannian Leapfrog integrator, adjusting the parameter trajectory step size proportionally to the local principal curvatures (the eigenvalues). This effectively 'warps' the optimization path, elongating steps in directions of low curvature and shortening them in directions of high curvature.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1. The local loss geometry of LLMs during fine-tuning is sufficiently smooth such that the top-$k$ Hessian eigenvectors accurately capture the principal directions of curvature for a given mini-batch. 2. The Pearlmutter HVP can be computed in $O(N)$ time with a minor constant overhead relative to the standard backpropagation pass. 3. The cost of running $k$ Lanczos iterations per step is vastly outweighed by the forward/backward pass of a multi-billion parameter LLM. 4. The top-$k$ principal curvature directions change slowly enough (continuous batch-to-batch geometry) that routing gradients along them does not introduce high-frequency trajectory oscillations.

This acts as a structural regularizer: the adversarial feedback loop penalizes policies that generate non-zero $d^1$ evaluations, mathematically forcing the code synthesis consensus toward a homologically trivial, globally stable state.

This requires estimating the Lyapunov spectrum of each token's local flow via power iteration on the attention Jacobian's singular values. We then define an adaptive, layer-specific truncation threshold $\tau^{(l)}(\mathcal{B})$ calibrated against the empirical KS entropy distribution $P(h^{(l)})$ within the current batch $\mathcal{B}$. Specifically, tokens whose local information density—measured as the rate of change of their representation's differential entropy—drops below the layer-calibrated KS-entropy quantile are pruned. ideas.topic: Dynamic Token Pruning via Layer-Wise Information Density Truncation

ideas.problem_statement: Existing dynamic token pruning methods use static or globally-allocated information density thresholds across layers, failing to capture the non-stationary, layer-dependent mixing dynamics of token representations. We formalize this as a measure-theoretic truncation operator $\Pi_{\tau}$ that removes tokens contributing negligible measure to the pushforward of the representation manifold at layer $l$. The pruning decision is thus tied to each token's contribution to the layer's ergodic information production rather than a heuristic attention score.

Tokens with low KS entropy rates at a given layer contribute proportionally less to downstream task performance, making them safe candidates for pruning.

A causal pivot for backtracking is triggered when the quadratic variation exceeds a threshold derived from the Dvoretzky-Kiefer-Wolfowitz confidence band on the branch's empirical value distribution, indicating that the heuristic evaluator's uncertainty has saturated and further expansion is unlikely to reduce regret. Conversely, if the predictable drift is positive but the quadratic variation is still growing, we insert a 'dilation' step—a低成本 intermediate node that gathers additional causal evidence before committing to the expensive full expansion. ideas.topic: Dynamic Token Pruning via Layer-Wise Information Density Truncation
ideas.title: Kolmogorov-Sinai Entropy Rate Thresholding for Layer-Localized Ergodic Token Pruning via Measure-Theoretic Density Truncation
ideas.problem_statement: Existing dynamic token pruning methods use static or globally-allocated information density thresholds across layers, failing to capture the non-stationary, layer-dependent mixing dynamics of token representations. As tokens traverse deeper layers, their representations undergo chaotic divergence or ergodic mixing depending on the input context. Applying a uniform truncation threshold ignores this layer-specific information flow, leading to either over-pruning of tokens undergoing transient representational shifts (destroying recoverable information) or under-pruning of tokens that have already reached semantic saturation (wasting compute).
ideas.core_mechanism: We model each transformer layer as a measure-preserving dynamical system on the token representation space. For each layer $l$ and token position $i$, we compute a local Kolmogorov-Sinai (KS) entropy rate $h^{(l)}_i$ by tracking the contraction/expansion of the Jacobian of the attention-weighted residual update restricted to token $i$'s orbit across the previous $k$ layers. This requires estimating the Lyapunov spectrum of each token's local flow via power iteration on the attention Jacobian's singular values. We then define an adaptive, layer-specific truncation threshold $\tau^{(l)}(\mathcal{B})$ calibrated against the empirical KS entropy distribution $P(h^{(l)})$ within the current batch $\mathcal{B}$. Specifically, tokens whose local information density—measured as the rate of change of their representation's differential entropy—drops below the layer-calibrated KS-entropy quantile are pruned. We formalize this as a measure-theoretic truncation operator $\Pi_{\tau}$ that removes tokens contributing negligible measure to the pushforward of the representation manifold at layer $l$. The pruning decision is thus tied to each token's contribution to the layer's ergodic information production rather than a heuristic attention score.

Token representations follow approximately measure-preserving dynamics within short layer windows, justifying the KS entropy framework.
The empirical distribution of local KS entropy rates within a batch is sufficiently smooth to yield stable truncation thresholds via quantile estimation.
Tokens with low KS entropy rates at a given layer contribute proportionally less to downstream task performance, making them safe candidates for pruning.
ideas.expected_impact: This approach introduces the first principled connection between dynamical systems theory (ergodic theory) and token pruning, replacing heuristic attention-score thresholds with a rigorous information-theoretic criterion. We expect a 15-25% reduction in unnecessary token retention compared to uniform-density truncation methods, with no measurable quality degradation on long-context benchmarks, because pruning decisions are grounded in each token's actual information flow contribution. The per-layer adaptive thresholding also enables finer-grained compute allocation, potentially reducing inference latency by 15-20% on sequences exceeding 8K tokens.

ideas.topic: Tree-of-Thought Search with Causal Pivot Backtracking for Hard Algorithmic Problems
ideas.title: Martingale Stopping-Time Backtracking with Doob Decomposition of Branch Potential in Tree-of-Thought Search
ideas.problem_statement: Tree-of-Thought (ToT) search for hard algorithmic problems suffers from inefficient exploration: standard heuristic evaluators provide point estimates of branch promise, causing the search to either waste compute on locally promising but globally dead-end branches or prematurely abandon difficult branches. Existing methods lack a principled mechanism to decide when accumulated evidence about a subtree is 'sufficient' to either commit to exploration or trigger causal backtracking, leading to poor sample efficiency on problems requiring deep, multi-step reasoning (e.g., competition-level mathematics, formal theorem proving).
ideas.core_mechanism: We model the ToT exploration trajectory as a submartingale process where the accumulated value signal along a reasoning path is decomposed via the Doob Decomposition Theorem into a predictable drift component (determined by the causal structure of prior reasoning steps) and a martingale difference noise component. At each node expansion, we compute the conditional variance process (quadratic variation) of this martingale component. A causal pivot for backtracking is triggered when the quadratic variation exceeds a threshold derived from the Dvoretzky-Kiefer-Wolfowitz confidence band on the branch's empirical value distribution, indicating that the heuristic evaluator's uncertainty has saturated and further expansion is unlikely to reduce regret. Conversely, if the predictable drift is positive but the quadratic variation is still growing, we insert a 'dilation' step—a低成本 intermediate node that gathers additional causal evidence before committing to the expensive full expansion. This transforms the backtracking decision from a threshold on point estimates into a measure-theoretic optimal stopping problem solved via the Snell envelope, guaranteeing that backtracking is causally justified by convergence of evidence rather than heuristic pessimism.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1. The LLM's per-step value heuristic produces evaluations whose conditional expectations form an adapted stochastic process to the filtration generated by reasoning history. 2. The Doob decomposition's predictable component captures genuine causal structure of the algorithmic problem (i.e., the drift reflects whether a mathematical/approach direction is fundamentally sound), while the martingale difference captures heuristic estimation noise. 3. The quadratic variation process is estimable from a bounded number of rollout samples per node (e.g., 3-5 GPT-4 evaluations suffice for convergence in practice). 4. Hard algorithmic problems have reasoning trees where dead-end branches exhibit characteristic variance signatures (stagnant drift with high variance) distinguishable from difficult-but-solvable branches (positive drift with decreasing variance).

ideas.topic: Formal Program Verification via LLM-Guided Theorem Prover Feedback

ideas.problem_statement: Existing LLM-guided interactive theorem provers (ITPs) treat proof search as discrete symbolic state transitions, where the LLM must predict exact tactic sequences. Tactic application is redefined as a continuous T-norm (specifically, the Łukasiewicz T-norm $T(x,y)=\max(0, x+y-1)$) over a bisimulation quotient space. When the LLM proposes a tactic, rather than executing it discretely, we compute a coinductive greatest-fixed-point (\nu) over the proof obligations. We train a spectral oracle to map the current proof state to an eigenfunction of a self-adjoint operator $\mathcal{L}$ defined on the coalgebra. The LLM receives feedback not on syntax, but on how its proposed tactic shifts the spectrum of $\mathcal{L}$. If the tactic's application forces the continuous truth valuation of all sub-goals to satisfy the T-norm identity (i.e., approaching 1.0 via continuous resolution), the coinductive proof state is deemed 'well-founded' and guided toward a Q.E.D. fixed-point.

An adversarial code patch is injected as a continuous perturbation function $\delta(x)$, and we formulate the detection objective as finding the perturbation's fixed-point in the operator's resolvent set: $\phi(x) = \delta(x) + \lambda \int K(x,y)\phi(y)dy$. An adversarial vulnerability scanner is formalized as a saddle-game: the attacker seeks $\delta(x)$ that shifts the fixed-point out of the resolvent's radius, while the reviewing agents collaboratively evaluate the operator's spectral radius to guarantee convergence. As new tokens arrive, they update the continuous eigenfunctions via a recurrent Legendre-Galerkin step. Attention is then computed by routing queries through the instantaneous S-L eigenvalues (which act as a continuous, topologically-aware frequency bottleneck), dynamically scaling the context retrieval without discrete window truncation.

Rather than computing the Hessian inverse, CAM runs a fixed, low-cost number of Lanczos iterations ($k \approx 5$) on the HVP operator to approximate the top-$k$ eigenvectors of the Hessian. The first-moment gradient is then orthogonally projected onto the span of these top-$k$ eigenvectors. To specifically escape sharp local minima and navigate ill-conditioned ravines, the momentum vector is dynamically routed through a Riemannian Leapfrog integrator, adjusting the parameter trajectory step size proportionally to the local principal curvatures (the eigenvalues). This effectively 'warps' the optimization path, elongating steps in directions of low curvature and shortening them in directions of high curvature.

ideas.topic: Causal Sub-space Disentanglement via Orthogonal Polynomial Projections

ideas.problem_statement: Standard causal disentanglement methods assume that the generative factors and their causal graph are stationary, and they typically rely on point-estimate encoders that cannot separate spurious correlations from genuine causal mechanisms when observational data is generated under non-stationary intervention distributions. The latent $z$ is projected onto the function space $L^2_w([-1,1])$ via the expansion $\hat{z}(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{N} c_n[z] \cdot P_n^{(\alpha,\beta)}(x)$, where the coefficients $c_n[z]$ are learned projection functionals. We then impose a Jacobi-Theta regularizer $\Theta_{\alpha,\beta} = \sum_{n \neq m} \langle c_n, c_m \rangle^2 / (|n - m|^s)$, which penalizes cross-spectral coupling between polynomial modes. We enforce this separation through a Sobolev-type adversarial loss that trains a discriminator to predict the intervention environment from high-degree coefficients $\{c_k, \ldots, c_N\}$ while being adversarially fooled on the low-degree causal subspace.

Interventional shifts across environments correspond to smooth perturbations in the Jacobi weight parameters $(\alpha, \beta)$, which is valid when the interventions modify conditional distributions via temperature-like or concentration-like reweighting rather than hard structural breaks.
The dimensionality $N$ of the polynomial expansion is sufficient to capture the spectral support of both causal and confounding factors without catastrophic truncation.

We then use a conformal prediction wrapper dynamically calibrated by the MWD volume to output a bounded credal set (a set of plausible reward intervals) rather than a point estimate. ideas.problem_statement: Existing LLM-guided interactive theorem provers (ITPs) treat proof search as discrete symbolic state transitions, where the LLM must predict exact tactic sequences. In this framework, unproven intermediate goals are assigned a continuous truth value in [0,1] derived from the LLM's latent logit confidence (belief state). Tactic application is redefined as a continuous T-norm (specifically, the Łukasiewicz T-norm $T(x,y)=\max(0, x+y-1)$) over a bisimulation quotient space. The optimal refactoring sequence is then formulated as finding the minimal-cost path in the traversal space that induces only acyclic bounded perturbations in the spectral sequence, guaranteeing all sheaf-local semantic constraints remain satisfiable at every step.

We then define an adaptive, layer-specific truncation threshold $\tau^{(l)}(\mathcal{B})$ calibrated against the empirical KS entropy distribution $P(h^{(l)})$ within the current batch $\mathcal{B}$. Tokens with low KS entropy rates at a given layer contribute proportionally less to downstream task performance, making them safe candidates for pruning.

A causal pivot for backtracking is triggered when the quadratic variation exceeds a threshold derived from the Dvoretzky-Kiefer-Wolfowitz confidence band on the branch's empirical value distribution, indicating that the heuristic evaluator's uncertainty has saturated and further expansion is unlikely to reduce regret. Conversely, if the predictable drift is positive but the quadratic variation is still growing, we insert a 'dilation' step—a低成本 intermediate node that gathers additional causal evidence before committing to the expensive full expansion. This transforms the backtracking decision from a threshold on point estimates into a measure-theoretic optimal stopping problem solved via the Snell envelope, guaranteeing that backtracking is causally justified by convergence of evidence rather than heuristic pessimism.

ideas.problem_statement: Standard causal disentanglement methods assume that the generative factors and their causal graph are stationary, and they typically rely on point-estimate encoders that cannot separate spurious correlations from genuine causal mechanisms when observational data is generated under non-stationary intervention distributions. We then use a conformal prediction wrapper dynamically calibrated by the MWD volume to output a bounded credal set (a set of plausible reward intervals) rather than a point estimate. ideas.topic: Dynamic Token Pruning via Layer-Wise Information Density Truncation
ideas.title: Kolmogorov-Sinai Entropy Rate Thresholding for Layer-Localized Ergodic Token Pruning via Measure-Theoretic Density Truncation
ideas.problem_statement: Existing dynamic token pruning methods use static or globally-allocated information density thresholds across layers, failing to capture the non-stationary, layer-dependent mixing dynamics of token representations. As tokens traverse deeper layers, their representations undergo chaotic divergence or ergodic mixing depending on the input context. Applying a uniform truncation threshold ignores this layer-specific information flow, leading to either over-pruning of tokens undergoing transient representational shifts (destroying recoverable information) or under-pruning of tokens that have already reached semantic saturation (wasting compute).
ideas.core_mechanism: We model each transformer layer as a measure-preserving dynamical system on the token representation space. For each layer $l$ and token position $i$, we compute a local Kolmogorov-Sinai (KS) entropy rate $h^{(l)}_i$ by tracking the contraction/expansion of the Jacobian of the attention-weighted residual update restricted to token $i$'s orbit across the previous $k$ layers. This requires estimating the Lyapunov spectrum of each token's local flow via power iteration on the attention Jacobian's singular values. We then define an adaptive, layer-specific truncation threshold $\tau^{(l)}(\mathcal{B})$ calibrated against the empirical KS entropy distribution $P(h^{(l)})$ within the current batch $\mathcal{B}$. Specifically, tokens whose local information density—measured as the rate of change of their representation's differential entropy—drops below the layer-calibrated KS-entropy quantile are pruned. We formalize this as a measure-theoretic truncation operator $\Pi_{\tau}$ that removes tokens contributing negligible measure to the pushforward of the representation manifold at layer $l$. The pruning decision is thus tied to each token's contribution to the layer's ergodic information production rather than a heuristic attention score.

Token representations follow approximately measure-preserving dynamics within short layer windows, justifying the KS entropy framework.
The empirical distribution of local KS entropy rates within a batch is sufficiently smooth to yield stable truncation thresholds via quantile estimation.
Tokens with low KS entropy rates at a given layer contribute proportionally less to downstream task performance, making them safe candidates for pruning.
ideas.expected_impact: This approach introduces the first principled connection between dynamical systems theory (ergodic theory) and token pruning, replacing heuristic attention-score thresholds with a rigorous information-theoretic criterion. We expect a 15-25% reduction in unnecessary token retention compared to uniform-density truncation methods, with no measurable quality degradation on long-context benchmarks, because pruning decisions are grounded in each token's actual information flow contribution. The per-layer adaptive thresholding also enables finer-grained compute allocation, potentially reducing inference latency by 15-20% on sequences exceeding 8K tokens.

ideas.topic: Tree-of-Thought Search with Causal Pivot Backtracking for Hard Algorithmic Problems
ideas.title: Martingale Stopping-Time Backtracking with Doob Decomposition of Branch Potential in Tree-of-Thought Search
ideas.problem_statement: Tree-of-Thought (ToT) search for hard algorithmic problems suffers from inefficient exploration: standard heuristic evaluators provide point estimates of branch promise, causing the search to either waste compute on locally promising but globally dead-end branches or prematurely abandon difficult branches. Existing methods lack a principled mechanism to decide when accumulated evidence about a subtree is 'sufficient' to either commit to exploration or trigger causal backtracking, leading to poor sample efficiency on problems requiring deep, multi-step reasoning (e.g., competition-level mathematics, formal theorem proving).
ideas.core_mechanism: We model the ToT exploration trajectory as a submartingale process where the accumulated value signal along a reasoning path is decomposed via the Doob Decomposition Theorem into a predictable drift component (determined by the causal structure of prior reasoning steps) and a martingale difference noise component. At each node expansion, we compute the conditional variance process (quadratic variation) of this martingale component. A causal pivot for backtracking is triggered when the quadratic variation exceeds a threshold derived from the Dvoretzky-Kiefer-Wolfowitz confidence band on the branch's empirical value distribution, indicating that the heuristic evaluator's uncertainty has saturated and further expansion is unlikely to reduce regret. Conversely, if the predictable drift is positive but the quadratic variation is still growing, we insert a 'dilation' step—a低成本 intermediate node that gathers additional causal evidence before committing to the expensive full expansion. This transforms the backtracking decision from a threshold on point estimates into a measure-theoretic optimal stopping problem solved via the Snell envelope, guaranteeing that backtracking is causally justified by convergence of evidence rather than heuristic pessimism.

The LLM's per-step value heuristic produces evaluations whose conditional expectations form an adapted stochastic process to the filtration generated by reasoning history. 2. The Doob decomposition's predictable component captures genuine causal structure of the algorithmic problem (i.e., the drift reflects whether a mathematical/approach direction is fundamentally sound), while the martingale difference captures heuristic estimation noise. 3. The quadratic variation process is estimable from a bounded number of rollout samples per node (e.g., 3-5 GPT-4 evaluations suffice for convergence in practice). 4. Hard algorithmic problems have reasoning trees where dead-end branches exhibit characteristic variance signatures (stagnant drift with high variance) distinguishable from difficult-but-solvable branches (positive drift with decreasing variance).

ideas.topic: Formal Program Verification via LLM-Guided Theorem Prover Feedback

ideas.problem_statement: Existing LLM-guided interactive theorem provers (ITPs) treat proof search as discrete symbolic state transitions, where the LLM must predict exact tactic sequences. Tactic application is redefined as a continuous T-norm (specifically, the Łukasiewicz T-norm $T(x,y)=\max(0, x+y-1)$) over a bisimulation quotient space. We train a spectral oracle to map the current proof state to an eigenfunction of a self-adjoint operator $\mathcal{L}$ defined on the coalgebra. The LLM receives feedback not on syntax, but on how its proposed tactic shifts the spectrum of $\mathcal{L}$. If the tactic's application forces the continuous truth valuation of all sub-goals to satisfy the T-norm identity (i.e., approaching 1.0 via continuous resolution), the coinductive proof state is deemed 'well-founded' and guided toward a Q.E.D. fixed-point.

The weight $w_l(i)$ is derived from the Bounded Mean Oscillation (BMO) norm of the attention output residual stream $r_l = y_l - y_{l-1}$: components of the spectral tail whose corresponding singular vectors have high alignment with high-BMO (rapidly fluctuating, information-dense) residual directions receive large $w_l(i)$, while low-BMO directions receive small weights. We prove a generalized weighted strong $(p,p)$-inequality: $\|T_l(f) - T_l^{(k)}(f)\|_{L^p(w_l)} \leq C \cdot [w_l]_{A_p}^{1/p} \cdot \left(\sum_{i>k} (\sigma_i^{(l)} w_l(i))^p\right)^{1/p}$, where $T_l^{(k)}$ denotes the rank-$k$ truncation. The per-layer truncation rank $k_l$ is then adaptively selected by enforcing a uniform weighted spectral tail bound $\sum_{i>k_l} (\sigma_i^{(l)} w_l(i))^p \leq \epsilon$, which naturally retains more rank in high-BMO layers and aggressively compresses low-BMO layers. The $A_p$ characteristic $[w_l]_{A_p}$ is estimated in $O(d)$ time per layer using a running max-to-mean ratio of attention pre-activation magnitudes projected onto singular vector pairs.

The singular value spectra of deep-layer KV matrices genuinely follow power-law decay $\sigma_i \sim c \cdot i^{-\alpha}$ with $\alpha \in (0.3, 0.8)$ for mid-layers, which is empirically verifiable. 2. We formalize this as a measure-theoretic truncation operator $\Pi_{\tau}$ that removes tokens contributing negligible measure to the pushforward of the representation manifold at layer $l$. ideas.title: Martingale Stopping-Time Backtracking with Doob Decomposition of Branch Potential in Tree-of-Thought Search
ideas.problem_statement: Tree-of-Thought (ToT) search for hard algorithmic problems suffers from inefficient exploration: standard heuristic evaluators provide point estimates of branch promise, causing the search to either waste compute on locally promising but globally dead-end branches or prematurely abandon difficult branches. A causal pivot for backtracking is triggered when the quadratic variation exceeds a threshold derived from the Dvoretzky-Kiefer-Wolfowitz confidence band on the branch's empirical value distribution, indicating that the heuristic evaluator's uncertainty has saturated and further expansion is unlikely to reduce regret. Conversely, if the predictable drift is positive but the quadratic variation is still growing, we insert a 'dilation' step—a低成本 intermediate node that gathers additional causal evidence before committing to the expensive full expansion. This transforms the backtracking decision from a threshold on point estimates into a measure-theoretic optimal stopping problem solved via the Snell envelope, guaranteeing that backtracking is causally justified by convergence of evidence rather than heuristic pessimism.

ideas.topic: Dynamic Token Pruning via Layer-Wise Information Density Truncation
ideas.title: Kolmogorov-Sinai Entropy Rate Thresholding for Layer-Localized Ergodic Token Pruning via Measure-Theoretic Density Truncation
ideas.problem_statement: Existing dynamic token pruning methods use static or globally-allocated information density thresholds across layers, failing to capture the non-stationary, layer-dependent mixing dynamics of token representations. As tokens traverse deeper layers, their representations undergo chaotic divergence or ergodic mixing depending on the input context. Applying a uniform truncation threshold ignores this layer-specific information flow, leading to either over-pruning of tokens undergoing transient representational shifts (destroying recoverable information) or under-pruning of tokens that have already reached semantic saturation (wasting compute).
ideas.core_mechanism: We model each transformer layer as a measure-preserving dynamical system on the token representation space. For each layer $l$ and token position $i$, we compute a local Kolmogorov-Sinai (KS) entropy rate $h^{(l)}_i$ by tracking the contraction/expansion of the Jacobian of the attention-weighted residual update restricted to token $i$'s orbit across the previous $k$ layers. This requires estimating the Lyapunov spectrum of each token's local flow via power iteration on the attention Jacobian's singular values. We then define an adaptive, layer-specific truncation threshold $\tau^{(l)}(\mathcal{B})$ calibrated against the empirical KS entropy distribution $P(h^{(l)})$ within the current batch $\mathcal{B}$. Specifically, tokens whose local information density—measured as the rate of change of their representation's differential entropy—drops below the layer-calibrated KS-entropy quantile are pruned. We formalize this as a measure-theoretic truncation operator $\Pi_{\tau}$ that removes tokens contributing negligible measure to the pushforward of the representation manifold at layer $l$. The pruning decision is thus tied to each token's contribution to the layer's ergodic information production rather than a heuristic attention score.

Token representations follow approximately measure-preserving dynamics within short layer windows, justifying the KS entropy framework.
The empirical distribution of local KS entropy rates within a batch is sufficiently smooth to yield stable truncation thresholds via quantile estimation.
Tokens with low KS entropy rates at a given layer contribute proportionally less to downstream task performance, making them safe candidates for pruning.
ideas.expected_impact: This approach introduces the first principled connection between dynamical systems theory (ergodic theory) and token pruning, replacing heuristic attention-score thresholds with a rigorous information-theoretic criterion. We expect a 15-25% reduction in unnecessary token retention compared to uniform-density truncation methods, with no measurable quality degradation on long-context benchmarks, because pruning decisions are grounded in each token's actual information flow contribution. The per-layer adaptive thresholding also enables finer-grained compute allocation, potentially reducing inference latency by 15-20% on sequences exceeding 8K tokens.

ideas.topic: Tree-of-Thought Search with Causal Pivot Backtracking for Hard Algorithmic Problems
ideas.title: Martingale Stopping-Time Backtracking with Doob Decomposition of Branch Potential in Tree-of-Thought Search
ideas.problem_statement: Tree-of-Thought (ToT) search for hard algorithmic problems suffers from inefficient exploration: standard heuristic evaluators provide point estimates of branch promise, causing the search to either waste compute on locally promising but globally dead-end branches or prematurely abandon difficult branches. Existing methods lack a principled mechanism to decide when accumulated evidence about a subtree is 'sufficient' to either commit to exploration or trigger causal backtracking, leading to poor sample efficiency on problems requiring deep, multi-step reasoning (e.g., competition-level mathematics, formal theorem proving).
ideas.core_mechanism: We model the ToT exploration trajectory as a submartingale process where the accumulated value signal along a reasoning path is decomposed via the Doob Decomposition Theorem into a predictable drift component (determined by the causal structure of prior reasoning steps) and a martingale difference noise component. At each node expansion, we compute the conditional variance process (quadratic variation) of this martingale component. A causal pivot for backtracking is triggered when the quadratic variation exceeds a threshold derived from the Dvoretzky-Kiefer-Wolfowitz confidence band on the branch's empirical value distribution, indicating that the heuristic evaluator's uncertainty has saturated and further expansion is unlikely to reduce regret. Conversely, if the predictable drift is positive but the quadratic variation is still growing, we insert a 'dilation' step—a低成本 intermediate node that gathers additional causal evidence before committing to the expensive full expansion. This transforms the backtracking decision from a threshold on point estimates into a measure-theoretic optimal stopping problem solved via the Snell envelope, guaranteeing that backtracking is causally justified by convergence of evidence rather than heuristic pessimism.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1. The LLM's per-step value heuristic produces evaluations whose conditional expectations form an adapted stochastic process to the filtration generated by reasoning history. 2. The Doob decomposition's predictable component captures genuine causal structure of the algorithmic problem (i.e., the drift reflects whether a mathematical/approach direction is fundamentally sound), while the martingale difference captures heuristic estimation noise. 3. The quadratic variation process is estimable from a bounded number of rollout samples per node (e.g., 3-5 GPT-4 evaluations suffice for convergence in practice). 4. Hard algorithmic problems have reasoning trees where dead-end branches exhibit characteristic variance signatures (stagnant drift with high variance) distinguishable from difficult-but-solvable branches (positive drift with decreasing variance).

ideas.topic: Formal Program Verification via LLM-Guided Theorem Prover Feedback

ideas.problem_statement: Existing LLM-guided interactive theorem provers (ITPs) treat proof search as discrete symbolic state transitions, where the LLM must predict exact tactic sequences. This creates a severe bottleneck: the exponentially branching proof tree forces the LLM to commit to hard decisions at each node, and feedback is binary (success/failure), providing no gradient for navigating partial proof states. In this framework, unproven intermediate goals are assigned a continuous truth value in [0,1] derived from the LLM's latent logit confidence (belief state). Tactic application is redefined as a continuous T-norm (specifically, the Łukasiewicz T-norm $T(x,y)=\max(0, x+y-1)$) over a bisimulation quotient space. When the LLM proposes a tactic, rather than executing it discretely, we compute a coinductive greatest-fixed-point (\nu) over the proof obligations. We train a spectral oracle to map the current proof state to an eigenfunction of a self-adjoint operator $\mathcal{L}$ defined on the coalgebra. The LLM receives feedback not on syntax, but on how its proposed tactic shifts the spectrum of $\mathcal{L}$. If the tactic's application forces the continuous truth valuation of all sub-goals to satisfy the T-norm identity (i.e., approaching 1.0 via continuous resolution), the coinductive proof state is deemed 'well-founded' and guided toward a Q.E.D. fixed-point.

By providing dense, differentiable feedback via coinductive T-norm convergence, it will drastically reduce the search depth required for complex theorems (e.g., in Coq or Lean). We expect a significant increase in pass@1 rates for formal verification tasks by allowing the model to 'slide' along proof trajectories rather than facing immediate hard-failures on imperfect tactics.

An adversarial vulnerability scanner is formalized as a saddle-game: the attacker seeks $\delta(x)$ that shifts the fixed-point out of the resolvent's radius, while the reviewing agents collaboratively evaluate the operator's spectral radius to guarantee convergence. Vulnerabilities are explicitly mathematically detected as bifurcations where the fixed-point loses stability.

The optimal refactoring sequence is then formulated as finding the minimal-cost path in the traversal space that induces only acyclic bounded perturbations in the spectral sequence, guaranteeing all sheaf-local semantic constraints remain satisfiable at every step.

ideas.topic: Multi-Agent Quality-Diversity Archive Search for Automated Scientific Discovery
ideas.title: Persistent Čech Coboundary Gradients for Topological Conflict Resolution in Multi-Agent Quality-Diversity Archives
ideas.problem_statement: In Multi-Agent Quality-Diversity Archive (MA-QDA) search, autonomous agents explore high-dimensional scientific hypothesis spaces. Because the archives rely on behavioral descriptors (e.g., structural or mechanistic traits of hypotheses), multiple agents frequently converge on adjacent cells, forming dense, overlapping clusters in the descriptor space. We model the explored scientific hypotheses of each agent as a topological space (a point cloud) which dynamically forms a Čech complex as the archive expands. When the topological supports of two or more agents overlap, they generate a non-trivial 1-cocycle. We compute the topological gradient of this cocycle using a discrete coboundary operator ($\delta$). By applying a custom backpropagation rule through the simplicial complex, we inject this topological gradient as a repulsive force into the agents' local policy gradients. This forces the interacting agents' search trajectories orthogonally away from the shared boundary (i.e., across the $H_1$ homology class), actively driving them into topologically distinct voids (holes) in the archive to discover maximally distinct scientific paradigms.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1) The behavioral descriptor space of scientific hypotheses can be effectively mapped into a metric space where a nerve theorem accurately captures intersection topology. 2) The discrete coboundary operator yields a gradient signal with sufficient directional information to reliably guide continuous policy optimization without causing catastrophic divergence. 3) The computational overhead of dynamically calculating persistent Čech complexes is tractable for the relatively sparse, high-dimensional descriptor spaces typical in automated scientific discovery.
ideas.expected_impact: This framework will fundamentally transform MA-QDA from a parallel random search into a geometrically coordinated topological exploration. By providing a mathematically rigorous penalty for overlapping scientific hypothesis spaces, it eliminates redundant exploration and actively steers agents toward unexplored mechanistic paradigms. We expect a significant increase in the global entropy of the final archive and a marked reduction in the time required to synthesize highly diverse, novel scientific theories, pushing the boundaries of automated scientific discovery.

The steering intervention is formulated as the exponential map $\exp_p(v)$ of a computed bracket-corrected control vector $v$ at the activation point $p$. This non-linear, curvature-aware steering vector is injected into the residual stream, dynamically forcing the trajectory to follow the intrinsic geodesics of the non-collapsed reasoning space rather than an arbitrary linear interpolation that intersects degenerate policy regions.

ideas.topic: Causal Sub-space Disentanglement via Orthogonal Polynomial Projections
ideas.title: Jacobi-Theta Spectral Sieving: Orthogonal Polynomial Projections for Causal-Invariant Subspace Disentanglement under Non-Stationary Interventions
ideas.problem_statement: Standard causal disentanglement methods assume that the generative factors and their causal graph are stationary, and they typically rely on point-estimate encoders that cannot separate spurious correlations from genuine causal mechanisms when observational data is generated under non-stationary intervention distributions. When multiple interventional environments induce smoothly varying spectral densities over the latent space (e.g., gradual domain shift or soft-policy interventions), existing variational or contrastive objectives entangle the causal content with the environment-specific spectral signatures, leading to representations that fail under compositionally novel interventions.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose decomposing the latent representation space into orthogonal causal subspaces via a continuous family of Jacobi orthogonal polynomial projections. Specifically, given an encoder $\phi$ producing latents $z \in \mathbb{R}^d$, we define a spectral integral operator $\mathcal{K}$ whose kernel is constructed from the weight function $w(x) = (1-x)^{\alpha}(1+x)^{\beta}$ of the Jacobi polynomials $P_n^{(\alpha,\beta)}(x)$. The latent $z$ is projected onto the function space $L^2_w([-1,1])$ via the expansion $\hat{z}(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{N} c_n[z] \cdot P_n^{(\alpha,\beta)}(x)$, where the coefficients $c_n[z]$ are learned projection functionals. We then impose a Jacobi-Theta regularizer $\Theta_{\alpha,\beta} = \sum_{n \neq m} \langle c_n, c_m \rangle^2 / (|n - m|^s)$, which penalizes cross-spectral coupling between polynomial modes. We prove that if the interventional distributions induce shifts that are smooth with respect to the Jacobi weight parameters $(\alpha, \beta)$, then the subspace spanned by the first $k$ polynomial projections $\text{span}\{c_0, \ldots, c_{k-1}\}$ is causally invariant—i.e., the interventional conditional $P(Y | \text{do}(X=x))$ depends only on the projection of $\phi(x)$ onto this low-degree polynomial subspace, while environment-specific confounders are absorbed into higher-degree modes. We enforce this separation through a Sobolev-type adversarial loss that trains a discriminator to predict the intervention environment from high-degree coefficients $\{c_k, \ldots, c_N\}$ while being adversarially fooled on the low-degree causal subspace.
key_assumptions: The true causal generative factors induce spectral representations whose power spectral density is concentrated in low-degree orthogonal polynomial modes, while spurious confounders contribute to higher-degree modes.

Interventional shifts across environments correspond to smooth perturbations in the Jacobi weight parameters $(\alpha, \beta)$, which is valid when the interventions modify conditional distributions via temperature-like or concentration-like reweighting rather than hard structural breaks.
The dimensionality $N$ of the polynomial expansion is sufficient to capture the spectral support of both causal and confounding factors without catastrophic truncation.
The adversarial Sobolev discriminator can reliably identify and isolate environment-specific spectral signatures from the high-degree polynomial coefficients.
ideas.expected_impact: This approach provides the first rigorous connection between orthogonal polynomial spectral theory and causal invariance, offering a constructive (rather than purely constraint-based) method for identifying causally sufficient subspaces. By leveraging the three-parameter tunability $(\alpha, \beta, N)$ of Jacobi polynomials, practitioners can adaptively control the causal-confounding spectral boundary without retraining the encoder. We expect measurable improvements in out-of-distribution generalization on benchmarks with smooth intervention families (e.g., procedural environment generation), and we anticipate the Jacobi-Theta regularizer will yield interpretable spectral fingerprints of confounding, enabling post-hoc diagnostics of which latent modes are causally relevant versus environment-specific artifacts.

ideas.topic: Von Neumann Entropy Density Heatmaps for Sparse Attention Pruning
