ideas.topic: Formal Program Verification via LLM-Guided Theorem Prover Feedback
ideas.title: Łukasiewicz-Spectral T-Norm Coinduction: Continuous Valued-Algebraic Proof-State Transitions for LLM-Guided Theorem Proving
ideas.problem_statement: Existing LLM-guided interactive theorem provers (ITPs) treat proof search as discrete symbolic state transitions, where the LLM must predict exact tactic sequences. This creates a severe bottleneck: the exponentially branching proof tree forces the LLM to commit to hard decisions at each node, and feedback is binary (success/failure), providing no gradient for navigating partial proof states. There is no mechanism to reason about the 'distance' of an intermediate proof state from a closed proof in a continuous, differentiable algebraic space that aligns with the LLM's internal representation.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose modeling the proof state space not as a discrete graph, but as a continuous coalgebraic manifold governed by Łukasiewicz infinite-valued logic. In this framework, unproven intermediate goals are assigned a continuous truth value in [0,1] derived from the LLM's latent logit confidence (belief state). Tactic application is redefined as a continuous T-norm (specifically, the Łukasiewicz T-norm $T(x,y)=\max(0, x+y-1)$) over a bisimulation quotient space. When the LLM proposes a tactic, rather than executing it discretely, we compute a coinductive greatest-fixed-point (\nu) over the proof obligations. We train a spectral oracle to map the current proof state to an eigenfunction of a self-adjoint operator $\mathcal{L}$ defined on the coalgebra. The LLM receives feedback not on syntax, but on how its proposed tactic shifts the spectrum of $\mathcal{L}$. If the tactic's application forces the continuous truth valuation of all sub-goals to satisfy the T-norm identity (i.e., approaching 1.0 via continuous resolution), the coinductive proof state is deemed 'well-founded' and guided toward a Q.E.D. fixed-point.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1) The LLM's internal latent space can be projected into a continuous algebraic structure amenable to infinite-valued logic. 2) The bisimulation quotient space of intermediate proof states forms a well-behaved manifold that supports a self-adjoint operator. 3) The spectral gap of this operator correlates strongly with the actual syntactic proof distance, allowing gradient-based semantic steering of the LLM's next-token prediction.
ideas.expected_impact: This approach will fundamentally shift LLM-guided theorem proving from discrete symbolic guessing to continuous manifold navigation. By providing dense, differentiable feedback via coinductive T-norm convergence, it will drastically reduce the search depth required for complex theorems (e.g., in Coq or Lean). We expect a significant increase in pass@1 rates for formal verification tasks by allowing the model to 'slide' along proof trajectories rather than facing immediate hard-failures on imperfect tactics.

ideas.topic: Multi-View Code Review Agents with Adversarial Vulnerability Scanning
ideas.title: Fredholm Integral Equation of the Second Kind for Adversarial Perturbation Fixed-Point Detection in Multi-View Code Review Semantic Kernels
ideas.problem_statement: Existing multi-view code review agents typically decompose vulnerability detection into independent classification tasks across different semantic perspectives (e.g., data-flow, control-flow, API-misuse). Adversarial vulnerabilities, however, exploit the *interactions* between these views—subtle semantic perturbations that appear benign in any single isolated view but introduce exploitable state inconsistencies at their intersection. Current approaches fail to formalize the continuous propagation of adversarial semantic perturbations across heterogeneous code review views, lacking a rigorous mathematical framework to detect the fixed-points where these perturbations converge into an actual security flaw.
ideas.core_mechanism: We model the multi-view code review process as a Fredholm Integral Equation of the Second Kind. We construct a continuous operator K acting on a Banach space of code semantics, where K represents the integral transform mapping latent code representations through a spectral kernel weighted by both inter-view attention scores and a formal vulnerability density function. An adversarial code patch is injected as a continuous perturbation function $\delta(x)$, and we formulate the detection objective as finding the perturbation's fixed-point in the operator's resolvent set: $\phi(x) = \delta(x) + \lambda \int K(x,y)\phi(y)dy$. By parameterizing the kernel $K(x,y)$ as a Neural Operator, we learn the exact resolvent $(I - \lambda K)^{-1}$. An adversarial vulnerability scanner is formalized as a saddle-game: the attacker seeks $\delta(x)$ that shifts the fixed-point out of the resolvent's radius, while the reviewing agents collaboratively evaluate the operator's spectral radius to guarantee convergence. Vulnerabilities are explicitly mathematically detected as bifurcations where the fixed-point loses stability.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1. The semantic representations of code can be continuously interpolated within a Banach space such that integral transforms meaningfully capture cross-view interactions. 2. Adversarial vulnerabilities correspond to perturbations that fundamentally alter the spectral properties (specifically the eigenvalues) of the inter-view interaction kernel. 3. The Neural Operator approximation of the Fredholm kernel converges sufficiently fast to make the saddle-game between the generative adversarial patcher and the multi-view evaluator computationally tractable.
ideas.expected_impact: This approach introduces a rigorous continuous-functional analytical framework for multi-agent vulnerability detection, fundamentally shifting the paradigm from discrete pattern-matching to spectral stability analysis. By forcing adversarial code mutations to defeat a mathematically proven fixed-point theorem rather than a discriminative classifier, the system gains provable robustness against entire classes of multi-view evasion attacks, significantly reducing false negative rates in zero-day code review scenarios.

ideas.topic: Automated Repository Refactoring via Dependency Graph Traversal
ideas.title: Persistent Sheaf Cohomology Obstruction Detection for Atomic Micro-Refactoring Sequencing via Spectral Sequence Filtration
ideas.problem_statement: Automated repository refactoring faces a critical ordering problem: large-scale structural changes (e.g., splitting a god-class, extracting a module) must be decomposed into sequences of atomic, behavior-preserving micro-refactorings (e.g., move field, pull-up method) that maintain compilability and semantic equivalence at every intermediate step. Existing graph-based dependency traversals identify structural coupling but fail to detect subtle semantic invariants and ordering obstructions—hidden constraints that make certain refactoring sequences infeasible. There is no rigorous topological framework that can quantify the 'refactorability distance' of a dependency graph or guarantee that a traversal sequence preserves all behavioral invariants across intermediate states.
ideas.core_mechanism: We model the repository's dependency graph as a dynamic simplicial complex $K$ equipped with a constructible sheaf $\mathcal{F}$ of program semantics, where each simplex (a clique of mutually-dependent code entities) is assigned a local semantic constraint space. As a candidate micro-refactoring traverses the graph, it induces a continuous deformation (a zig-zag of sheaf pushforwards and pullbacks) on $K$, which we track using the spectral sequence associated with the sheaf cohomology $H^*(K, \mathcal{F})$. We detect refactorability obstructions by tracking the birth and death of non-trivial cohomology classes in $E_r^{p,q}$ pages across the filtration induced by the traversal. Specifically, if a proposed micro-refactoring sequence causes a persistent non-zero class in the $E_\infty$ page of the spectral sequence, this algebraically certifies an invariant violation (e.g., a cyclic dependency that cannot be broken without an intermediate compilable state). The optimal refactoring sequence is then formulated as finding the minimal-cost path in the traversal space that induces only acyclic bounded perturbations in the spectral sequence, guaranteeing all sheaf-local semantic constraints remain satisfiable at every step.
key_assumptions: Program invariants and behavioral contracts can be faithfully encoded as local sections of a sheaf over the dependency simplicial complex, with gluing conditions representing cross-module type-checking or data-flow constraints.
The spectral sequence of sheaf cohomology converges sufficiently rapidly for dependency graphs of real-world software repositories (bounded $k$-skeleton depth) to be computationally tractable.
Non-trivial persistent cohomology classes in the spectral sequence filtration correlate with genuine semantic invariant violations during refactoring, rather than topological noise.

The cost of computing sheaf cohomology group boundaries is dominated by the combinatorial structure of the dependency graph, which is typically sparse enough ($O(n)$ edges for $O(n)$ nodes in well-architected code) to render spectral sequence page-turning feasible.
ideas.expected_impact: This research introduces the first rigorous algebraic-topological framework for guaranteeing semantic preservation during automated micro-refactoring sequencing. By replacing heuristic greedy traversal with spectral sequence-guided navigation, it enables refactoring engines to provably identify feasible atomic sequences for large-scale structural transformations that current tools abort on due to undetectable intermediate invariant violations. This unlocks safe, fully autonomous refactoring of deeply entangled legacy codebases where no single safe path is obvious, fundamentally advancing the reliability of automated software evolution in industrial-scale repositories.

ideas.topic: Sobolev Space L2 Bounds for Continuous Trajectory Sequence Approximations
ideas.title: Wavelet-Galerkin Variational Crimes: Sobolev $H^s$ Norm Discretization for Trajectory-Level GFlowNet Action-Space Rectification via Mesh-Adaptive Lax-Wendroff
ideas.problem_statement: Existing continuous trajectory approximation frameworks treat sequence generation as discrete token-level sampling, which fundamentally fails to respect the Sobolev $H^s(\mathcal{X})$ bounds required for guaranteeing Lipschitz continuity in the underlying probability flows. When GFlowNets or RL policies approximate continuous trajectories via discrete tokenization, 'variational crimes' are committed: the discrete sampling measure diverges from the target continuous Sobolev measure by an unbounded margin. This manifests as high-frequency oscillatory artifacts in trajectory distributions and a loss of weak differentiability, violating the assumptions required for stable amortized inference and causing catastrophic forgetting of long-horizon dependencies.

The sequence's latent state is continuously parameterized by a hierarchy of scaling functions $\phi_{j,k}$ and wavelets $\psi_{j,k}$ satisfying a Sobolev embedding theorem. To enforce L2 bounds on the continuous trajectory, we introduce a Mesh-Adaptive Lax-Wendroff (MALW) residual term: instead of purely minimizing forward/reverse KL divergence, we minimize the variational crime error $||u - I_h u||_{H^s}$ between the idealized continuous trajectory $u$ and its interpolant $I_h u$ on the discrete action mesh $h$. The sequence generator implicitly solves the weak formulation $a(u, v) = L(v)$ for all test functions $v \in H^s_0(\mathcal{X})$, where the bilinear form $a(\cdot, \cdot)$ encodes the token-transition operator. We dynamically refine the wavelet mesh in regions where the Sobolev residual exceeds a theoretical Lax-Wendroff stability bound $C h^{\min(k, s)} ||u||_{H^k}$, locally allocating representational capacity (layers/heads) exactly where the continuous approximation is breaking down.

The wavelet basis can be made sufficiently localized in both spatial and frequency domains to allow a computationally tractable $O(N \log N)$ sparse matrix representation of the transition operator. 3. The 'variational crimes' (non-conformity between discrete sampling and continuous flow) are predominantly localized and can be bounded by Strang's first lemma in this non-Euclidean sequence space. 4. The underlying target distribution's density is sufficiently smooth that adaptive mesh refinement strictly dominates uniform-capacity tokenization.

Empirically, it will eliminate high-frequency, degenerative sampling loops in long-horizon generation tasks by mathematically enforcing a hard Sobolev L2 limit on sequential variation. ideas.topic: Givens Unitary Rotations in SO(D) for High-Dimensional Vector Compression
ideas.title: Sesquilinear Jacobi Operator Tridiagonalization for Optimal-Depth Givens Rotation Cascades via Sturm-Liouville Zero-Counting

Existing heuristics select rotation pairs (i, j) greedily based on magnitude, yielding suboptimal cascade depths and preventing provably minimal compression schedules. By mapping the problem of identifying the optimal sequence of zero-targeting rotations to finding the spectral gaps of an associated Sturm-Liouville (S-L) system, we prove that the minimal number of Givens rotations equals the oscillation count (zero crossings) of the S-L eigenfunctions. Specifically, we construct a sesquilinear form over the vector's amplitude density and solve a continuous eigenvalue problem. The zero-counting theorem for S-L systems yields an exact, discrete sequence of Jacobi angles $\theta_k$. These angles are then directly mapped to the parameters of a sequence of Givens rotation matrices $G(i_k, j_k, \theta_k)$ that forms a numerically stable, provably minimal-depth cascade for projecting the high-dimensional vector into the desired low-rank SO(D) subspace.

The target compression dimension k is sufficiently smaller than the ambient dimension D (k << D) such that the Jacobi operator's spectrum exhibits distinct, isolated gaps. 2. The L2-norm of the vector is bounded, ensuring the Sturm-Liouville system converges to a self-adjoint solution without singularities in the domain. 3. The cost of solving the S-L eigenvalue problem (O(D log D) via spectral methods) is fundamentally cheaper than the combinatorial search cost, which holds true for high dimensions.

ideas.topic: Spectral Decay Properties of Transformer Residual Key-Value Matrices
ideas.title: Zygmund-Class Muckenhoupt $A_p$ Weighted Norm Inequalities for BMO-Controlled Spectral Tail Truncation in Residual KV Matrices
ideas.problem_statement: Empirical observations across transformer families reveal that the singular value spectra of residual-stream key-value matrices exhibit heavy-tailed power-law decay with layer-dependent exponents $\alpha_l$. This estimated $\alpha$ acts as a symplectic integrator time-scaling factor $h \propto \alpha^{-1}$, which continuously warps the local Fisher metric. When the environment shifts abruptly ($\alpha \to 0$), the symplectic integration step expands the Riemannian volume element, explicitly enlarging the KL trust region to allow rapid policy adaptation. Conversely, during stable periods ($\alpha \to 1$), the integration step contracts, mathematically enforcing tighter KL constraints to guarantee stable monotonic improvement.

Deep MWD trajectories indicate concentrated, high-confidence agreement (aleatoric), while shallow trajectories indicate dispersed, OOD disagreement (epistemic). We then use a conformal prediction wrapper dynamically calibrated by the MWD volume to output a bounded credal set (a set of plausible reward intervals) rather than a point estimate. The RLHF policy gradient is constrained to strictly operate within the intersection of these conformal bounds, causing gradient masking to automatically zero out updates that violate the conformal guarantee.

ideas.topic: Dynamic Token Pruning via Layer-Wise Information Density Truncation

ideas.problem_statement: Existing dynamic token pruning methods use static or globally-allocated information density thresholds across layers, failing to capture the non-stationary, layer-dependent mixing dynamics of token representations. As tokens traverse deeper layers, their representations undergo chaotic divergence or ergodic mixing depending on the input context. Applying a uniform truncation threshold ignores this layer-specific information flow, leading to either over-pruning of tokens undergoing transient representational shifts (destroying recoverable information) or under-pruning of tokens that have already reached semantic saturation (wasting compute).

For each layer $l$ and token position $i$, we compute a local Kolmogorov-Sinai (KS) entropy rate $h^{(l)}_i$ by tracking the contraction/expansion of the Jacobian of the attention-weighted residual update restricted to token $i$'s orbit across the previous $k$ layers. This requires estimating the Lyapunov spectrum of each token's local flow via power iteration on the attention Jacobian's singular values. We then define an adaptive, layer-specific truncation threshold $\tau^{(l)}(\mathcal{B})$ calibrated against the empirical KS entropy distribution $P(h^{(l)})$ within the current batch $\mathcal{B}$. Specifically, tokens whose local information density—measured as the rate of change of their representation's differential entropy—drops below the layer-calibrated KS-entropy quantile are pruned. We formalize this as a measure-theoretic truncation operator $\Pi_{\tau}$ that removes tokens contributing negligible measure to the pushforward of the representation manifold at layer $l$. The pruning decision is thus tied to each token's contribution to the layer's ergodic information production rather than a heuristic attention score.

Token representations follow approximately measure-preserving dynamics within short layer windows, justifying the KS entropy framework.
The empirical distribution of local KS entropy rates within a batch is sufficiently smooth to yield stable truncation thresholds via quantile estimation.
Tokens with low KS entropy rates at a given layer contribute proportionally less to downstream task performance, making them safe candidates for pruning.
ideas.expected_impact: This approach introduces the first principled connection between dynamical systems theory (ergodic theory) and token pruning, replacing heuristic attention-score thresholds with a rigorous information-theoretic criterion. We expect a 15-25% reduction in unnecessary token retention compared to uniform-density truncation methods, with no measurable quality degradation on long-context benchmarks, because pruning decisions are grounded in each token's actual information flow contribution. ideas.topic: Tree-of-Thought Search with Causal Pivot Backtracking for Hard Algorithmic Problems
ideas.title: Martingale Stopping-Time Backtracking with Doob Decomposition of Branch Potential in Tree-of-Thought Search
ideas.problem_statement: Tree-of-Thought (ToT) search for hard algorithmic problems suffers from inefficient exploration: standard heuristic evaluators provide point estimates of branch promise, causing the search to either waste compute on locally promising but globally dead-end branches or prematurely abandon difficult branches. At each node expansion, we compute the conditional variance process (quadratic variation) of this martingale component. A causal pivot for backtracking is triggered when the quadratic variation exceeds a threshold derived from the Dvoretzky-Kiefer-Wolfowitz confidence band on the branch's empirical value distribution, indicating that the heuristic evaluator's uncertainty has saturated and further expansion is unlikely to reduce regret. Conversely, if the predictable drift is positive but the quadratic variation is still growing, we insert a 'dilation' step—a低成本 intermediate node that gathers additional causal evidence before committing to the expensive full expansion. This transforms the backtracking decision from a threshold on point estimates into a measure-theoretic optimal stopping problem solved via the Snell envelope, guaranteeing that backtracking is causally justified by convergence of evidence rather than heuristic pessimism.

As a candidate micro-refactoring traverses the graph, it induces a continuous deformation (a zig-zag of sheaf pushforwards and pullbacks) on $K$, which we track using the spectral sequence associated with the sheaf cohomology $H^*(K, \mathcal{F})$. We detect refactorability obstructions by tracking the birth and death of non-trivial cohomology classes in $E_r^{p,q}$ pages across the filtration induced by the traversal. Specifically, if a proposed micro-refactoring sequence causes a persistent non-zero class in the $E_\infty$ page of the spectral sequence, this algebraically certifies an invariant violation (e.g., a cyclic dependency that cannot be broken without an intermediate compilable state). The optimal refactoring sequence is then formulated as finding the minimal-cost path in the traversal space that induces only acyclic bounded perturbations in the spectral sequence, guaranteeing all sheaf-local semantic constraints remain satisfiable at every step.

Existing gradient clipping or norm-based anomaly detection fails to isolate these faults because the poisoned transitions often exhibit perfectly normal gradient magnitudes, making fail-closed enforcement impossible without discarding massive amounts of legitimate exploration data.
ideas.core_mechanism: We introduce Topological Replay Auditing (TRA), a mechanism that constructs a dynamic Čech complex filtration from the point-cloud of per-agent gradient update vectors at each training epoch. By tracking the birth and death of topological holes (1-dimensional homology classes) in this gradient complex, TRA identifies 'topological consensus'. A localized ZVF artifact caused by a deterministic replay fault alters the local geometry of the policy update, creating an anomalous topological void that breaks the expected Betti numbers for consensus. When TRA detects an unexpected homology class, it deterministically traces the bounding simplices back to their exact agent and replay timestep, triggering a fail-closed rollback specifically for the compromised agent.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1) In a healthy, highly-coupled MARL environment, the local policy update gradients of agents form a topological manifold (specifically, a connected 1-cycle) that remains structurally consistent across epochs. 2) Silent localized faults and ZVF injections alter the angular trajectory of specific agent gradients sufficiently to tear this manifold, creating detectable 1-dimensional homology classes. 3) The computational overhead of tracking 1-dimensional Čech complex persistence across periodic replay updates is mitigated by the fail-closed guarantee, as topological auditing is only executed on asynchronous gradient sync intervals.
ideas.expected_impact: This research will enable mathematical fail-closed isolation of single-agent faults in decentralized MARL without requiring a global training halt or rolling back the entire multi-agent replay buffer. By shifting anomaly detection from magnitude-based heuristics to topological invariants, distributed RL systems can achieve provable integrity against silent data corruption, significantly increasing the reliability of large-scale policy training.

ideas.topic: Absorbing State Identification in Reward-Trajectory Quotient Spaces
ideas.title: Persistent Homology-based Quasi-Cycle Detection in Persistent Entropy Quotient Spaces
ideas.problem_statement: When analyzing complex RL trajectories, traditional absorbing state identification methods rely on discrete, exact state-matching techniques. This fails to recognize 'practically absorbing' sets—regions where the agent exhibits perpetual cyclic behavior (e.g., pacing in a corner) without technically triggering a terminal state. Furthermore, mapping trajectories with vastly different syntactic structures but similar underlying intents into a single quotient space often obscures these behavioral sinks due to high-frequency syntactic noise, making them indistinguishable from purposeful exploratory trajectories.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose modeling the reward-trajectory quotient space as a time-varying simplicial complex derived from k-nearest-neighbor graphs of quotient-embedded trajectory segments. We apply persistent homology to compute the 1-dimensional Betti numbers ($\beta_1$) to identify topological loops. Instead of looking for strict terminal states, we define an 'Absorbing Quasi-Cycle' as a topological feature whose persistence interval (lifetime) exceeds a dynamically scaled threshold based on the system's persistent entropy. When a trajectory enters a region of the quotient space that generates a high-persistence 1-dimensional hole, we mathematically identify this as a functional absorbing state, despite the lack of an explicit terminal signal.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1) Meaningless cyclic behaviors (behavioral sinks) manifest as closed loops in the chosen reward-trajectory quotient embedding, whereas purposeful exploration forms contractible paths. 2) The topological noise of syntactic variations can be filtered out using persistence diagrams without erasing the signal of true behavioral loops. 3) The computational overhead of computing Betti numbers on sliding windows of trajectory embeddings is tractable when accelerated via sparse Ricci flow graph pre-processing.
ideas.expected_impact: This research will fundamentally shift absorbing state detection from a discrete, syntactic-level event to a robust, topological-level phenomenon. It will allow RL practitioners to automatically detect and prevent agent oscillation, pacing, and infinite loops in sparse-reward or glitched environments. Furthermore, it provides a mathematically rigorous method for equivalence-class partitioning in trajectory quotient spaces, ensuring that functional failure modes are identified even when disguised by stochastic environmental noise.

ideas.problem_statement: Current spectral attention mechanisms rely on static, segment-wise orthogonal polynomial projections (like Legendre polynomials applied to fixed chunk sizes). Instead of projecting fixed token chunks onto a static Legendre basis, we treat the token stream as a continuous signal governed by an S-L differential operator. The network learns the spatially-varying 'weight' and 'diffusion' functions of this operator per attention head. As new tokens arrive, they update the continuous eigenfunctions via a recurrent Legendre-Galerkin step. Attention is then computed by routing queries through the instantaneous S-L eigenvalues (which act as a continuous, topologically-aware frequency bottleneck), dynamically scaling the context retrieval without discrete window truncation.

ideas.problem_statement: In autoregressive Large Language Models, the Key-Value (KV) cache suffers from extreme activation noise sparsity—often amplified in long contexts. By treating the KV cache as a quantum state vector subject to entropic drift and stochastic noise diffusion, the Givens rotations are optimized not just as static orthogonal projectors, but as continuous-time unitary operators. The model derives a modified Itô isometry for the attention head, where the entropic noise elimination boundary is mathematically defined by the commutator $[G_t, dW_t]$, allowing the network to dynamically filter sparse KV noise via the predictable quadratic variation of the attention trajectory.
key_assumptions: The sparse noise present in the KV cache is accurately modeled as a Brownian motion (Wiener process) operating within a complex Hilbert space.
The deterministic baseline of the attention mechanism can be abstracted as the drift component of a quantum SDE.
The baseline Givens rotation matrices can be successfully parameterized as time-ordered unitary operators (analogous to a product formula in stochastic quantum mechanics).
The attention head can be efficiently trained to approximate the predictable quadratic variation of this stochastic process using standard backpropagation through a stochastic computational graph.

By allowing the Givens entropic attention to adapt to the statistical variance of KV noise dynamically, it is expected to significantly improve perplexity and retrieval accuracy in infinite-context or heavily quantized settings. ideas.topic: Curvature-Aware Gradient Routing for Ill-Conditioned LLM Fine-Tuning
ideas.title: Riemannian Leapfrog Hessian-Vector Products for Curvature-Aligned Momentum in LLM Fine-Tuning
ideas.problem_statement: Standard optimizers like AdamW approximate curvature using diagonal second-moment estimates, completely ignoring the off-diagonal Hessian structure. This forces the optimizer to rely on heavy-tuned learning rates and momentum coefficients to navigate ill-conditioned loss landscapes, often resulting in catastrophic forgetting or training instability during LLM fine-tuning. Capturing exact curvature requires O(N^3) matrix inversions, which is computationally intractable for multi-billion parameter models. The problem is to dynamically guide gradient updates using local curvature *without* explicit Hessian inversion, enabling stable traversal of narrow, steep ravines in the loss landscape.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose Curvature-Aligned Momentum (CAM), an optimizer that leverages implicit Hessian-Vector Products (HVPs) via the Pearlmutter trick to route standard gradients along a Riemannian manifold defined by the local loss geometry. Rather than computing the Hessian inverse, CAM runs a fixed, low-cost number of Lanczos iterations ($k \approx 5$) on the HVP operator to approximate the top-$k$ eigenvectors of the Hessian. The first-moment gradient is then orthogonally projected onto the span of these top-$k$ eigenvectors. To specifically escape sharp local minima and navigate ill-conditioned ravines, the momentum vector is dynamically routed through a Riemannian Leapfrog integrator, adjusting the parameter trajectory step size proportionally to the local principal curvatures (the eigenvalues). This effectively 'warps' the optimization path, elongating steps in directions of low curvature and shortening them in directions of high curvature.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1. The local loss geometry of LLMs during fine-tuning is sufficiently smooth such that the top-$k$ Hessian eigenvectors accurately capture the principal directions of curvature for a given mini-batch. 2. The Pearlmutter HVP can be computed in $O(N)$ time with a minor constant overhead relative to the standard backpropagation pass. 3. The cost of running $k$ Lanczos iterations per step is vastly outweighed by the forward/backward pass of a multi-billion parameter LLM. 4. The top-$k$ principal curvature directions change slowly enough (continuous batch-to-batch geometry) that routing gradients along them does not introduce high-frequency trajectory oscillations.

ideas.title: Martingale Stopping-Time Backtracking with Doob Decomposition of Branch Potential in Tree-of-Thought Search
ideas.problem_statement: Tree-of-Thought (ToT) search for hard algorithmic problems suffers from inefficient exploration: standard heuristic evaluators provide point estimates of branch promise, causing the search to either waste compute on locally promising but globally dead-end branches or prematurely abandon difficult branches. Existing methods lack a principled mechanism to decide when accumulated evidence about a subtree is 'sufficient' to either commit to exploration or trigger causal backtracking, leading to poor sample efficiency on problems requiring deep, multi-step reasoning (e.g., competition-level mathematics, formal theorem proving).
ideas.core_mechanism: We model the ToT exploration trajectory as a submartingale process where the accumulated value signal along a reasoning path is decomposed via the Doob Decomposition Theorem into a predictable drift component (determined by the causal structure of prior reasoning steps) and a martingale difference noise component. At each node expansion, we compute the conditional variance process (quadratic variation) of this martingale component. A causal pivot for backtracking is triggered when the quadratic variation exceeds a threshold derived from the Dvoretzky-Kiefer-Wolfowitz confidence band on the branch's empirical value distribution, indicating that the heuristic evaluator's uncertainty has saturated and further expansion is unlikely to reduce regret. Conversely, if the predictable drift is positive but the quadratic variation is still growing, we insert a 'dilation' step—a低成本 intermediate node that gathers additional causal evidence before committing to the expensive full expansion. This transforms the backtracking decision from a threshold on point estimates into a measure-theoretic optimal stopping problem solved via the Snell envelope, guaranteeing that backtracking is causally justified by convergence of evidence rather than heuristic pessimism.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1. The LLM's per-step value heuristic produces evaluations whose conditional expectations form an adapted stochastic process to the filtration generated by reasoning history. 2. The Doob decomposition's predictable component captures genuine causal structure of the algorithmic problem (i.e., the drift reflects whether a mathematical/approach direction is fundamentally sound), while the martingale difference captures heuristic estimation noise. 3. The quadratic variation process is estimable from a bounded number of rollout samples per node (e.g., 3-5 GPT-4 evaluations suffice for convergence in practice). 4. Hard algorithmic problems have reasoning trees where dead-end branches exhibit characteristic variance signatures (stagnant drift with high variance) distinguishable from difficult-but-solvable branches (positive drift with decreasing variance).

ideas.topic: Formal Program Verification via LLM-Guided Theorem Prover Feedback
ideas.title: Łukasiewicz-Spectral T-Norm Coinduction: Continuous Valued-Algebraic Proof-State Transitions for LLM-Guided Theorem Proving
ideas.problem_statement: Existing LLM-guided interactive theorem provers (ITPs) treat proof search as discrete symbolic state transitions, where the LLM must predict exact tactic sequences. This creates a severe bottleneck: the exponentially branching proof tree forces the LLM to commit to hard decisions at each node, and feedback is binary (success/failure), providing no gradient for navigating partial proof states. There is no mechanism to reason about the 'distance' of an intermediate proof state from a closed proof in a continuous, differentiable algebraic space that aligns with the LLM's internal representation.

In this framework, unproven intermediate goals are assigned a continuous truth value in [0,1] derived from the LLM's latent logit confidence (belief state). Tactic application is redefined as a continuous T-norm (specifically, the Łukasiewicz T-norm $T(x,y)=\max(0, x+y-1)$) over a bisimulation quotient space. When the LLM proposes a tactic, rather than executing it discretely, we compute a coinductive greatest-fixed-point (\nu) over the proof obligations. We train a spectral oracle to map the current proof state to an eigenfunction of a self-adjoint operator $\mathcal{L}$ defined on the coalgebra. The LLM receives feedback not on syntax, but on how its proposed tactic shifts the spectrum of $\mathcal{L}$. If the tactic's application forces the continuous truth valuation of all sub-goals to satisfy the T-norm identity (i.e., approaching 1.0 via continuous resolution), the coinductive proof state is deemed 'well-founded' and guided toward a Q.E.D. fixed-point.

By providing dense, differentiable feedback via coinductive T-norm convergence, it will drastically reduce the search depth required for complex theorems (e.g., in Coq or Lean). We expect a significant increase in pass@1 rates for formal verification tasks by allowing the model to 'slide' along proof trajectories rather than facing immediate hard-failures on imperfect tactics.

ideas.problem_statement: Existing multi-view code review agents typically decompose vulnerability detection into independent classification tasks across different semantic perspectives (e.g., data-flow, control-flow, API-misuse). Adversarial vulnerabilities, however, exploit the *interactions* between these views—subtle semantic perturbations that appear benign in any single isolated view but introduce exploitable state inconsistencies at their intersection. An adversarial code patch is injected as a continuous perturbation function $\delta(x)$, and we formulate the detection objective as finding the perturbation's fixed-point in the operator's resolvent set: $\phi(x) = \delta(x) + \lambda \int K(x,y)\phi(y)dy$. By parameterizing the kernel $K(x,y)$ as a Neural Operator, we learn the exact resolvent $(I - \lambda K)^{-1}$. An adversarial vulnerability scanner is formalized as a saddle-game: the attacker seeks $\delta(x)$ that shifts the fixed-point out of the resolvent's radius, while the reviewing agents collaboratively evaluate the operator's spectral radius to guarantee convergence. Vulnerabilities are explicitly mathematically detected as bifurcations where the fixed-point loses stability.

The optimal refactoring sequence is then formulated as finding the minimal-cost path in the traversal space that induces only acyclic bounded perturbations in the spectral sequence, guaranteeing all sheaf-local semantic constraints remain satisfiable at every step.

ideas.topic: Spectral Decay Properties of Transformer Residual Key-Value Matrices

ideas.title: Stochastic Arendt-Batty Liouville Semigroup Regularization for Holomorphic Descriptor Trajectories in Multi-Modal Quality-Diversity Experiment Archives
ideas.problem_statement: Multi-modal Quality-Diversity (QD) archives for scientific experiment design increasingly rely on heterogeneous descriptor spaces (e.g., combining mass-spectrometry signatures, genomic sequences, and thermodynamic curves). When mapping these fundamentally different physical modalities into a unified behavioral descriptor space for MAP-Elites, the archive's cell occupancy dynamics exhibit discontinuous, shock-like jumps if a newly discovered experiment drastically out-performs an incumbent. These shocks cause catastrophic forgetting of viable experimental lineages and destabilize the QD gradient flow. Standard MAP-Elites replacement mechanisms lack the mathematical continuity required to maintain a stable, differentiable archive manifold across modalities.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose modeling the continuous-time evolution of the QD archive's state as a strongly continuous semigroup of bounded linear operators $T(t)$ on the Banach space $X$ of fitness-weighted experiment descriptor distributions. Instead of discrete MAP-Elites replacement, we formulate the archive update as an abstract Cauchy problem: $\frac{du}{dt} = Au(t) + f(t)$, where $A$ is the infinitesimal generator governing archive dynamics and $f(t)$ represents the injection of new multi-modal experiments. We leverage the Arendt-Batty theorem to ensure stability: by proving that the spectrum $\sigma(A)$ is contained within a sector $|\arg(\lambda)| \le \theta$ in the right half-plane and that no residual spectrum lies on the imaginary axis, we guarantee that the semigroup $T(t)$ is exponentially stable. To enforce multi-modal consistency, we apply a stochastic Liouville perturbation $\sum \gamma_i(u) \circ dW_i$ that holomorphically extends the descriptor trajectories into the complex plane, allowing smooth interpolation between physically incompatible modalities. The archive update mechanism is resolved via a holomorphic functional calculus, replacing the discrete argmax replacement with a spectral multiplier $\Phi(A)$ that smoothly transitions cell occupancy based on the resolvent $(\lambda I - A)^{-1}$ evaluated at novel experiments.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1. The mapping from heterogeneous experimental data to the unified descriptor space can be continuously parameterized such that the archive state space $X$ admits a Banach space structure with sufficient regularity for semigroup generation. 2. The infinitesimal generator $A$ of the archive dynamics can be spectrally characterized a priori to ensure the Arendt-Batty stability conditions hold (specifically, boundedness of the resolvent on the imaginary axis). 3. The stochastic Liouville perturbation faithfully captures cross-modal transition probabilities without violating the strongly continuous nature of the semigroup. 4. The computational cost of evaluating the holomorphic functional calculus operator $\Phi(A)$ can be mitigated via Krylov subspace approximations to maintain tractable experiment generation throughput.
ideas.expected_impact: This framework will fundamentally eliminate mode-collapse and catastrophic forgetting in multi-modal QD-driven experiment design by guaranteeing mathematically bounded archive transitions. By enforcing a holomorphic descriptor trajectory, the archive will naturally interpolate between distinct scientific domains (e.g., smoothly transitioning between chemical and biological experimental modalities), uncovering novel, cross-disciplinary experiment designs. This will lead to a measurable increase in the Illumination metric (coverage × uniformity) and enable the discovery of robust experimental protocols that exist at the mathematical boundaries of traditionally siloed scientific fields.

ideas.topic: Sparse Entropic Gating for Real-Time Streaming Audio Generation
ideas.title: Gâteaux-Derivative Kernel Interpolation over Fréchet-Carrier Hölder Exponents for Causal Acoustic Envelope Extrapolation in Sparse Entropic Gating
ideas.problem_statement: Real-time streaming audio generation systems utilizing sparse entropic gating face a fundamental limitation: the top-$k$ sparsity mask must be computed autoregressively, introducing an irreducible sequential bottleneck that violates strict latency constraints. Current methods either rely on heuristic spectral gating that fails to capture non-stationary transient acoustic features (e.g., percussive attacks, consonants), or use opaque neural gating predictors that are mathematically uninterpretable and fail to provide causal guarantees, leading to temporal aliasing and pre-echo artifacts during streaming inference.
ideas.core_mechanism: We introduce the Fréchet-Carrier Hölder Extrapolator (FCHE), which models the temporal evolution of the sparse gating distribution's log-magnitudes as a continuous curve in a Banach space equipped with a local Hölder regularity measure. By computing the Gâteaux derivative of the entropic gating functional with respect to infinitesimal time-shifts along this curve, we derive a kernel operator that acts on the historical trajectory of sparse gate activations. This operator explicitly estimates the local Hölder exponent (quantifying the temporal smoothness/sharpness of acoustic transients). We interpolate these Gâteaux-derived, Hölder-weighted gradients using a causal Nyquist-limited Sinc-Kernel to analytically extrapolate the sparse gating support and continuous weights for the next $\Delta t$ inference steps, allowing the gating network to be bypassed entirely for a bounded future horizon without breaking causality.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1) The temporal evolution of the optimal sparse entropic gating distribution in the latent space is sufficiently smooth to be modeled as a continuous Fréchet curve, except at localized acoustic transients which are captured by sharp drops in the Hölder exponent. 2) The Gâteaux derivative of the entropic functional provides an unbiased, mathematically rigorous first-order approximation of the temporal gating dynamics. 3) The computational cost of evaluating the causal Sinc-Kernel interpolation is asymptotically bounded by $O(k \log k)$, making it strictly faster than a forward pass of the gating network for sufficiently large hidden dimensions.
ideas.expected_impact: This framework will provide the first mathematically rigorous, causally-guaranteed mechanism for speculative sparse gating in streaming audio. It is expected to reduce end-to-end generation latency by over 40% by parallelizing the temporal dependency of the gating mechanism. Furthermore, by grounding the sparse mask prediction in functional analysis and Hölder continuity, it entirely eliminates pre-echo artifacts and temporal aliasing during fast acoustic transients, setting a new theoretical standard for structural interpretability in continuous audio generation systems.

ideas.topic: Zero-Variance Starvation (ZVF) Mitigation in GRPO via Spectral Trajectory Gating
ideas.title: Manifold-Anchored Reference Trajectory Projection for ZVF Mitigation in GRPO
ideas.problem_statement: Zero-Variance Failure (ZVF) in GRPO occurs when an exploration policy collapses onto a single trajectory, causing the group advantage variance to drop to zero and ceasing gradient flow. Existing solutions (e.g., KL penalties) require sampling from the frozen reference model, which has a large compute footprint and disrupts the sequential inference pipeline. Without a reference model, dynamically penalizing exact trajectory repetitions in a computationally efficient, single-pass manner remains an unsolved problem.
ideas.core_mechanism: We introduce a Spectral Projection Memory module that continuously generates a low-dimensional 'anchor' for high-frequency intermediate trajectories using a streaming Hashing Trick combined with Random Fourier Features. During GRPO generation, each newly decoded token sequence is projected into this spectral space. The policy network's output logits are then subjected to a 'Manifold Repulsion Gate'—a dynamic regularization term applied directly in the attention head that penalizes token generation if the intermediate spectral signature aligns too closely with the current anchor. This creates a continuous anti-correlation pressure that breaks zero-variance states in real-time without storing or re-evaluating full reference trajectories.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1. ZVF behavioral collapse is fundamentally observable in the high-frequency variance of intermediate layer activations (which the spectral projection captures), rather than just the final output tokens. 2. The sequential alignment between the streaming hash space and the policy's latent manifold is sufficiently linear to allow an efficient dot-product repulsion gate. 3. The additional floating-point operations required for the spectral projection impose a negligible latency overhead compared to standard transformer auto-regressive decoding.
ideas.expected_impact: This mechanism will entirely eliminate Zero-Variance Starvation in GRPO without the memory and compute overhead of loading a reference policy or retaining large trajectory batches. By maintaining a steady non-zero advantage variance during deep reinforcement fine-tuning, it will prevent mode collapse, accelerate convergence on reasoning tasks, and enable stable GRPO training on edge hardware with highly constrained VRAM.

ideas.topic: Adaptive Reward-Trajectory Entropy Regularization in Policy Gradient Methods
ideas.title: Cauchy-Schwarz Trajectory Entropy Bound for Mode-Collapse Prevention in On-Policy RL
ideas.problem_statement: Standard policy gradient methods employ maximum entropy regularization to encourage exploration. However, this objective optimizes the marginal state entropy, creating an 'exploration distribution' that is uniform across the state space. When the environment contains large, reward-neutral regions (e.g., wide corridors), maximizing marginal entropy leads to policy bifurcation and mode-collapse, where the agent randomly oscillates between disconnected high-return trajectories, destroying the continuity of the policy manifold and destabilizing value estimation.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose replacing the standard marginal Shannon entropy with a trajectory-level Cauchy-Schwarz (CS) entropy bound. The CS divergence naturally penalizes overlaps between distinct sampled trajectories. By maximizing the CS trajectory entropy bound, we formulate an objective that explicitly maximizes the pairwise 'distance' between entire state-action sequences in the trajectory space (pushing the policy to discover diverse high-return paths) while inherently minimizing intra-trajectory variance (ensuring each individual path is smooth, continuous, and deterministic). We implement this via a dual-critic architecture where an auxiliary network approximates the kernel distance between current batch trajectories and a replay bank of previous diverse modes.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1. Bifurcation and mode-collapse in wide state-spaces are primarily driven by the uniform-distribution bias of marginal Shannon entropy. 2. The trajectory-level kernel distance can be accurately approximated using a bounded context window (e.g., the last $K$ states) without suffering from the curse of dimensionality. 3. The computational overhead of the pairwise kernel matrix calculation during the update phase is negligible compared to the cost of environment interaction.
ideas.expected_impact: This regularization will yield highly cohesive multi-modal policies capable of smoothly navigating vast, reward-sparse environments without the 'flickering' behavior characteristic of traditional maximum-entropy methods. It will fundamentally shift policy gradient exploration from state-marginal uniformity to trajectory-level distinctness, resulting in improved sample efficiency and stable convergence in complex continuous control tasks with multiple viable solutions.

ideas.topic: Group Relative Advantage Estimation with Dynamic Variational Baselines
ideas.title: Hyperbolic GRPO: Poincaré Disk-Embedded Relative Advantage Geometry for Hierarchical Policy Topology
ideas.problem_statement: Standard Group Relative Advantage Estimation (GRAE) treats all sample trajectories as residing in a flat Euclidean space, computing pairwise advantages without acknowledging latent hierarchical or taxonomic relationships between behaviors. This forces the optimizer to penalize semantically similar but syntactically distinct successful trajectories as high-variance outliers. In environments with multi-modal hierarchical solution spaces, this Euclidean assumption leads to the catastrophic collapse of intermediate structural behaviors, destroying the learned policy's behavioral tree in favor of a single, locally optimal flat trajectory.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose embedding the group's sampled trajectories into the Poincaré disk model of hyperbolic space prior to advantage calculation. By modeling policy behaviors as a continuously expanding tree, the variational baseline is computed as the weighted Fréchet mean of the group in hyperbolic space, rather than the arithmetic mean in parameter/action space. Relative advantages are then computed using the hyperbolic distance metric (which naturally discounts the distance between points near the root and exponentially penalizes divergence near the boundary). This curvature dynamically expands the optimization gradient to explicitly preserve hierarchical taxonomic diversity, structurally anchoring the variational baseline to the semantic behavior tree.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1) The underlying optimal policy structure for complex tasks exhibits a learnable, tree-like hierarchical topology; 2) Standard policy networks can be successfully projected into and optimized over a Riemannian manifold (specifically, a hyperbolic space with constant negative curvature) without severe vanishing gradients; 3) The computational overhead of calculating Fréchet means and hyperbolic distances during the GRPO update is tractable and offset by a significant reduction in required overall sample complexity.
ideas.expected_impact: This framework will transform GRPO from a purely statistical variance-reduction technique into a topologically aware optimizer. It will entirely prevent mode collapse in environments with deep behavioral hierarchies (e.g., robotic tool-use, multi-step logical reasoning), discover naturally branching sub-policies without requiring hard-coded hierarchical reinforcement learning architectures, and establish the first mathematical bridge between Riemannian geometry and group-relative advantage estimation.

ideas.topic: Deterministic Multi-Agent Replay and Gradient Receipt Auditing for Fail-Closed RL
ideas.title: Topological Consensus Z-Vector Detection via Cech Complex Filtration in Multi-Agent Replay
ideas.problem_statement: In multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) distributed training, a single agent's hardware fault (e.g., a drifting weight or silent NaN gradient) generates localized Zero-Vector Force (ZVF) artifacts that poison the shared global trajectory replay buffer. Existing gradient clipping or norm-based anomaly detection fails to isolate these faults because the poisoned transitions often exhibit perfectly normal gradient magnitudes, making fail-closed enforcement impossible without discarding massive amounts of legitimate exploration data.
ideas.core_mechanism: We introduce Topological Replay Auditing (TRA), a mechanism that constructs a dynamic Čech complex filtration from the point-cloud of per-agent gradient update vectors at each training epoch. By tracking the birth and death of topological holes (1-dimensional homology classes) in this gradient complex, TRA identifies 'topological consensus'. A localized ZVF artifact caused by a deterministic replay fault alters the local geometry of the policy update, creating an anomalous topological void that breaks the expected Betti numbers for consensus. When TRA detects an unexpected homology class, it deterministically traces the bounding simplices back to their exact agent and replay timestep, triggering a fail-closed rollback specifically for the compromised agent.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1) In a healthy, highly-coupled MARL environment, the local policy update gradients of agents form a topological manifold (specifically, a connected 1-cycle) that remains structurally consistent across epochs. 2) Silent localized faults and ZVF injections alter the angular trajectory of specific agent gradients sufficiently to tear this manifold, creating detectable 1-dimensional homology classes. 3) The computational overhead of tracking 1-dimensional Čech complex persistence across periodic replay updates is mitigated by the fail-closed guarantee, as topological auditing is only executed on asynchronous gradient sync intervals.
ideas.expected_impact: This research will enable mathematical fail-closed isolation of single-agent faults in decentralized MARL without requiring a global training halt or rolling back the entire multi-agent replay buffer. By shifting anomaly detection from magnitude-based heuristics to topological invariants, distributed RL systems can achieve provable integrity against silent data corruption, significantly increasing the reliability of large-scale policy training.

ideas.topic: Absorbing State Identification in Reward-Trajectory Quotient Spaces
ideas.title: Persistent Homology-based Quasi-Cycle Detection in Persistent Entropy Quotient Spaces
ideas.problem_statement: When analyzing complex RL trajectories, traditional absorbing state identification methods rely on discrete, exact state-matching techniques. This fails to recognize 'practically absorbing' sets—regions where the agent exhibits perpetual cyclic behavior (e.g., pacing in a corner) without technically triggering a terminal state. Furthermore, mapping trajectories with vastly different syntactic structures but similar underlying intents into a single quotient space often obscures these behavioral sinks due to high-frequency syntactic noise, making them indistinguishable from purposeful exploratory trajectories.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose modeling the reward-trajectory quotient space as a time-varying simplicial complex derived from k-nearest-neighbor graphs of quotient-embedded trajectory segments. We apply persistent homology to compute the 1-dimensional Betti numbers ($\beta_1$) to identify topological loops. Instead of looking for strict terminal states, we define an 'Absorbing Quasi-Cycle' as a topological feature whose persistence interval (lifetime) exceeds a dynamically scaled threshold based on the system's persistent entropy. When a trajectory enters a region of the quotient space that generates a high-persistence 1-dimensional hole, we mathematically identify this as a functional absorbing state, despite the lack of an explicit terminal signal.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1) Meaningless cyclic behaviors (behavioral sinks) manifest as closed loops in the chosen reward-trajectory quotient embedding, whereas purposeful exploration forms contractible paths. 2) The topological noise of syntactic variations can be filtered out using persistence diagrams without erasing the signal of true behavioral loops. 3) The computational overhead of computing Betti numbers on sliding windows of trajectory embeddings is tractable when accelerated via sparse Ricci flow graph pre-processing.
ideas.expected_impact: This research will fundamentally shift absorbing state detection from a discrete, syntactic-level event to a robust, topological-level phenomenon. It will allow RL practitioners to automatically detect and prevent agent oscillation, pacing, and infinite loops in sparse-reward or glitched environments. Furthermore, it provides a mathematically rigorous method for equivalence-class partitioning in trajectory quotient spaces, ensuring that functional failure modes are identified even when disguised by stochastic environmental noise.

ideas.problem_statement: Current spectral attention mechanisms rely on static, segment-wise orthogonal polynomial projections (like Legendre polynomials applied to fixed chunk sizes). Instead of projecting fixed token chunks onto a static Legendre basis, we treat the token stream as a continuous signal governed by an S-L differential operator. The network learns the spatially-varying 'weight' and 'diffusion' functions of this operator per attention head. As new tokens arrive, they update the continuous eigenfunctions via a recurrent Legendre-Galerkin step. Attention is then computed by routing queries through the instantaneous S-L eigenvalues (which act as a continuous, topologically-aware frequency bottleneck), dynamically scaling the context retrieval without discrete window truncation.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1) Long-range semantic dependencies in transformer representations can be accurately approximated by the smooth eigenfunctions of a learned differential operator. 2) The continuous S-L eigenstates can be discretized and updated recurrently in linear time $O(N)$ relative to the sequence length via an efficient Legendre-Galerkin approximation. 3) The gradient of the eigenvalues of the S-L operator with respect to the network weights can be effectively optimized via implicit differentiation without causing training instability.

ideas.topic: Quantum-Inspired Givens Entropic Attention for Sparse KV Noise Elimination
ideas.title: Non-Commutative Itô Calculus for KV-Cache Noise Filtration via Quantum Givens Stochastic Flow
ideas.problem_statement: In autoregressive Large Language Models, the Key-Value (KV) cache suffers from extreme activation noise sparsity—often amplified in long contexts. While quantum-inspired Givens rotations can theoretically compress and filter attention matrices, they currently operate deterministically and fail to model the stochastic, non-commutative nature of attention noise propagation. The problem is that without a mathematical framework to model the cumulative, noisy perturbation of keys and values over time, deterministic Givens entropic attention either over-compresses vital context or fails to eliminate dynamic noise, leading to degraded long-context reasoning.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose modeling the sequential application of Givens rotation matrices ($G_i$) over the KV cache as a Non-Commutative Quantum Itô Stochastic Differential Equation (SDE). By treating the KV cache as a quantum state vector subject to entropic drift and stochastic noise diffusion, the Givens rotations are optimized not just as static orthogonal projectors, but as continuous-time unitary operators. The model derives a modified Itô isometry for the attention head, where the entropic noise elimination boundary is mathematically defined by the commutator $[G_t, dW_t]$, allowing the network to dynamically filter sparse KV noise via the predictable quadratic variation of the attention trajectory.
key_assumptions: The sparse noise present in the KV cache is accurately modeled as a Brownian motion (Wiener process) operating within a complex Hilbert space.
The deterministic baseline of the attention mechanism can be abstracted as the drift component of a quantum SDE.
The baseline Givens rotation matrices can be successfully parameterized as time-ordered unitary operators (analogous to a product formula in stochastic quantum mechanics).
The attention head can be efficiently trained to approximate the predictable quadratic variation of this stochastic process using standard backpropagation through a stochastic computational graph.
ideas.expected_impact: This research will establish a rigorous stochastic-geometric foundation for quantum-inspired attention mechanisms. By allowing the Givens entropic attention to adapt to the statistical variance of KV noise dynamically, it is expected to significantly improve perplexity and retrieval accuracy in infinite-context or heavily quantized settings. Token representations are mapped into canonical coordinates: 'position' (semantic key states) and 'momentum' (temporal value derivatives). By performing an action-angle coordinate transformation, the oscillatory dynamics of highly attended token pairs are converted into invariant 'action' variables (representing conserved global context energy) and cyclic 'angle' variables. KV-cache compression is then executed as a canonical transformation (specifically, a controlled energy truncation) that selectively discards tokens with negligible action magnitudes. Because symplectic integration exactly preserves the geometric phase-space volume and the system's Hamiltonian invariants, the compression is structurally reversible and non-destructive to the long-term global context topology.

The computational overhead of implicit symplectic integration is mitigated by the drastic reduction in sequence length during subsequent attention operations.

ideas.topic: Curvature-Aware Gradient Routing for Ill-Conditioned LLM Fine-Tuning
ideas.title: Riemannian Leapfrog Hessian-Vector Products for Curvature-Aligned Momentum in LLM Fine-Tuning
ideas.problem_statement: Standard optimizers like AdamW approximate curvature using diagonal second-moment estimates, completely ignoring the off-diagonal Hessian structure. This forces the optimizer to rely on heavy-tuned learning rates and momentum coefficients to navigate ill-conditioned loss landscapes, often resulting in catastrophic forgetting or training instability during LLM fine-tuning. Capturing exact curvature requires O(N^3) matrix inversions, which is computationally intractable for multi-billion parameter models. The problem is to dynamically guide gradient updates using local curvature *without* explicit Hessian inversion, enabling stable traversal of narrow, steep ravines in the loss landscape.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose Curvature-Aligned Momentum (CAM), an optimizer that leverages implicit Hessian-Vector Products (HVPs) via the Pearlmutter trick to route standard gradients along a Riemannian manifold defined by the local loss geometry. Rather than computing the Hessian inverse, CAM runs a fixed, low-cost number of Lanczos iterations ($k \approx 5$) on the HVP operator to approximate the top-$k$ eigenvectors of the Hessian. The first-moment gradient is then orthogonally projected onto the span of these top-$k$ eigenvectors. To specifically escape sharp local minima and navigate ill-conditioned ravines, the momentum vector is dynamically routed through a Riemannian Leapfrog integrator, adjusting the parameter trajectory step size proportionally to the local principal curvatures (the eigenvalues). This effectively 'warps' the optimization path, elongating steps in directions of low curvature and shortening them in directions of high curvature.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1. The local loss geometry of LLMs during fine-tuning is sufficiently smooth such that the top-$k$ Hessian eigenvectors accurately capture the principal directions of curvature for a given mini-batch. 2. The Pearlmutter HVP can be computed in $O(N)$ time with a minor constant overhead relative to the standard backpropagation pass. 3. The cost of running $k$ Lanczos iterations per step is vastly outweighed by the forward/backward pass of a multi-billion parameter LLM. 4. The top-$k$ principal curvature directions change slowly enough (continuous batch-to-batch geometry) that routing gradients along them does not introduce high-frequency trajectory oscillations.

ideas.topic: Content-Addressed Cryptographic Provenance Verification in Multi-Agent Pipelines
ideas.title: Cayley-Menger Determinantal Codification for Incidence-Algebraic Provenance in Multi-Agent Directed Acyclic Graphs
ideas.problem_statement: In complex multi-agent LLM pipelines, verifying content-addressed provenance requires cryptographic attestation of how discrete token manifolds mutate from one agent to the next. Current approaches either rely on localized, vulnerable cryptographic hashes of local KV-caches—which fail to capture the combinatorial geometry of token-level transformations across agent boundaries—or require expensive zero-knowledge proofs of the entire inference execution. There is currently no mathematically rigorous mechanism to cryptographically bind the structural mutation of a text sequence to its exact lineage using the manifold geometry of the latent token space.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose embedding the input and output token manifolds of each agent into a high-dimensional metric space. We compute the Cayley-Menger determinant of these $n$-point configurations to generate a volume-based topological invariant (the hypervolume of the token simplicial complex). This geometric invariant is then algebraically hashed using the incidence algebra of the pipeline's Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). The Möbius function of the DAG acts as an invertible operator over the sequence of Cayley-Menger invariants. By taking the inverse zeta transform of the operator, we derive an exact, content-addressed cryptographic fingerprint of the structural transformations. If an intermediate agent in the pipeline alters the semantic core of the text while syntactically masquerading as the original, the discrete hypervolume shifts, irrevocably breaking the Möbius inversion constraint.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1) The latent representations of semantically distinct texts form measurably different volumetric simplicial complexes in high-dimensional embedding space. 2) The Cayley-Menger determinant can be adapted to efficiently scale with the context window size ($N$ tokens) via localized sliding-window volumetric hashing. 3) The topological constraints imposed by the DAG's incidence algebra are sufficiently rigid to prevent second-preimage attacks on the generated invariant.
ideas.expected_impact: This framework introduces an entirely new paradigm for LLM provenance: 'Geometric Cryptography'. We then use a conformal prediction wrapper dynamically calibrated by the MWD volume to output a bounded credal set (a set of plausible reward intervals) rather than a point estimate. ideas.topic: Dynamic Token Pruning via Layer-Wise Information Density Truncation

ideas.problem_statement: Existing dynamic token pruning methods use static or globally-allocated information density thresholds across layers, failing to capture the non-stationary, layer-dependent mixing dynamics of token representations. As tokens traverse deeper layers, their representations undergo chaotic divergence or ergodic mixing depending on the input context. This requires estimating the Lyapunov spectrum of each token's local flow via power iteration on the attention Jacobian's singular values. We then define an adaptive, layer-specific truncation threshold $\tau^{(l)}(\mathcal{B})$ calibrated against the empirical KS entropy distribution $P(h^{(l)})$ within the current batch $\mathcal{B}$. Specifically, tokens whose local information density—measured as the rate of change of their representation's differential entropy—drops below the layer-calibrated KS-entropy quantile are pruned. We formalize this as a measure-theoretic truncation operator $\Pi_{\tau}$ that removes tokens contributing negligible measure to the pushforward of the representation manifold at layer $l$. The pruning decision is thus tied to each token's contribution to the layer's ergodic information production rather than a heuristic attention score.

Token representations follow approximately measure-preserving dynamics within short layer windows, justifying the KS entropy framework.
The empirical distribution of local KS entropy rates within a batch is sufficiently smooth to yield stable truncation thresholds via quantile estimation.
Tokens with low KS entropy rates at a given layer contribute proportionally less to downstream task performance, making them safe candidates for pruning.
ideas.expected_impact: This approach introduces the first principled connection between dynamical systems theory (ergodic theory) and token pruning, replacing heuristic attention-score thresholds with a rigorous information-theoretic criterion. We expect a 15-25% reduction in unnecessary token retention compared to uniform-density truncation methods, with no measurable quality degradation on long-context benchmarks, because pruning decisions are grounded in each token's actual information flow contribution. ideas.title: Martingale Stopping-Time Backtracking with Doob Decomposition of Branch Potential in Tree-of-Thought Search
ideas.problem_statement: Tree-of-Thought (ToT) search for hard algorithmic problems suffers from inefficient exploration: standard heuristic evaluators provide point estimates of branch promise, causing the search to either waste compute on locally promising but globally dead-end branches or prematurely abandon difficult branches. At each node expansion, we compute the conditional variance process (quadratic variation) of this martingale component. A causal pivot for backtracking is triggered when the quadratic variation exceeds a threshold derived from the Dvoretzky-Kiefer-Wolfowitz confidence band on the branch's empirical value distribution, indicating that the heuristic evaluator's uncertainty has saturated and further expansion is unlikely to reduce regret. Conversely, if the predictable drift is positive but the quadratic variation is still growing, we insert a 'dilation' step—a低成本 intermediate node that gathers additional causal evidence before committing to the expensive full expansion. This transforms the backtracking decision from a threshold on point estimates into a measure-theoretic optimal stopping problem solved via the Snell envelope, guaranteeing that backtracking is causally justified by convergence of evidence rather than heuristic pessimism.

ideas.title: Zygmund-Class Muckenhoupt $A_p$ Weighted Norm Inequalities for BMO-Controlled Spectral Tail Truncation in Residual KV Matrices
ideas.problem_statement: Empirical observations across transformer families reveal that the singular value spectra of residual-stream key-value matrices exhibit heavy-tailed power-law decay with layer-dependent exponents $\alpha_l$. Standard SVD-based KV-cache truncation assumes a uniform, rapidly decaying spectrum; however, in mid-to-deep residual layers, the slow spectral decay (small $\alpha_l$) causes aggressive truncation to incur unbounded operator norm errors under standard $L^2$ measures, even when discarded singular components carry low semantic importance. The core problem is the absence of a principled truncation criterion that accounts for the non-uniform, anisotropic sensitivity of the output distribution to individual spectral tail components—some tail directions are semantically critical while others are highly redundant.
ideas.core_mechanism: We model the residual KV matrix at layer $l$ as an integral operator $T_l$ whose singular values $\{\sigma_i^{(l)}\}$ are reweighted by a dynamically computed Muckenhoupt $A_p$-weight function $w_l(i)$ over the singular index $i$. The weight $w_l(i)$ is derived from the Bounded Mean Oscillation (BMO) norm of the attention output residual stream $r_l = y_l - y_{l-1}$: components of the spectral tail whose corresponding singular vectors have high alignment with high-BMO (rapidly fluctuating, information-dense) residual directions receive large $w_l(i)$, while low-BMO directions receive small weights. We prove a generalized weighted strong $(p,p)$-inequality: $\|T_l(f) - T_l^{(k)}(f)\|_{L^p(w_l)} \leq C \cdot [w_l]_{A_p}^{1/p} \cdot \left(\sum_{i>k} (\sigma_i^{(l)} w_l(i))^p\right)^{1/p}$, where $T_l^{(k)}$ denotes the rank-$k$ truncation. The per-layer truncation rank $k_l$ is then adaptively selected by enforcing a uniform weighted spectral tail bound $\sum_{i>k_l} (\sigma_i^{(l)} w_l(i))^p \leq \epsilon$, which naturally retains more rank in high-BMO layers and aggressively compresses low-BMO layers. The $A_p$ characteristic $[w_l]_{A_p}$ is estimated in $O(d)$ time per layer using a running max-to-mean ratio of attention pre-activation magnitudes projected onto singular vector pairs.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1. The singular value spectra of deep-layer KV matrices genuinely follow power-law decay $\sigma_i \sim c \cdot i^{-\alpha}$ with $\alpha \in (0.3, 0.8)$ for mid-layers, which is empirically verifiable. 2. The BMO semi-norm of the residual stream increment $r_l$ is a valid proxy for semantic information density—high local oscillation correlates with fine-grained reasoning content. 3. The $A_p$-weight constructed from BMO projections satisfies the Muckenhoupt $A_p$ condition $[w_l]_{A_p} < \infty$ within practical numerical precision, ensuring the boundedness of the Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator on the weighted space. 4. The computational overhead of maintaining a running rank-1 SVD update plus the $O(d)$ weight estimation is amortizable within the attention forward pass without significant latency degradation.
ideas.expected_impact: This framework replaces the universal rank-selection heuristic in KV-cache compression with a principled, layer-adaptive criterion grounded in harmonic analysis. We expect a 30-50% improvement in compression ratios at iso-perplexity compared to uniform spectral truncation, particularly benefiting long-context generation where mid-layer spectral tails are most pronounced. The weighted norm inequality provides the first rigorous truncation error bound for heavy-tailed transformer spectra, bridging the gap between observed power-law phenomena and practical compression theory. The BMO-$A_p$ coupling also yields a diagnostic tool: the layer-wise $[w_l]_{A_p}$ trajectory serves as a training-time regularizer that can detect and penalize pathological spectral flatting during fine-tuning.

ideas.topic: Sub-Linear Long-Document Summarization via Entropic Block Truncation
ideas.title: Universal Teichmüller Deformation via Beltrami Coefficients for Conformally Invariant Entropic Block Truncation in Long-Document Summarization
ideas.problem_statement: Long-document summarization requires processing token sequences that scale super-linearly in both memory and compute. Existing entropic block truncation methods operate on a fixed, Euclidean token representation space, requiring computationally expensive brute-force or heuristic search to identify optimal truncation boundaries. When document blocks exhibit non-uniform semantic distortions (e.g., narrative shifts, topic transitions, or density variations), flat Euclidean distance metrics fundamentally fail to capture the true informational geometry, leading to the loss of critical salient content during aggressive sub-linear truncation. There is currently no mathematically rigorous framework for dynamically conformally warping the token space to minimize the topological entropy loss of truncated blocks.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose modeling the latent semantic block geometry of a long document as a Riemann surface and applying Universal Teichmüller Theory to dynamically optimize block truncation. Specifically, we compute a Beltrami coefficient $\mu(z)$ for the token block sequence, which quantifies the local conformal distortion required to map high-density informational regions to a standard unit disk. The entropic block truncation boundary is then determined by solving a Beltrami equation $\frac{\partial f}{\partial \bar{z}} = \mu(z) \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}$, identifying the quasiconformal mapping $f$ that minimizes the distortion of the informational measure (differential entropy). Blocks exhibiting high semantic entropy are assigned non-zero Beltrami coefficients, dynamically stretching the conformal metric to preserve them. Intractable boundaries are continuously warped so that the truncation threshold acts as a Jordan curve on the conformal disk, allowing sub-linear O(n^{1/2}) pruning of low-information tokens while perfectly preserving the quasiconformal moduli of the semantic dependencies.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1. The hidden states of long-document transformer blocks can be continuously projected as local coordinates onto a complex plane, allowing the application of quasiconformal mappings. 2. The relative semantic shift between adjacent text blocks can be accurately approximated by the modulus of the computed Beltrami coefficient. 3. There exists an analytically tractable or efficiently approximable numerical solver (e.g., Laplacian smoothing or a small neural solver) for the Beltrami equation that runs in strictly sub-linear time relative to the sequence length.
ideas.expected_impact: This framework will introduce a topologically invariant method for document truncation, mathematically guaranteeing minimal distortion of semantic dependencies regardless of local text density. By shifting the optimization space from discrete Euclidean heuristics to continuous conformal geometry, it enables dramatically more aggressive sub-linear context reduction (targeting $O(n^{1/2})$ scaling) without the hallucination or fact-retrieval degradation typically seen in standard truncation methods. Furthermore, it opens a novel research direction applying Complex Analysis and Riemann surface topology to sequence modeling.
