ideas.topic: Automated Literature Survey Generation with Citation Graph Traversal
ideas.title: Discrete Hodge-Laplacian Saliency Propagation via Middle-Dimensional Simplicial Sheaves for Cycle-Aware Literature Survey Generation
ideas.problem_statement: Existing automated literature survey systems model citation networks as directed graphs, restricting relevance propagation to pairwise (0-dimensional) node relationships via Graph Neural Networks. This fundamentally fails to capture higher-order epistemic structures: cliques of mutually citing papers that form cohesive 'research schools', or structural holes (cycles) indicating unresolved academic debates or paradigm clashes. Consequently, generated surveys flatten multi-perspective controversies into homogeneous, non-representative narratives, missing the topological 'holes' in the citation graph that often represent the most critical open problems.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose constructing a time-varying $k$-dimensional simplicial complex $K$ from the citation network, where nodes, edges, triangles, and tetrahedra represent papers, direct citations, shared reference pools (research cliques), and core_SYNTHESIZED_concepts, respectively. We define a discrete sheaf $\mathcal{F}$ over $K$, assigning a vector space of semantic embeddings $V_\sigma$ to each simplex $\sigma$. Instead of standard graph Laplacians, we compute the $k$-th Hodge-Laplacian ($L_k$) to govern the survey generation mechanism. Specifically, an LLM decoder is conditioned on the $1$-homology group ($H_1$) generators—eigenvectors of $L_1$ with zero eigenvalue—which mathematically isolate citation cycles (papers A cites B, B cites C, C cites A) representing academic controversies or unassimilated research branches. We introduce a 'Hodge-attention' mechanism that cross-attends to the orthogonal complement of the boundary space ($\text{im}(\partial_1)$), ensuring the generated text preserves the directional flow of citations (im $\partial_2$) while explicitly allocating text generation tokens to describe the topological 'holes' representing open research gaps.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1. The topological invariants of the citation graph (specifically Betti numbers $\beta_1$) strongly correlate with the presence of distinct academic debates, conflicting methodologies, or critical unsolved problems. 2. Semantic embeddings of papers can be validly discretized into stalks of a sheaf such that the restriction maps preserve citation directionality. 3. The computational overhead of persistent homology computation on dynamic citation subgraphs can be mitigated via localized matrix-deflation techniques, allowing real-time Hodge decomposition during LLM decoding.
ideas.expected_impact: This framework will shift automated survey generation from 'flat' aggregation to dialectic mapping. By mathematically guaranteeing the representation of multi-perspective conflicts and structural holes, the system will produce surveys that explicitly map out open problems and paradigm clashes, achieving a structurally complete overview of the literature rather than a biased consensus.

ideas.topic: Deterministic Replay Verification for Autonomous Robotic Control
ideas.title: Quillen-Suslin Theoretic State-Space Completion for Module-Theoretic Deterministic Replay in Free-Space Robotic Control
ideas.problem_statement: Deterministic replay verification of autonomous robotic control fundamentally breaks when a system transitions from highly constrained environments (fully actuated, holonomic) to free-space environments (underactuated, non-holonomic). In these open conditions, the control state space loses its algebraic closure, rendering the affine subspace of physical sensory states non-stably-free. Consequently, attempting to deterministically replay a policy execution fails because the geometrically observed actuator kinematics cannot be uniquely mapped to their originating deterministic control parameters, leading to what is known as 'replay divergence' in free-space dynamics.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose modeling the robotic control-state execution trace as a finitely generated module over a polynomial ring $R = K[x_1, ..., x_n]$ (representing kinematic degrees of freedom and time). When the system enters underactuated free-space, the recorded replay trace generates a non-stably free module $M$, preventing direct deterministic re-execution. We introduce a Quillen-Suslin Completion Operator that dynamically identifies the missing algebraic degrees of freedom. By treating the divergence between the recorded physical observables and the actuator parameters as an obstruction in the projective dimension of $M$, the operator algorithmically constructs the exact unimodular rows required to patch $M$ into a free module $R^k$. This is achieved by localizing the Quillen patching step at the zero-measure singular sets of the robot's Jacobian inverse, guaranteeing that the extended free module $R^k$ precisely completes the missing affine transformations, thus bounding the replay execution strictly to the original policy's deterministic trajectory.
key_assumptions: The kinematic state transitions of the autonomous robot can be accurately discretized and algebraically encoded as coordinates in a multivariate polynomial ring.

The deterministic replay divergences in free-space environments are fundamentally driven by sudden drops in the actuation rank, which algebraically maps to a loss of stable freeness in the module quotient.
The computational overhead of calculating the Quillen-Suslin unimodular matrix patch is sufficiently low to be calculated synchronously alongside the real-time replay verification loop.
ideas.expected_impact: This research will provide a rigorous algebraic foundation for verifying control policies in highly degenerate, real-world robotic environments (such as aerial drones in turbulent wind or quadrupeds recovering from slips). By mathematically guaranteeing deterministic replay fidelity even in non-holonomic, underactuated state spaces, it eliminates the 'sim-to-real' verification gap, enabling the safe certification of deep reinforcement learning policies for safety-critical autonomous deployments.

ideas.topic: Multi-Modal Quality-Diversity Ideation for Scientific Experiment Design
ideas.title: Stochastic Arendt-Batty Liouville Semigroup Regularization for Holomorphic Descriptor Trajectories in Multi-Modal Quality-Diversity Experiment Archives
ideas.problem_statement: Multi-modal Quality-Diversity (QD) archives for scientific experiment design increasingly rely on heterogeneous descriptor spaces (e.g., combining mass-spectrometry signatures, genomic sequences, and thermodynamic curves). When mapping these fundamentally different physical modalities into a unified behavioral descriptor space for MAP-Elites, the archive's cell occupancy dynamics exhibit discontinuous, shock-like jumps if a newly discovered experiment drastically out-performs an incumbent. These shocks cause catastrophic forgetting of viable experimental lineages and destabilize the QD gradient flow. Standard MAP-Elites replacement mechanisms lack the mathematical continuity required to maintain a stable, differentiable archive manifold across modalities.

Instead of discrete MAP-Elites replacement, we formulate the archive update as an abstract Cauchy problem: $\frac{du}{dt} = Au(t) + f(t)$, where $A$ is the infinitesimal generator governing archive dynamics and $f(t)$ represents the injection of new multi-modal experiments. We leverage the Arendt-Batty theorem to ensure stability: by proving that the spectrum $\sigma(A)$ is contained within a sector $|\arg(\lambda)| \le \theta$ in the right half-plane and that no residual spectrum lies on the imaginary axis, we guarantee that the semigroup $T(t)$ is exponentially stable. To enforce multi-modal consistency, we apply a stochastic Liouville perturbation $\sum \gamma_i(u) \circ dW_i$ that holomorphically extends the descriptor trajectories into the complex plane, allowing smooth interpolation between physically incompatible modalities. The archive update mechanism is resolved via a holomorphic functional calculus, replacing the discrete argmax replacement with a spectral multiplier $\Phi(A)$ that smoothly transitions cell occupancy based on the resolvent $(\lambda I - A)^{-1}$ evaluated at novel experiments.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1. The mapping from heterogeneous experimental data to the unified descriptor space can be continuously parameterized such that the archive state space $X$ admits a Banach space structure with sufficient regularity for semigroup generation. 2. The infinitesimal generator $A$ of the archive dynamics can be spectrally characterized a priori to ensure the Arendt-Batty stability conditions hold (specifically, boundedness of the resolvent on the imaginary axis). 3. The stochastic Liouville perturbation faithfully captures cross-modal transition probabilities without violating the strongly continuous nature of the semigroup. 4. The computational cost of evaluating the holomorphic functional calculus operator $\Phi(A)$ can be mitigated via Krylov subspace approximations to maintain tractable experiment generation throughput.
ideas.expected_impact: This framework will fundamentally eliminate mode-collapse and catastrophic forgetting in multi-modal QD-driven experiment design by guaranteeing mathematically bounded archive transitions. By enforcing a holomorphic descriptor trajectory, the archive will naturally interpolate between distinct scientific domains (e.g., smoothly transitioning between chemical and biological experimental modalities), uncovering novel, cross-disciplinary experiment designs. ideas.topic: Sparse Entropic Gating for Real-Time Streaming Audio Generation
ideas.title: Gâteaux-Derivative Kernel Interpolation over Fréchet-Carrier Hölder Exponents for Causal Acoustic Envelope Extrapolation in Sparse Entropic Gating
ideas.problem_statement: Real-time streaming audio generation systems utilizing sparse entropic gating face a fundamental limitation: the top-$k$ sparsity mask must be computed autoregressively, introducing an irreducible sequential bottleneck that violates strict latency constraints. By computing the Gâteaux derivative of the entropic gating functional with respect to infinitesimal time-shifts along this curve, we derive a kernel operator that acts on the historical trajectory of sparse gate activations. This operator explicitly estimates the local Hölder exponent (quantifying the temporal smoothness/sharpness of acoustic transients). We interpolate these Gâteaux-derived, Hölder-weighted gradients using a causal Nyquist-limited Sinc-Kernel to analytically extrapolate the sparse gating support and continuous weights for the next $\Delta t$ inference steps, allowing the gating network to be bypassed entirely for a bounded future horizon without breaking causality.

ideas.topic: Causal Inference Engine for Automated Bug Diagnosis in Large Codebases
ideas.title: Gröbner Basis Syzygy Resolution for Ideal-Theoretic Root-Cause Isolation in Static Single Assignment Dataflow Graphs
ideas.problem_statement: Automated bug diagnosis in large codebases struggles to pinpoint root-cause defects because observed execution failures are typically syntactically and temporally distant from the originating faulty instruction. Existing causal inference engines model program dataflow probabilistically (e.g., via Bayesian networks or causal DAGs), which introduces uncertainty and fails to capture the deterministic, algebraic nature of variable dependencies. When multiple interacting variables cause a failure state, current methods cannot rigorously isolate the exact minimal subset of program instructions (the root cause) from the broader execution milieu.
ideas.core_mechanism: We model the Static Single Assignment (SSA) form of a codebase as a multivariate polynomial ideal $I$ over a finite field, where monomials represent program variables and polynomial generators $\{f_1, \dots, f_n\}$ represent deterministic dataflow operations (e.g., assignments, branch constraints). We map an observed bug to a specific 'failure monomial' $m_{fail}$. To diagnose the root cause, we construct the module of syzygies over $I$—the set of algebraic relations among the generators—and compute the minimal Gröbner basis $G$ with respect to a fault-localization monomial ordering (e.g., a weighted degree ordering prioritizing temporally distant operations). The core mechanism proves that the leading monomials of the Gröbner basis dictate the exact 'annihilator' algebraic conditions. By resolving the specific syzygy that produces $m_{fail}$ in the quotient ring $K[x_1, \dots, x_n]/I$, we deterministically invert the causal dataflow, yielding the mathematically minimal generator subset $\{f_k\}$ that acts as the root-cause defect.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1. Codebase execution dataflow and logical branching can be losslessly abstracted as polynomial generators over a computable algebraic field without poly-exponential blowup in the intermediate representation. 2. The Gröbner basis fault-localization monomial ordering can be heuristically seeded with static analysis call-graph depth to keep computational complexity tractable for large-scale codebases. 3. Observed failures manifest as observable 'target polynomials' or monomials that mathematically reside in the ideal generated by the codebase's normal dataflow constraints.
ideas.expected_impact: This approach transitions automated bug diagnosis from probabilistic causal inference to formal, deterministic ideal-theoretic refutation. It eliminates false positives by mathematically proving that non-root-cause variables annihilate out of the quotient ring, offering absolute guarantees of fault localization. This mechanism will enable debugging engines to pinpoint exact anomalous assignments in complex, deeply nested, multi-threaded dataflows with zero empirical uncertainty, vastly reducing Mean Time to Resolution (MTTR) in enterprise-scale legacy codebases.

This creates a continuous anti-correlation pressure that breaks zero-variance states in real-time without storing or re-evaluating full reference trajectories.

ideas.topic: Deterministic Multi-Agent Replay and Gradient Receipt Auditing for Fail-Closed RL
ideas.title: Topological Consensus Z-Vector Detection via Cech Complex Filtration in Multi-Agent Replay
ideas.problem_statement: In multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) distributed training, a single agent's hardware fault (e.g., a drifting weight or silent NaN gradient) generates localized Zero-Vector Force (ZVF) artifacts that poison the shared global trajectory replay buffer. By tracking the birth and death of topological holes (1-dimensional homology classes) in this gradient complex, TRA identifies 'topological consensus'. A localized ZVF artifact caused by a deterministic replay fault alters the local geometry of the policy update, creating an anomalous topological void that breaks the expected Betti numbers for consensus. ideas.topic: Causal Sub-space Disentanglement via Orthogonal Polynomial Projections

The latent $z$ is projected onto the function space $L^2_w([-1,1])$ via the expansion $\hat{z}(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{N} c_n[z] \cdot P_n^{(\alpha,\beta)}(x)$, where the coefficients $c_n[z]$ are learned projection functionals. They implicitly assume a static environmental MDP, causing the learned policy to collapse into local optima when the transition dynamics drift. The core issue is that standard Trust Region Policy Optimization evaluates the KL divergence between the current and old policies using a static Euclidean geometry, treating the policy distribution as a fixed point in state-space rather than a dynamically evolving entity coupled to environmental shifts. There is no mechanism to organically align the policy's KL-constrained update step with the underlying Hölder-continuous drift of the environment's transition kernel.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose modeling the policy search trajectory not as discrete gradient steps, but as a continuous symplectic Hamiltonian flow over the Fisher-Rao Information Metric manifold. The algorithm, Hölder-Aware Symplectic Policy Flow (HASPF), reparameterizes the standard KL constraint as a Hamiltonian energy function. To handle non-stationarity, we introduce a Bregman divergence-based dual estimator that dynamically estimates the Hölder continuity exponent ($\alpha \in (0,1)$) of the transition kernel's shift between timesteps. This estimated $\alpha$ acts as a symplectic integrator time-scaling factor $h \propto \alpha^{-1}$, which continuously warps the local Fisher metric. When the environment shifts abruptly ($\alpha \to 0$), the symplectic integration step expands the Riemannian volume element, explicitly enlarging the KL trust region to allow rapid policy adaptation. Conversely, during stable periods ($\alpha \to 1$), the integration step contracts, mathematically enforcing tighter KL constraints to guarantee stable monotonic improvement.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1. The non-stationary shifts in the environment's transition kernel $P(s'|s,a)$ are locally Hölder continuous in time, meaning the degree of environmental drift exhibits measurable, estimable bounds over finite horizons. 2. The underlying dynamics of the policy network parameters can be continuously approximated by a symplectic manifold, allowing reversible leapfrog integration without structural dissipation of the information geometry. 3. A reliable auxiliary estimator network can implicitly infer the instantaneous Hölder exponent $\alpha$ from high-dimensional state representations without requiring explicit environmental reward signals.
ideas.expected_impact: HASPF will theoretically guarantee bounded regret even under adversarial non-stationary shifts by mathematically tying the adaptive KL trust region bound to the true intrinsic drift of the environment. Empirically, it is expected to eliminate the catastrophic forgetting and brittle collapse currently observed in TRPO-based algorithms operating in non-stationary MDPs, yielding significant sample efficiency improvements and yielding a robust, dynamically scaling policy search paradigm for real-world, drifting environments.

ideas.topic: Self-Refining Multi-Objective Evaluation for Complex Reasoning Tasks
ideas.title: Riesz s-Energy Equilibrium on Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces for Pareto-Optimal Self-Refinement of Reasoning Chains
ideas.problem_statement: Existing self-refining multi-objective evaluation methods treat objectives (e.g., factual accuracy, logical coherence, fluency) as independently weighted scalar rewards. This additive aggregation fails to capture non-linear objective trade-offs, leading to self-refinement trajectories that over-optimize easily distinguishable surrogate metrics while fundamentally degrading the complex structural reasoning capabilities. There is no mathematical guarantee that the self-refinement process converges to a Pareto-optimal frontier that properly balances multi-objective trade-offs without catastrophic forgetting of specific reasoning skills.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose mapping the LLM's reasoning state (represented by its Chain-of-Thought hidden representations) into a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS) structured as a Riesz s-energy equilibrium. Each active evaluation objective $i$ exerts a virtual repulsive force field defined by a kernel-induced potential $V_i(x) = \sum_{j \neq i} \frac{w_j}{d_\mathcal{H}(x_i, x_j)^s}$, where $s$ is an adaptively tuned repulsion exponent based on the current reward gradient entropy. The self-refinement generation step is formulated as seeking the variational minimizer of the total energy $E(x) = \sum_{i \neq j} \frac{1}{d_\mathcal{H}(x_i, x_j)^s}$. Instead of applying a linearized update to maximize scalar reward, the model samples the next reasoning token by projecting the locally estimated Pareto gradient onto the tangent space of this Riesz energy manifold. This forces the reasoning chain to dynamically distribute its semantic mass across the objective axes, mathematically guaranteeing a well-spaced exploration of the Pareto frontier via the equilibrium properties of the s-energy potential.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1) The complex reasoning capabilities of the model can be effectively embedded into an RKHS where semantic distances $d_\mathcal{H}$ accurately reflect functional differences in multi-objective outputs. 2) The gradient signals from independent evaluation models (or reward heads) can be locally approximated as conservative vector fields equivalent to virtual repulsive forces. 3) The computational overhead of approximating the pairwise Riesz potential online during decoding is tractable via random Fourier feature approximations of the RKHS kernel.
ideas.expected_impact: This framework will fundamentally shift multi-objective LLM evaluation from static scalar weighting to dynamic, geometry-aware equilibrium seeking. It is expected to eliminate the 'reward hacking' phenomenon where one metric dominates self-refinement, ensuring that generated reasoning chains strictly reside on the true Pareto frontier. This will result in significantly higher data efficiency for self-refining loops and improved structural integrity in complex reasoning tasks (e.g., mathematical or logical deduction) where objective trade-offs are highly non-linear.

ideas.topic: Reward Model Calibration via Uncertainty-Weighted Ensemble Variance
ideas.title: Conformal Dirichlet-Calibrated Credal Reward Ensembles via Mahalanobis-Wasserstein Depth Trajectories
ideas.problem_statement: Reward models (RMs) in RLHF are notoriously overconfident on out-of-distribution (OOD) prompts, leading to reward hacking. Existing uncertainty-weighted ensembles rely on scalar variance or heuristic disagreement metrics, which fail to distinguish epistemic uncertainty (lack of knowledge) from aleatoric ambiguity (inherent prompt subjectivity). Scalar variance collapses the multi-dimensional disagreement trajectory of the ensemble into a single noisy scalar, providing no geometric guarantees on coverage or calibration, ultimately resulting in the policy exploiting transient, spurious reward peaks.
ideas.core_mechanism: We introduce Conformal Dirichlet Calibration (CDC), which models the ensemble's continuous reward output trajectories not as independent scalars, but as a multivariate Dirichlet distribution mapped onto a probability simplex. We evaluate these trajectories using a statistical Mahalanobis-Wasserstein Depth (MWD) metric. The MWD continuously tracks the geometric trajectory of the ensemble's output distribution across decoder layers, quantifying the shape and divergence of the reward manifold. Deep MWD trajectories indicate concentrated, high-confidence agreement (aleatoric), while shallow trajectories indicate dispersed, OOD disagreement (epistemic). We then use a conformal prediction wrapper dynamically calibrated by the MWD volume to output a bounded credal set (a set of plausible reward intervals) rather than a point estimate. The RLHF policy gradient is constrained to strictly operate within the intersection of these conformal bounds, causing gradient masking to automatically zero out updates that violate the conformal guarantee.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1. The continuous reward signals provided by the ensemble members can be meaningfully L1-normalized and projected into a Dirichlet distribution over the probability simplex without breaking temporal coherence across transformer layers. 2. The Mahalanobis-Wasserstein depth of the ensemble's hidden-state trajectory provides a strictly more informative geometric signal for differentiating aleatoric vs. epistemic uncertainty than unidirectional output scalar variance. 3. The computational overhead of computing MWD and conformal bounds online is amortizable through asynchronous ensemble forward-passes and does not introduce training instabilities during PPO.
ideas.expected_impact: This research will fundamentally shift RM calibration from point-estimate variance minimization to geometric trajectory depth analysis. By guaranteeing distribution-free conformal coverage adapted to the ensemble's Wasserstein geometry, the policy will demonstrably eliminate catastrophic reward hacking on OOD prompts while maintaining fast convergence on well-defined alignment tasks, bridging the gap between statistical conformal prediction and practical LLM alignment.

ideas.topic: Entropy-Regularized Optimal Transport Routing in Sparse Mixture-of-Experts
ideas.title: Kantorovich Dual Network Pruning via Optimal Transport Discrepancy Equilibrium in Sparse MoE Gating
ideas.problem_statement: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures suffer from representation collapse, where the router consistently over-utilizes a small fraction of experts for semantically similar inputs, causing capacity bottlenecks and leaving other experts under-trained. Current routing solutions rely on auxiliary load-balancing losses or greedy top-$k$ token assignment, which fail to capture global distributional discrepancies between the token demand and the actual expert capacity supply.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose modeling the MoE routing objective as a regularized Optimal Transport (OT) problem between a continuous measure of token representations (demand) and a discrete measure of expert capacities (supply). Instead of standard entropy-regularized OT (e.g., Sinkhorn iterations) which adds a static temperature constant, we introduce a learnable, attention-driven Kantorovich Dual Network. This network dynamically parameterizes the OT dual potentials $f(x)$ and $g(y)$ for tokens and experts respectively. The routing mechanism is computed as the exact c-transform of these dual potentials, yielding a transport plan that inherently satisfies marginal capacity constraints. We optimize the potentials by minimizing the $L^2$-norm of the marginal violation (the equilibrium gap), replacing standard auxiliary load-balancing losses entirely.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1. The representations of input tokens in a sequence form a continuous probability measure that can be optimally transported to the discrete expert capacity manifold. 2. The dual potentials of the Kantorovich OT problem can be accurately parameterized by a lightweight, shared multi-layer perceptron rather than requiring iterative fixed-point algorithms like Sinkhorn. 3. Constraining the gradient updates to minimize the equilibrium gap of the marginal constraints is strictly more efficient for load balancing than penalizing variance across expert dispatch frequencies.
ideas.expected_impact: This mechanism will mathematically eliminate routing collapse and eliminate the need to tune load-balancing penalty hyperparameters, leading to strictly enforced expert capacity utilization. By leveraging dynamic dual potentials rather than static entropic regularization, the model will achieve lower transport cost (higher specialization efficiency), yielding lower perplexity and more robust generalization on downstream tasks without increasing inference latency.

ideas.topic: Quantization-Aware Spectral Decomposition for Low-Bit KV-Cache Acceleration
ideas.title: Hausdorff-Continuum Mixed-Adicity Hyperdimensional State Folding for Bit-Width Adaptive KV-Cache Quantization
ideas.problem_statement: Existing quantization-aware mechanisms for KV-cache compression enforce static bit-width allocations (e.g., INT4 or INT8) across the continuous token stream. This discrete step-function approach forces a rigid trade-off between numerical fidelity and memory conservation: salient tokens are restricted by the bit-budget ceiling, while redundant tokens waste precious memory, ultimately bottlenecking maximum sequence length and generation throughput.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose replacing the discrete bit-allocation layer with a continuous Hausdorff-Continuum State Folder (HCSF). Instead of quantizing a state $x$ to a fixed $2^b$ grid, HCSF projects $x$ onto a mixed-adic dynamical system constructed from coprime moduli $\{p_1, p_2, \dots\}$ using the Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT). State preservation is modeled by a Hausdorff measure on a fractional-dimensional manifold. Using a lightweight online controller, the system continuously interpolates the moduli set based on the real-time estimated information curvature of the incoming token. This dynamically scales the effective bit-width to a continuous floating value (e.g., exactly 3.7 bits for a specific token), effectively folding the token's state into an optimal continuous-integer hypersphere.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1. The cryptographic and mathematical operations required for CRT-based mixed-adic folding can be executed via parallelized tensor operations (e.g., using custom Triton kernels) without introducing prohibitive inference latency. 2. The 'information curvature' of a token's Key/Value vectors serves as a highly reliable, causally safe proxy for determining the exact amount of numerical precision required to prevent attention divergence. 3. The transformer's subsequent attention mechanism can inherently process and attend over holographically folded mixed-adic representations.
ideas.expected_impact: This mechanism fundamentally redefines quantization from a static, discrete architectural constraint to a continuous, fluid state-space transformation. It allows for the granular, sub-integer allocation of memory across sequence lengths, theoretically reducing KV-cache memory footprints by an additional 30-45% over standard INT4 baselines while preserving exact parity with FP16 attention maps. This unlocks near-infinite context windows for edge devices strictly constrained by VRAM ceilings.

ideas.topic: Dynamic Token Pruning via Layer-Wise Information Density Truncation
ideas.title: Kolmogorov-Sinai Entropy Rate Thresholding for Layer-Localized Ergodic Token Pruning via Measure-Theoretic Density Truncation
ideas.problem_statement: Existing dynamic token pruning methods use static or globally-allocated information density thresholds across layers, failing to capture the non-stationary, layer-dependent mixing dynamics of token representations. As tokens traverse deeper layers, their representations undergo chaotic divergence or ergodic mixing depending on the input context. Applying a uniform truncation threshold ignores this layer-specific information flow, leading to either over-pruning of tokens undergoing transient representational shifts (destroying recoverable information) or under-pruning of tokens that have already reached semantic saturation (wasting compute).
ideas.core_mechanism: We model each transformer layer as a measure-preserving dynamical system on the token representation space. For each layer $l$ and token position $i$, we compute a local Kolmogorov-Sinai (KS) entropy rate $h^{(l)}_i$ by tracking the contraction/expansion of the Jacobian of the attention-weighted residual update restricted to token $i$'s orbit across the previous $k$ layers. This requires estimating the Lyapunov spectrum of each token's local flow via power iteration on the attention Jacobian's singular values. We then define an adaptive, layer-specific truncation threshold $\tau^{(l)}(\mathcal{B})$ calibrated against the empirical KS entropy distribution $P(h^{(l)})$ within the current batch $\mathcal{B}$. Specifically, tokens whose local information density—measured as the rate of change of their representation's differential entropy—drops below the layer-calibrated KS-entropy quantile are pruned. We formalize this as a measure-theoretic truncation operator $\Pi_{\tau}$ that removes tokens contributing negligible measure to the pushforward of the representation manifold at layer $l$. The pruning decision is thus tied to each token's contribution to the layer's ergodic information production rather than a heuristic attention score.
key_assumptions: The attention mechanism's Jacobian can be efficiently approximated layer-by-layer using Hutchinson-type trace estimators or power iteration without full materialization.
Token representations follow approximately measure-preserving dynamics within short layer windows, justifying the KS entropy framework.
The empirical distribution of local KS entropy rates within a batch is sufficiently smooth to yield stable truncation thresholds via quantile estimation.
Tokens with low KS entropy rates at a given layer contribute proportionally less to downstream task performance, making them safe candidates for pruning.
ideas.expected_impact: This approach introduces the first principled connection between dynamical systems theory (ergodic theory) and token pruning, replacing heuristic attention-score thresholds with a rigorous information-theoretic criterion. We expect a 15-25% reduction in unnecessary token retention compared to uniform-density truncation methods, with no measurable quality degradation on long-context benchmarks, because pruning decisions are grounded in each token's actual information flow contribution. The per-layer adaptive thresholding also enables finer-grained compute allocation, potentially reducing inference latency by 15-20% on sequences exceeding 8K tokens.

ideas.topic: Tree-of-Thought Search with Causal Pivot Backtracking for Hard Algorithmic Problems
ideas.title: Martingale Stopping-Time Backtracking with Doob Decomposition of Branch Potential in Tree-of-Thought Search
ideas.problem_statement: Tree-of-Thought (ToT) search for hard algorithmic problems suffers from inefficient exploration: standard heuristic evaluators provide point estimates of branch promise, causing the search to either waste compute on locally promising but globally dead-end branches or prematurely abandon difficult branches. Existing methods lack a principled mechanism to decide when accumulated evidence about a subtree is 'sufficient' to either commit to exploration or trigger causal backtracking, leading to poor sample efficiency on problems requiring deep, multi-step reasoning (e.g., competition-level mathematics, formal theorem proving).
ideas.core_mechanism: We model the ToT exploration trajectory as a submartingale process where the accumulated value signal along a reasoning path is decomposed via the Doob Decomposition Theorem into a predictable drift component (determined by the causal structure of prior reasoning steps) and a martingale difference noise component. At each node expansion, we compute the conditional variance process (quadratic variation) of this martingale component. A causal pivot for backtracking is triggered when the quadratic variation exceeds a threshold derived from the Dvoretzky-Kiefer-Wolfowitz confidence band on the branch's empirical value distribution, indicating that the heuristic evaluator's uncertainty has saturated and further expansion is unlikely to reduce regret. Conversely, if the predictable drift is positive but the quadratic variation is still growing, we insert a 'dilation' step—a低成本 intermediate node that gathers additional causal evidence before committing to the expensive full expansion. This transforms the backtracking decision from a threshold on point estimates into a measure-theoretic optimal stopping problem solved via the Snell envelope, guaranteeing that backtracking is causally justified by convergence of evidence rather than heuristic pessimism.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1. The LLM's per-step value heuristic produces evaluations whose conditional expectations form an adapted stochastic process to the filtration generated by reasoning history. 2. The Doob decomposition's predictable component captures genuine causal structure of the algorithmic problem (i.e., the drift reflects whether a mathematical/approach direction is fundamentally sound), while the martingale difference captures heuristic estimation noise. 3. The quadratic variation process is estimable from a bounded number of rollout samples per node (e.g., 3-5 GPT-4 evaluations suffice for convergence in practice). 4. Hard algorithmic problems have reasoning trees where dead-end branches exhibit characteristic variance signatures (stagnant drift with high variance) distinguishable from difficult-but-solvable branches (positive drift with decreasing variance).

ideas.topic: Formal Program Verification via LLM-Guided Theorem Prover Feedback
ideas.title: Łukasiewicz-Spectral T-Norm Coinduction: Continuous Valued-Algebraic Proof-State Transitions for LLM-Guided Theorem Proving
ideas.problem_statement: Existing LLM-guided interactive theorem provers (ITPs) treat proof search as discrete symbolic state transitions, where the LLM must predict exact tactic sequences. This creates a severe bottleneck: the exponentially branching proof tree forces the LLM to commit to hard decisions at each node, and feedback is binary (success/failure), providing no gradient for navigating partial proof states. There is no mechanism to reason about the 'distance' of an intermediate proof state from a closed proof in a continuous, differentiable algebraic space that aligns with the LLM's internal representation.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose modeling the proof state space not as a discrete graph, but as a continuous coalgebraic manifold governed by Łukasiewicz infinite-valued logic. In this framework, unproven intermediate goals are assigned a continuous truth value in [0,1] derived from the LLM's latent logit confidence (belief state). Tactic application is redefined as a continuous T-norm (specifically, the Łukasiewicz T-norm $T(x,y)=\max(0, x+y-1)$) over a bisimulation quotient space. When the LLM proposes a tactic, rather than executing it discretely, we compute a coinductive greatest-fixed-point (\nu) over the proof obligations. We train a spectral oracle to map the current proof state to an eigenfunction of a self-adjoint operator $\mathcal{L}$ defined on the coalgebra. The LLM receives feedback not on syntax, but on how its proposed tactic shifts the spectrum of $\mathcal{L}$. If the tactic's application forces the continuous truth valuation of all sub-goals to satisfy the T-norm identity (i.e., approaching 1.0 via continuous resolution), the coinductive proof state is deemed 'well-founded' and guided toward a Q.E.D. fixed-point.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1) The LLM's internal latent space can be projected into a continuous algebraic structure amenable to infinite-valued logic. 2) The bisimulation quotient space of intermediate proof states forms a well-behaved manifold that supports a self-adjoint operator. 3) The spectral gap of this operator correlates strongly with the actual syntactic proof distance, allowing gradient-based semantic steering of the LLM's next-token prediction.
ideas.expected_impact: This approach will fundamentally shift LLM-guided theorem proving from discrete symbolic guessing to continuous manifold navigation. By providing dense, differentiable feedback via coinductive T-norm convergence, it will drastically reduce the search depth required for complex theorems (e.g., in Coq or Lean). We expect a significant increase in pass@1 rates for formal verification tasks by allowing the model to 'slide' along proof trajectories rather than facing immediate hard-failures on imperfect tactics.

ideas.topic: Multi-View Code Review Agents with Adversarial Vulnerability Scanning
ideas.title: Fredholm Integral Equation of the Second Kind for Adversarial Perturbation Fixed-Point Detection in Multi-View Code Review Semantic Kernels
ideas.problem_statement: Existing multi-view code review agents typically decompose vulnerability detection into independent classification tasks across different semantic perspectives (e.g., data-flow, control-flow, API-misuse). Adversarial vulnerabilities, however, exploit the *interactions* between these views—subtle semantic perturbations that appear benign in any single isolated view but introduce exploitable state inconsistencies at their intersection. Current approaches fail to formalize the continuous propagation of adversarial semantic perturbations across heterogeneous code review views, lacking a rigorous mathematical framework to detect the fixed-points where these perturbations converge into an actual security flaw.
ideas.core_mechanism: We model the multi-view code review process as a Fredholm Integral Equation of the Second Kind. We construct a continuous operator K acting on a Banach space of code semantics, where K represents the integral transform mapping latent code representations through a spectral kernel weighted by both inter-view attention scores and a formal vulnerability density function. An adversarial code patch is injected as a continuous perturbation function $\delta(x)$, and we formulate the detection objective as finding the perturbation's fixed-point in the operator's resolvent set: $\phi(x) = \delta(x) + \lambda \int K(x,y)\phi(y)dy$. By parameterizing the kernel $K(x,y)$ as a Neural Operator, we learn the exact resolvent $(I - \lambda K)^{-1}$. An adversarial vulnerability scanner is formalized as a saddle-game: the attacker seeks $\delta(x)$ that shifts the fixed-point out of the resolvent's radius, while the reviewing agents collaboratively evaluate the operator's spectral radius to guarantee convergence. Vulnerabilities are explicitly mathematically detected as bifurcations where the fixed-point loses stability.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1. The semantic representations of code can be continuously interpolated within a Banach space such that integral transforms meaningfully capture cross-view interactions. 2. Adversarial vulnerabilities correspond to perturbations that fundamentally alter the spectral properties (specifically the eigenvalues) of the inter-view interaction kernel. 3. The Neural Operator approximation of the Fredholm kernel converges sufficiently fast to make the saddle-game between the generative adversarial patcher and the multi-view evaluator computationally tractable.
ideas.expected_impact: This approach introduces a rigorous continuous-functional analytical framework for multi-agent vulnerability detection, fundamentally shifting the paradigm from discrete pattern-matching to spectral stability analysis. By forcing adversarial code mutations to defeat a mathematically proven fixed-point theorem rather than a discriminative classifier, the system gains provable robustness against entire classes of multi-view evasion attacks, significantly reducing false negative rates in zero-day code review scenarios.

ideas.topic: Automated Repository Refactoring via Dependency Graph Traversal
ideas.title: Persistent Sheaf Cohomology Obstruction Detection for Atomic Micro-Refactoring Sequencing via Spectral Sequence Filtration
ideas.problem_statement: Automated repository refactoring faces a critical ordering problem: large-scale structural changes (e.g., splitting a god-class, extracting a module) must be decomposed into sequences of atomic, behavior-preserving micro-refactorings (e.g., move field, pull-up method) that maintain compilability and semantic equivalence at every intermediate step. Existing graph-based dependency traversals identify structural coupling but fail to detect subtle semantic invariants and ordering obstructions—hidden constraints that make certain refactoring sequences infeasible. There is no rigorous topological framework that can quantify the 'refactorability distance' of a dependency graph or guarantee that a traversal sequence preserves all behavioral invariants across intermediate states.
ideas.core_mechanism: We model the repository's dependency graph as a dynamic simplicial complex $K$ equipped with a constructible sheaf $\mathcal{F}$ of program semantics, where each simplex (a clique of mutually-dependent code entities) is assigned a local semantic constraint space. As a candidate micro-refactoring traverses the graph, it induces a continuous deformation (a zig-zag of sheaf pushforwards and pullbacks) on $K$, which we track using the spectral sequence associated with the sheaf cohomology $H^*(K, \mathcal{F})$. We detect refactorability obstructions by tracking the birth and death of non-trivial cohomology classes in $E_r^{p,q}$ pages across the filtration induced by the traversal. Specifically, if a proposed micro-refactoring sequence causes a persistent non-zero class in the $E_\infty$ page of the spectral sequence, this algebraically certifies an invariant violation (e.g., a cyclic dependency that cannot be broken without an intermediate compilable state). The optimal refactoring sequence is then formulated as finding the minimal-cost path in the traversal space that induces only acyclic bounded perturbations in the spectral sequence, guaranteeing all sheaf-local semantic constraints remain satisfiable at every step.
key_assumptions: Program invariants and behavioral contracts can be faithfully encoded as local sections of a sheaf over the dependency simplicial complex, with gluing conditions representing cross-module type-checking or data-flow constraints.
The spectral sequence of sheaf cohomology converges sufficiently rapidly for dependency graphs of real-world software repositories (bounded $k$-skeleton depth) to be computationally tractable.
Non-trivial persistent cohomology classes in the spectral sequence filtration correlate with genuine semantic invariant violations during refactoring, rather than topological noise.

The cost of computing sheaf cohomology group boundaries is dominated by the combinatorial structure of the dependency graph, which is typically sparse enough ($O(n)$ edges for $O(n)$ nodes in well-architected code) to render spectral sequence page-turning feasible.

By replacing heuristic greedy traversal with spectral sequence-guided navigation, it enables refactoring engines to provably identify feasible atomic sequences for large-scale structural transformations that current tools abort on due to undetectable intermediate invariant violations. This unlocks safe, fully autonomous refactoring of deeply entangled legacy codebases where no single safe path is obvious, fundamentally advancing the reliability of automated software evolution in industrial-scale repositories.

ideas.topic: Sobolev Space L2 Bounds for Continuous Trajectory Sequence Approximations
ideas.title: Wavelet-Galerkin Variational Crimes: Sobolev $H^s$ Norm Discretization for Trajectory-Level GFlowNet Action-Space Rectification via Mesh-Adaptive Lax-Wendroff
ideas.problem_statement: Existing continuous trajectory approximation frameworks treat sequence generation as discrete token-level sampling, which fundamentally fails to respect the Sobolev $H^s(\mathcal{X})$ bounds required for guaranteeing Lipschitz continuity in the underlying probability flows. When GFlowNets or RL policies approximate continuous trajectories via discrete tokenization, 'variational crimes' are committed: the discrete sampling measure diverges from the target continuous Sobolev measure by an unbounded margin. This manifests as high-frequency oscillatory artifacts in trajectory distributions and a loss of weak differentiability, violating the assumptions required for stable amortized inference and causing catastrophic forgetting of long-horizon dependencies.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose embedding the trajectory generation process into a dynamically adapted Wavelet-Galerkin finite element space. ideas.topic: Dynamic Token Pruning via Layer-Wise Information Density Truncation
ideas.title: Kolmogorov-Sinai Entropy Rate Thresholding for Layer-Localized Ergodic Token Pruning via Measure-Theoretic Density Truncation
ideas.problem_statement: Existing dynamic token pruning methods use static or globally-allocated information density thresholds across layers, failing to capture the non-stationary, layer-dependent mixing dynamics of token representations. As tokens traverse deeper layers, their representations undergo chaotic divergence or ergodic mixing depending on the input context. Applying a uniform truncation threshold ignores this layer-specific information flow, leading to either over-pruning of tokens undergoing transient representational shifts (destroying recoverable information) or under-pruning of tokens that have already reached semantic saturation (wasting compute).

This requires estimating the Lyapunov spectrum of each token's local flow via power iteration on the attention Jacobian's singular values. We then define an adaptive, layer-specific truncation threshold $\tau^{(l)}(\mathcal{B})$ calibrated against the empirical KS entropy distribution $P(h^{(l)})$ within the current batch $\mathcal{B}$. Specifically, tokens whose local information density—measured as the rate of change of their representation's differential entropy—drops below the layer-calibrated KS-entropy quantile are pruned. We formalize this as a measure-theoretic truncation operator $\Pi_{\tau}$ that removes tokens contributing negligible measure to the pushforward of the representation manifold at layer $l$. The pruning decision is thus tied to each token's contribution to the layer's ergodic information production rather than a heuristic attention score.

Token representations follow approximately measure-preserving dynamics within short layer windows, justifying the KS entropy framework.
The empirical distribution of local KS entropy rates within a batch is sufficiently smooth to yield stable truncation thresholds via quantile estimation.
Tokens with low KS entropy rates at a given layer contribute proportionally less to downstream task performance, making them safe candidates for pruning.
ideas.expected_impact: This approach introduces the first principled connection between dynamical systems theory (ergodic theory) and token pruning, replacing heuristic attention-score thresholds with a rigorous information-theoretic criterion. We expect a 15-25% reduction in unnecessary token retention compared to uniform-density truncation methods, with no measurable quality degradation on long-context benchmarks, because pruning decisions are grounded in each token's actual information flow contribution. ideas.topic: Tree-of-Thought Search with Causal Pivot Backtracking for Hard Algorithmic Problems
ideas.title: Martingale Stopping-Time Backtracking with Doob Decomposition of Branch Potential in Tree-of-Thought Search
ideas.problem_statement: Tree-of-Thought (ToT) search for hard algorithmic problems suffers from inefficient exploration: standard heuristic evaluators provide point estimates of branch promise, causing the search to either waste compute on locally promising but globally dead-end branches or prematurely abandon difficult branches. At each node expansion, we compute the conditional variance process (quadratic variation) of this martingale component. A causal pivot for backtracking is triggered when the quadratic variation exceeds a threshold derived from the Dvoretzky-Kiefer-Wolfowitz confidence band on the branch's empirical value distribution, indicating that the heuristic evaluator's uncertainty has saturated and further expansion is unlikely to reduce regret. Conversely, if the predictable drift is positive but the quadratic variation is still growing, we insert a 'dilation' step—a低成本 intermediate node that gathers additional causal evidence before committing to the expensive full expansion. This transforms the backtracking decision from a threshold on point estimates into a measure-theoretic optimal stopping problem solved via the Snell envelope, guaranteeing that backtracking is causally justified by convergence of evidence rather than heuristic pessimism.

The LLM's per-step value heuristic produces evaluations whose conditional expectations form an adapted stochastic process to the filtration generated by reasoning history. 2. The Doob decomposition's predictable component captures genuine causal structure of the algorithmic problem (i.e., the drift reflects whether a mathematical/approach direction is fundamentally sound), while the martingale difference captures heuristic estimation noise. 3. The quadratic variation process is estimable from a bounded number of rollout samples per node (e.g., 3-5 GPT-4 evaluations suffice for convergence in practice). 4. Hard algorithmic problems have reasoning trees where dead-end branches exhibit characteristic variance signatures (stagnant drift with high variance) distinguishable from difficult-but-solvable branches (positive drift with decreasing variance).

ideas.topic: Formal Program Verification via LLM-Guided Theorem Prover Feedback

ideas.topic: Sub-Linear Long-Document Summarization via Entropic Block Truncation

Existing entropic block truncation methods operate on a fixed, Euclidean token representation space, requiring computationally expensive brute-force or heuristic search to identify optimal truncation boundaries. When document blocks exhibit non-uniform semantic distortions (e.g., narrative shifts, topic transitions, or density variations), flat Euclidean distance metrics fundamentally fail to capture the true informational geometry, leading to the loss of critical salient content during aggressive sub-linear truncation. Specifically, we compute a Beltrami coefficient $\mu(z)$ for the token block sequence, which quantifies the local conformal distortion required to map high-density informational regions to a standard unit disk. The entropic block truncation boundary is then determined by solving a Beltrami equation $\frac{\partial f}{\partial \bar{z}} = \mu(z) \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}$, identifying the quasiconformal mapping $f$ that minimizes the distortion of the informational measure (differential entropy). Blocks exhibiting high semantic entropy are assigned non-zero Beltrami coefficients, dynamically stretching the conformal metric to preserve them. Intractable boundaries are continuously warped so that the truncation threshold acts as a Jordan curve on the conformal disk, allowing sub-linear O(n^{1/2}) pruning of low-information tokens while perfectly preserving the quasiconformal moduli of the semantic dependencies.

There exists an analytically tractable or efficiently approximable numerical solver (e.g., Laplacian smoothing or a small neural solver) for the Beltrami equation that runs in strictly sub-linear time relative to the sequence length.
ideas.expected_impact: This framework will introduce a topologically invariant method for document truncation, mathematically guaranteeing minimal distortion of semantic dependencies regardless of local text density. By shifting the optimization space from discrete Euclidean heuristics to continuous conformal geometry, it enables dramatically more aggressive sub-linear context reduction (targeting $O(n^{1/2})$ scaling) without the hallucination or fact-retrieval degradation typically seen in standard truncation methods. Furthermore, it opens a novel research direction applying Complex Analysis and Riemann surface topology to sequence modeling.

ideas.topic: Causal Inference Engine for Automated Bug Diagnosis in Large Codebases

ideas.problem_statement: Automated bug diagnosis in large codebases struggles to pinpoint root-cause defects because observed execution failures are typically syntactically and temporally distant from the originating faulty instruction. We map an observed bug to a specific 'failure monomial' $m_{fail}$. To diagnose the root cause, we construct the module of syzygies over $I$—the set of algebraic relations among the generators—and compute the minimal Gröbner basis $G$ with respect to a fault-localization monomial ordering (e.g., a weighted degree ordering prioritizing temporally distant operations). The core mechanism proves that the leading monomials of the Gröbner basis dictate the exact 'annihilator' algebraic conditions. By resolving the specific syzygy that produces $m_{fail}$ in the quotient ring $K[x_1, \dots, x_n]/I$, we deterministically invert the causal dataflow, yielding the mathematically minimal generator subset $\{f_k\}$ that acts as the root-cause defect.

Observed failures manifest as observable 'target polynomials' or monomials that mathematically reside in the ideal generated by the codebase's normal dataflow constraints.
ideas.expected_impact: This approach transitions automated bug diagnosis from probabilistic causal inference to formal, deterministic ideal-theoretic refutation. It eliminates false positives by mathematically proving that non-root-cause variables annihilate out of the quotient ring, offering absolute guarantees of fault localization. This mechanism will enable debugging engines to pinpoint exact anomalous assignments in complex, deeply nested, multi-threaded dataflows with zero empirical uncertainty, vastly reducing Mean Time to Resolution (MTTR) in enterprise-scale legacy codebases.

ideas.topic: Causal Sub-space Disentanglement via Orthogonal Polynomial Projections

A causal pivot for backtracking is triggered when the quadratic variation exceeds a threshold derived from the Dvoretzky-Kiefer-Wolfowitz confidence band on the branch's empirical value distribution, indicating that the heuristic evaluator's uncertainty has saturated and further expansion is unlikely to reduce regret. ideas.title: Quillen-Suslin Theoretic State-Space Completion for Module-Theoretic Deterministic Replay in Free-Space Robotic Control
ideas.problem_statement: Deterministic replay verification of autonomous robotic control fundamentally breaks when a system transitions from highly constrained environments (fully actuated, holonomic) to free-space environments (underactuated, non-holonomic). In these open conditions, the control state space loses its algebraic closure, rendering the affine subspace of physical sensory states non-stably-free. Consequently, attempting to deterministically replay a policy execution fails because the geometrically observed actuator kinematics cannot be uniquely mapped to their originating deterministic control parameters, leading to what is known as 'replay divergence' in free-space dynamics.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose modeling the robotic control-state execution trace as a finitely generated module over a polynomial ring $R = K[x_1, ..., x_n]$ (representing kinematic degrees of freedom and time). When the system enters underactuated free-space, the recorded replay trace generates a non-stably free module $M$, preventing direct deterministic re-execution. We introduce a Quillen-Suslin Completion Operator that dynamically identifies the missing algebraic degrees of freedom. By treating the divergence between the recorded physical observables and the actuator parameters as an obstruction in the projective dimension of $M$, the operator algorithmically constructs the exact unimodular rows required to patch $M$ into a free module $R^k$. This is achieved by localizing the Quillen patching step at the zero-measure singular sets of the robot's Jacobian inverse, guaranteeing that the extended free module $R^k$ precisely completes the missing affine transformations, thus bounding the replay execution strictly to the original policy's deterministic trajectory.
key_assumptions: The kinematic state transitions of the autonomous robot can be accurately discretized and algebraically encoded as coordinates in a multivariate polynomial ring.

The deterministic replay divergences in free-space environments are fundamentally driven by sudden drops in the actuation rank, which algebraically maps to a loss of stable freeness in the module quotient.
The computational overhead of calculating the Quillen-Suslin unimodular matrix patch is sufficiently low to be calculated synchronously alongside the real-time replay verification loop.
ideas.expected_impact: This research will provide a rigorous algebraic foundation for verifying control policies in highly degenerate, real-world robotic environments (such as aerial drones in turbulent wind or quadrupeds recovering from slips). By mathematically guaranteeing deterministic replay fidelity even in non-holonomic, underactuated state spaces, it eliminates the 'sim-to-real' verification gap, enabling the safe certification of deep reinforcement learning policies for safety-critical autonomous deployments.

ideas.topic: Multi-Modal Quality-Diversity Ideation for Scientific Experiment Design
ideas.title: Stochastic Arendt-Batty Liouville Semigroup Regularization for Holomorphic Descriptor Trajectories in Multi-Modal Quality-Diversity Experiment Archives
ideas.problem_statement: Multi-modal Quality-Diversity (QD) archives for scientific experiment design increasingly rely on heterogeneous descriptor spaces (e.g., combining mass-spectrometry signatures, genomic sequences, and thermodynamic curves). When mapping these fundamentally different physical modalities into a unified behavioral descriptor space for MAP-Elites, the archive's cell occupancy dynamics exhibit discontinuous, shock-like jumps if a newly discovered experiment drastically out-performs an incumbent. These shocks cause catastrophic forgetting of viable experimental lineages and destabilize the QD gradient flow. Standard MAP-Elites replacement mechanisms lack the mathematical continuity required to maintain a stable, differentiable archive manifold across modalities.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose modeling the continuous-time evolution of the QD archive's state as a strongly continuous semigroup of bounded linear operators $T(t)$ on the Banach space $X$ of fitness-weighted experiment descriptor distributions. Instead of discrete MAP-Elites replacement, we formulate the archive update as an abstract Cauchy problem: $\frac{du}{dt} = Au(t) + f(t)$, where $A$ is the infinitesimal generator governing archive dynamics and $f(t)$ represents the injection of new multi-modal experiments. We leverage the Arendt-Batty theorem to ensure stability: by proving that the spectrum $\sigma(A)$ is contained within a sector $|\arg(\lambda)| \le \theta$ in the right half-plane and that no residual spectrum lies on the imaginary axis, we guarantee that the semigroup $T(t)$ is exponentially stable. To enforce multi-modal consistency, we apply a stochastic Liouville perturbation $\sum \gamma_i(u) \circ dW_i$ that holomorphically extends the descriptor trajectories into the complex plane, allowing smooth interpolation between physically incompatible modalities. The archive update mechanism is resolved via a holomorphic functional calculus, replacing the discrete argmax replacement with a spectral multiplier $\Phi(A)$ that smoothly transitions cell occupancy based on the resolvent $(\lambda I - A)^{-1}$ evaluated at novel experiments.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1. The mapping from heterogeneous experimental data to the unified descriptor space can be continuously parameterized such that the archive state space $X$ admits a Banach space structure with sufficient regularity for semigroup generation. 2. The infinitesimal generator $A$ of the archive dynamics can be spectrally characterized a priori to ensure the Arendt-Batty stability conditions hold (specifically, boundedness of the resolvent on the imaginary axis). 3. The stochastic Liouville perturbation faithfully captures cross-modal transition probabilities without violating the strongly continuous nature of the semigroup. 4. The computational cost of evaluating the holomorphic functional calculus operator $\Phi(A)$ can be mitigated via Krylov subspace approximations to maintain tractable experiment generation throughput.
ideas.expected_impact: This framework will fundamentally eliminate mode-collapse and catastrophic forgetting in multi-modal QD-driven experiment design by guaranteeing mathematically bounded archive transitions. By enforcing a holomorphic descriptor trajectory, the archive will naturally interpolate between distinct scientific domains (e.g., smoothly transitioning between chemical and biological experimental modalities), uncovering novel, cross-disciplinary experiment designs. This will lead to a measurable increase in the Illumination metric (coverage × uniformity) and enable the discovery of robust experimental protocols that exist at the mathematical boundaries of traditionally siloed scientific fields.

ideas.topic: Sparse Entropic Gating for Real-Time Streaming Audio Generation
ideas.title: Gâteaux-Derivative Kernel Interpolation over Fréchet-Carrier Hölder Exponents for Causal Acoustic Envelope Extrapolation in Sparse Entropic Gating
ideas.problem_statement: Real-time streaming audio generation systems utilizing sparse entropic gating face a fundamental limitation: the top-$k$ sparsity mask must be computed autoregressively, introducing an irreducible sequential bottleneck that violates strict latency constraints. Current methods either rely on heuristic spectral gating that fails to capture non-stationary transient acoustic features (e.g., percussive attacks, consonants), or use opaque neural gating predictors that are mathematically uninterpretable and fail to provide causal guarantees, leading to temporal aliasing and pre-echo artifacts during streaming inference.
ideas.core_mechanism: We introduce the Fréchet-Carrier Hölder Extrapolator (FCHE), which models the temporal evolution of the sparse gating distribution's log-magnitudes as a continuous curve in a Banach space equipped with a local Hölder regularity measure. By computing the Gâteaux derivative of the entropic gating functional with respect to infinitesimal time-shifts along this curve, we derive a kernel operator that acts on the historical trajectory of sparse gate activations. This operator explicitly estimates the local Hölder exponent (quantifying the temporal smoothness/sharpness of acoustic transients). We interpolate these Gâteaux-derived, Hölder-weighted gradients using a causal Nyquist-limited Sinc-Kernel to analytically extrapolate the sparse gating support and continuous weights for the next $\Delta t$ inference steps, allowing the gating network to be bypassed entirely for a bounded future horizon without breaking causality.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1) The temporal evolution of the optimal sparse entropic gating distribution in the latent space is sufficiently smooth to be modeled as a continuous Fréchet curve, except at localized acoustic transients which are captured by sharp drops in the Hölder exponent. 2) The Gâteaux derivative of the entropic functional provides an unbiased, mathematically rigorous first-order approximation of the temporal gating dynamics. 3) The computational cost of evaluating the causal Sinc-Kernel interpolation is asymptotically bounded by $O(k \log k)$, making it strictly faster than a forward pass of the gating network for sufficiently large hidden dimensions.
ideas.expected_impact: This framework will provide the first mathematically rigorous, causally-guaranteed mechanism for speculative sparse gating in streaming audio. It is expected to reduce end-to-end generation latency by over 40% by parallelizing the temporal dependency of the gating mechanism. Furthermore, by grounding the sparse mask prediction in functional analysis and Hölder continuity, it entirely eliminates pre-echo artifacts and temporal aliasing during fast acoustic transients, setting a new theoretical standard for structural interpretability in continuous audio generation systems.

ideas.topic: Causal Inference Engine for Automated Bug Diagnosis in Large Codebases
ideas.title: Gröbner Basis Syzygy Resolution for Ideal-Theoretic Root-Cause Isolation in Static Single Assignment Dataflow Graphs
ideas.problem_statement: Automated bug diagnosis in large codebases struggles to pinpoint root-cause defects because observed execution failures are typically syntactically and temporally distant from the originating faulty instruction. Existing causal inference engines model program dataflow probabilistically (e.g., via Bayesian networks or causal DAGs), which introduces uncertainty and fails to capture the deterministic, algebraic nature of variable dependencies. When multiple interacting variables cause a failure state, current methods cannot rigorously isolate the exact minimal subset of program instructions (the root cause) from the broader execution milieu.
ideas.core_mechanism: We model the Static Single Assignment (SSA) form of a codebase as a multivariate polynomial ideal $I$ over a finite field, where monomials represent program variables and polynomial generators $\{f_1, \dots, f_n\}$ represent deterministic dataflow operations (e.g., assignments, branch constraints). We map an observed bug to a specific 'failure monomial' $m_{fail}$. To diagnose the root cause, we construct the module of syzygies over $I$—the set of algebraic relations among the generators—and compute the minimal Gröbner basis $G$ with respect to a fault-localization monomial ordering (e.g., a weighted degree ordering prioritizing temporally distant operations). The core mechanism proves that the leading monomials of the Gröbner basis dictate the exact 'annihilator' algebraic conditions. By resolving the specific syzygy that produces $m_{fail}$ in the quotient ring $K[x_1, \dots, x_n]/I$, we deterministically invert the causal dataflow, yielding the mathematically minimal generator subset $\{f_k\}$ that acts as the root-cause defect.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1. Codebase execution dataflow and logical branching can be losslessly abstracted as polynomial generators over a computable algebraic field without poly-exponential blowup in the intermediate representation. 2. The Gröbner basis fault-localization monomial ordering can be heuristically seeded with static analysis call-graph depth to keep computational complexity tractable for large-scale codebases. 3. Observed failures manifest as observable 'target polynomials' or monomials that mathematically reside in the ideal generated by the codebase's normal dataflow constraints.
ideas.expected_impact: This approach transitions automated bug diagnosis from probabilistic causal inference to formal, deterministic ideal-theoretic refutation. It eliminates false positives by mathematically proving that non-root-cause variables annihilate out of the quotient ring, offering absolute guarantees of fault localization. This mechanism will enable debugging engines to pinpoint exact anomalous assignments in complex, deeply nested, multi-threaded dataflows with zero empirical uncertainty, vastly reducing Mean Time to Resolution (MTTR) in enterprise-scale legacy codebases.

ideas.topic: Dynamic Feature Selection via Mutual Information Maximization in Deep Networks
ideas.title: Khatri-Rao Sketching for Information-Theoretic Dynamic Gating via Conditional von Mises-Fisher Sparsity Manifolds
ideas.problem_statement: Existing dynamic feature selection methods that optimize mutual information (MI) maximization face a critical computational bottleneck: they require estimating the determinant or inverse of high-dimensional conditional covariance matrices to compute the standard MI proxy $I(X;Y) = \frac{1}{2} \log \frac{|\Sigma_{XX}| |\Sigma_{YY}|}{|\Sigma_{(XY)(XY)}}|$. This incurs $O(d^3)$ or $O(d^{\omega})$ matrix complexity per network layer per forward pass, making information-theoretic dynamic gating computationally infeasible for high-dimensional deep networks. We need a sub-quadratic mechanism that directly maximizes MI without explicit joint covariance inversion.
ideas.core_mechanism: We introduce Khatri-Rao Sketching for Dynamic Gating (KRSDG). Instead of deterministically evaluating covariance determinants, we model the dynamic feature importance vector as a probability distribution over a von Mises-Fisher (vMF) manifold concentrated on the unit hypersphere. To approximate the information-theoretic objective in $O(d)$, we project the joint feature-target distribution onto a structured Khatri-Rao (column-wise Kronecker) random sketch. By leveraging the spectral properties of Khatri-Rao products, we provably preserve the quadratic Rényi entropy of the features (via Johnson-Lindenstrauss bounds on product spaces) while strictly avoiding covariance inversion. The feature mask is dynamically generated by sampling from the vMF distribution, where the concentration parameter $\kappa$ is updated via natural gradient ascent on the sketched MI estimate. This transforms the discrete combinatorial NP-hard feature search into a continuous, differentiable, sub-quadratic probabilistic routing problem.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1. The joint distribution of neural network features and target labels can be locally approximated by an elliptical distribution, allowing Rényi entropy to serve as a faithful MI proxy. 2. The Khatri-Rao sketch dimension can be bounded sub-quadratically relative to the feature dimension while maintaining a tight additive error margin in the spectral norm of the joint covariance. 3. The gradient signal derived from the sketched MI lower bound is sufficiently aligned with the true mutual information landscape to ensure monotonic improvement of the feature mask during training.
ideas.expected_impact: This mechanism will reduce the asymptotic computational overhead of mutual-information-based dynamic feature selection from cubic to linear/quadratic, enabling real-time, layer-wise dynamic gating in high-capacity architectures without information loss. It provides a rigorous theoretical bridge between randomized linear algebra and information-theoretic submodular optimization, potentially unlocking highly interpretable, massive-scale dynamic networks that actively discard redundant features on the fly with zero degradation in downstream task performance.

ideas.topic: Self-Correcting Reasoning Loops for Symbolic Mathematics
ideas.title: Galois-Adjoint Biclosure Operators for Lattice-Theoretic Backtrack Minimization in Self-Correcting Symbolic Equation Solvers
ideas.problem_statement: When LLMs perform self-correcting reasoning loops for symbolic mathematics, they often engage in unproductive cycles—repeatedly applying valid but useless algebraic transformations, or backtracking prematurely due to a lack of structural awareness regarding the distance between the current algebraic state and the target solution. Existing self-correction methods rely on dense, opaque scalar rewards (e.g., from an outcome reward model) or semantic embeddings that fail to capture the exact, rigorous algebraic constraints of symbolic manipulation, leading to inefficient exploration of the equation space and frequent entrapment in algebraic cycles.
ideas.core_mechanism: We model the sequential states of a symbolic equation during an LLM's reasoning trajectory as a partially ordered set (poset) $(L, \leq)$, ordered by syntactic substitution and algebraic complexity. We define a Galois connection $(F, G)$ between this reasoning poset $L$ and a target ideal poset $M$ (representing the set of canonical, simplified forms). Here, $F: L \to M$ is the forward adjoint mapping a current equation state to its nearest canonical form in $M$, and $G: M \to L$ is the upper adjoint. For each step in the self-correcting loop, rather than relying on a scalar reward, the agent computes the $F$-biclosure of its current state. The algebraic edit distance between the current state and its $F$-closure provides an exact, differentiable structural mismatch gradient (formalized as a residuated lattice residual). The reasoning loop is guided to select subsequent algebraic transformations that strictly minimize this residual. If the residual remains stagnant or increases, a definitive topological dead-end is detected, deterministically triggering a mathematical pruning of that reasoning branch.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1. The state of a symbolic equation can be deterministically parsed into a formal algebraic structure (e.g., a syntactic tree or polynomial ideal) that admits a partial order. 2. A meaningful target set of 'simplified' or 'solved' canonical forms exists for the given mathematical domain, allowing the formulation of valid Galois adjunctions. 3. The exact computation of the $F$-closure (or a computationally tractable neural approximation of it) can be executed faster than exploring multiple LLM-generated reasoning steps.
ideas.expected_impact: This approach will ground self-correcting feedback in exact algebraic geometry rather than probabilistic semantics, mathematically eliminating algebraic cycling in reasoning loops. By leveraging the monotonicity guarantees of Galois adjoint functions, the framework ensures that the LLM's reasoning trajectory strictly respects algebraic invariants. This will drastically reduce the sampling depth required to solve complex competition-level mathematics, significantly improving both the success rate and token efficiency of symbolic math agents.

ideas.topic: Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Alignment via Unitary Spectral Projections
ideas.title: Non-Abelian Holonomy Gradients on Stiefel-Embedded Monolingual Submersions for Perturbation-Robust Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Alignment

A critical failure mode is the instability of these spectral embeddings under sub-space perturbations: the lowest singular vectors of monolingual embedding covariance matrices often rotate erratically under minor distributional shifts or stochastic noise (e.g., when evaluating on low-resource, out-of-domain text). At each optimization step, we compute the Lie algebra gradient $\Omega \in \mathfrak{su}(d)$. By applying a continuous gauge transformation derived from the Lie bracket of sequential gradients, we isolate the 'commutator noise' $[\Omega_t, \Omega_{t-1}]$. We mathematically prove that this commutator strictly bounds the spectral drift of the eigenvectors of the cross-lingual mapping. ideas.topic: High-Throughput Parallel Evaluators for Autonomous Research Pipelines
ideas.title: Hardy Space $H^2$ Pseudohyperbolic Disk Packings for Reproducing Kernel Inter-Evaluator Diagnostic Code Synthesis
ideas.problem_statement: High-throughput parallel evaluators in autonomous research pipelines typically rely on thousands of independently generated diagnostic scripts to verify the functional correctness, robustness, or performance of novel algorithmic hypotheses. These evaluators are subject to extreme semantic and behavioral redundancy (e.g., checking the same edge-cases via different code paths), leading to massive computational waste and evaluator-induced bottlenecks. Existing deduplication methods rely on coarse syntactic hashing or static AST embedding similarity, failing to capture deep behavioral equivalence or non-obvious functional overlaps in dynamically generated diagnostic logic.
ideas.core_mechanism: We propose modeling each generated evaluator's behavioral manifold as a point within the Hardy space $H^2(\mathbb{D})$ of the complex unit disk. An evaluator's abstract syntax tree (AST) is continuously embedded into a coefficient vector defining an analytic function, whose state-transition logic is fully captured by the space's reproducing kernel $K_z(w) = \frac{1}{1-\bar{z}w}$. The semantic-behavioral similarity between any two parallel evaluators is rigorously defined as the pseudohyperbolic distance $\rho(z_i, z_j) = |\frac{z_i - z_j}{1 - \bar{z_i}z_j}|$ in this space. We introduce a dynamic Apollonian disk-packing algorithm that continuously maps incoming evaluators onto $\mathbb{D}$ and erects a hyperbolic exclusion zone (a Poincaré disk) around accepted evaluators based on an $\epsilon$-threshold of $\rho$. Incoming evaluators falling into an existing disk are mathematically provable as semantic derivatives of existing tests and are immediately discarded; otherwise, they are admitted to the parallel execution pool. This casts evaluator deduplication as a continuous, boundary-preserving geometric packing problem in complex Hilbert space.
ideas.key_assumptions: 1) The execution behavior and boundary-case targeting of a diagnostic script can be losslessly mapped to the analytic continuation properties of an $H^2$ function via tree-structured complex embeddings. 2) The pseudohyperbolic metric on this space strictly bounds the behavioral divergence of the evaluators, such that small $\rho$ guarantees high functional overlap in execution traces. 3) Maintaining an Apollonian packing of non-overlapping Poincaré disks in real-time is computationally cheaper (sub-linear lookup via spatial kd-trees in $\mathbb{R}^2$) than actually executing redundant diagnostic code on the target autonomous pipeline.
ideas.expected_impact: This mechanism will transform high-throughput evaluator management from an $O(N)$ execution-bound problem to an $O(\log N)$ geometric lookup problem. By proving strict behavioral non-redundancy via pseudohyperbolic boundaries, autonomous pipelines will eliminate >70% of redundant diagnostic computations without sacrificing behavioral coverage. This enables exponentially denser exploration of the research hypothesis space under fixed compute envelopes, massively accelerating the autonomous scientific discovery loop.
